c0598aa63dbbe6e2: OSLO, Nov 27 — The head of the Norwegian Football Federation Lise Klaveness, a fierce critic of Fifa president Gianni Infantino, acknowledged Thursday it would be "difficult" to topple him but the possibility was "still in play".

Klaveness has been critical of Infantino since 2022 when the World Cup was held in Qatar, and called for his resignation in August after several controversies during this year's World Cup hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico.
"It will be difficult" to dethrone Infantino, Klaveness, a lawyer and former national squad player, told foreign media in Oslo yesterday.

While European football confederation Uefa has rallied around French football chief Philippe Diallo's candidacy to take over the Fifa presidency in a March election, Infantino, who is running for re-election, still enjoys the support of the African, South American and Asian confederations, and is seen as the favourite.
"You cannot really know what's going to happen in such a volatile political world," Klaveness, 45, argued.
"So it might end up with a different candidate than Infantino for very many reasons."
"But as it seems now, he has a lot of support."

While the African (CAF) and South American (Conmebol) football confederations have reaffirmed their backing for Infantino, Klaveness pointed out that it is not they who vote, but the national federations, and that each vote is secret.
"That's why it's still in play," she said.
She also said she hoped that Diallo and the third candidate, Kozo Tashima, honorary president of the Japanese federation, would manage to join forces against Infantino.

At the head of Fifa since 2016, Infantino has been involved in several recent controversies, including accusations of running a one-man show, awarding a Fifa "peace prize" to Donald Trump, lifting the suspension of USA forward Folarin Balogun during the 2026 World Cup, and floating plans — later abandoned — to sell stakes in World Cup commercial rights. — AFP
9b9adbde09128670: MADRID: No coach in the history of Spanish football has won more LaLiga matches than Atletico Madrid's Diego Simeone.
The Argentine claimed his 345th league victory last weekend to keep the Rojiblancos in the race to chase down Spain's traditional giants, Barcelona and Real Madrid.
Third-placed Atletico visit Elche on Saturday with Simeone looking to keep adding to his record and deliver a third LaLiga title, adding to his conquests in 2014 and 2021.
Atletico trail leaders Barcelona by five points before they face the Catalans on Dec 2, in a match brought forward because of the teams' participation in the Spanish Super Cup in January.
Barcelona visit Deportivo La Coruna on Sunday, while Real Madrid, second and two points ahead of Atletico, host Alaves on Saturday.
Simeone surpassed the late Luis Aragones, on 344 league victories, to stand alone at the top of the all-time list.
"I would like to share this number with all the people behind these 345 victories," said Simeone, speaking of his family, current and former staff and players.
"I don't usually get excited about many things, but getting to this point has taken incredible work."
Prying two league titles away from giants Real Madrid and Barcelona was an impressive achievement, and Atletico have shown this season they have the tools to do it again.
Until their defeat by Barcelona before the international break, Atletico won their seven prior league matches, including a derby victory over Real Madrid.
Their strong start has come without star player Julian Alvarez being at his best, which shows they can still find a higher gear.
The Argentine forward wanted to leave in the summer and tried to force through a move to Barcelona, but Atletico staunchly resisted.
Alvarez started the season at a low ebb and struggling for fitness, and has scored just three goals across all competitions to date.
However the 2022 World Cup winner has started to show some of his quality in recent appearances and tensions with the supporters have eased.
'Same ambition, hunger'
Alvarez set up Atletico's first two goals against Getafe in their win last weekend and scored with a free-kick against Viking in the Champions League on Wednesday.
"He's truly an incredible player, fantastic. I like him as a person, I'll support him as a footballer, I understand him as a player," said Simeone on Wednesday.

"Even though he hasn't scored in previous matches, there isn't an attacking move that doesn't go through him, and he always contributes important things. To get where we want to be, we need the best Julian Alvarez."
Simeone's other two title successes were powered by goals from South American strikers, with Brazilian Diego Costa key in 2014, and Uruguay's Luis Suarez vital in 2021.
A resurgent Alvarez would help Atletico's bid for a third crown under Simeone.
Atletico midfielder Koke said Simeone has not changed since arriving at the club in 2011, even though his football has become more progressive in recent years.
"I think practically nothing has changed, because he still has the same drive, the same ambition, the same hunger, and I think that will never change," said the veteran midfielder.

"Obviously, he's a bit older but everything else remains the same... he's still very demanding in training, he doesn't let us relax for a second, and that's what makes the difference and allows us to compete against the best."
b548002f670d35c0: HANOI, Nov 27 — On the dusty fringes of the Vietnamese capital, Kieu Minh Phuong walks along rows of rusted wire cages, peering into crowded pens filled with animals awaiting an uncertain fate as either household companions or restaurant ingredients.

The 40-year-old ceramics trader is searching for Dom, a nine-year-old calico cat he nurtured from infancy before she disappeared overnight. His search led him to this open-air depot after he read accounts across online neighbourhood forums, where distraught owners frequently recount tracking their stolen companions to roadside animal markets, according to a Reuters report.
“There is a high chance that Dom was stolen,” Phuong said, convinced of foul play after several neighbours reported pets missing in the very same nocturnal sweep.

Phuong’s grief reflects an escalating cultural friction across Vietnam, where a burgeoning culture of companion animal care is colliding with a deeply entrenched, legally sanctioned meat trade. While pet snatching constitutes larceny under domestic property law, trading, butchering, and serving cat and dog meat remains entirely permissible. This regulatory contradiction has fostered organised theft syndicates, with roving crews combing residential alleys on motorbikes after midnight, utilizing adhesive tape and improvised stun devices to snatch family pets before owners can react.

State media reports highlight the industrial scale of the racket. Recent operations in Ho Chi Minh City dismantled an operation accused of trapping 2,700 felines for provincial abattoirs, while police in Hanoi arrested five men caught with over 300 animals. The illicit trade thrives on compelling financial incentives: live dogs fetch roughly US$1.50 per kilogram, while live cats command nearly US$5 per kilogram, lucrative windfalls in an economy where entry-level wages hover below a dollar an hour.
For older generations and blue-collar workers, the cuisine remains tied to custom and folklore, with traditional beliefs suggesting the meat enhances vitality or dispels misfortune.

“Cat meat is a favourite ⁠dish for working-class people,” explained Tran Thanh, a 50-year-old truck driver from Haiphong. “Mostly people of my age or older keep the habit,” he said, noting that an informal hot-pot feast shared among coworkers provides unique culinary appeal. “We choose cat meat instead of pork or chicken because it goes well with rice wine.”

Animal protection groups such as Four Paws International estimated in 2020 that over six million dogs and cats enter Vietnam’s slaughterhouses each year. Yet commercial appetite is experiencing a steady generational decline, dampened by municipal rabies advisories and shifting domestic values among younger city dwellers.

“Young people nowadays keep dogs indoors and treat them like members of the family,” observed Tran Huu Thanh, who shuttered his long-running dog-meat diner in 2019 following an unsustainable collapse in patronage.

Municipal authorities in Hanoi have also stepped in with vocational transition grants, successfully assisting 28 trade-related businesses to pivot into mainstream commercial sectors over the past year.

Although livestock regulations require traders to document animal origins, enforcement at wet markets remains virtually non-existent, leaving overloaded welfare shelters to stem the bleeding. At the SNNC Rescue Centre, volunteers regularly pool personal contributions to outbid abattoir middlemen and intercept transport cages, though severe resource constraints and an existing sanctuary population of 1,400 animals have forced the shelter to curtail new rescue missions.

Four weeks after Dom disappeared, Phuong continues to comb clandestine digital marketplaces where animal traffickers post photos of snatched pets, seeking extortionate payouts from owners desperate for their return.
“Dom was my emotional support,” he said quietly. “The house is empty without her.”
80218933677b7449: TAWAU, Nov 26 — An 18-year-old student who pleaded guilty to uploading a teenage girl’s photograph on social media with threatening captions was discharged with a warning by the Magistrate’s Court here today after personally apologising to the victim.
Magistrate Don Stiwin Malanjum made the ruling under Section 91(1)(a) of the Child Act 2001 (Amendment 2016) after taking into account recommendations from the Social Welfare Department (JKM).
The court also took into account that the eldest of five siblings regretted his actions, promised not to reoffend and wanted to focus on his studies.
The court also ordered the return of RM500 bail.

According to the charge, the accused, who was 17 at the time of the offence, allegedly uploaded the photograph of the 13-year-old victim at a restaurant here at noon on April 17 under Section 507E of the Penal Code, which provides for a maximum prison term of 20 years and whipping upon conviction.

Based on the facts of the case, the victim’s mother received a message via WhatsApp from a friend who sent a screenshot showing her daughter’s photograph on Instagram along with several captions containing allegations of bullying and threats.

Investigations found that the accused uploaded the victim’s photograph after reading a WhatsApp group conversation claiming that a friend’s cousin had been bullied by the victim and another individual.
The boy admitted he got carried away by emotion before obtaining the victim’s photograph and uploading it to an Instagram Story through his own account with threatening captions.
Prosecuting Officer ASP Jeffery Kadison conducted the prosecution, while the accused was unrepresented. — Bernama
d50a8955b92f69ef: IPOH, Nov 27 — Introducing rural remote working hub programmes to encourage youths to remain or return to their hometowns needs comprehensive study and planning, Perak Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Saarani Mohamad said today.

He was replying to Simpang Pulai assemblyman Wong Chai Yi had asked whether or not the state government plans to introduce rental incentives, rural community housing or rural remote working hubs to encourage young people to remain in or return to their hometowns.

Speaking in the Perak State Legislative Assembly, Saarani said the proposal, which could also include rental incentives and a rural community housing scheme, needed to be studied further as it involved comprehensive planning of the local economic sector.
He said the local economic landscape was the main catalyst in encouraging young people to remain in their respective villages.

“In this regard, a balanced economic landscape in the areas surrounding the New Villages should be able to provide employment opportunities and competitive wages to ensure that young people choose to remain in the New Villages.
“Only then they would not migrate to major cities such as Singapore and the Klang Valley, which offer greater income opportunities,” he said.
61468adbbd101bf0: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 27 — Throughout his more than three decades in the legal profession, former Attorney General Tan Sri Abdul Gani Patail played a pivotal role in several high-profile cases that captured public attention, establishing himself as a prominent figure in Malaysia’s legal landscape.

Among the high-profile prosecutions Abdul Gani handled were the corruption case involving former Sabah Chief Minister Datuk Joseph Pairin Kitingan in 1993 and the case involving the Al-Ma’unah militant group in 2000.

The Lahad Datu-born legal figure also led the prosecution team in the case involving 30 individuals, including Philippine nationals, charged with waging war against the Yang di-Pertuan Agong and involvement in various terrorism-related activities in Lahad Datu, Sabah, in 2013.
Abdul Gani, who served as Attorney General for 13 years from 2002 to 2015, died at a private hospital here tonight due to an infection.
Attorney General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar, who confirmed the news of his death, also extended his condolences to Abdul Gani’s family.
“The entire Attorney General’s Chambers (AGC) extends its condolences to his family and prays that Allah showers His blessings upon his soul,” Mohd Dusuki said when contacted.
Abdul Gani was also part of the prosecution team in the 2006 murder case involving Mongolian national Altantuya Shaariibuu.

He also led the prosecution of former Transport Minister Tun Dr Ling Liong Sik, who was charged in 2010 with cheating the Malaysian government in connection with the Port Klang Free Zone (PKFZ) scandal involving the RM1.08 billion purchase of land in Pulau Indah.
Abdul Gani also handled the prosecution of former Selangor Menteri Besar Dr Mohamad Khir Toyo on corruption charges relating to a property purchase.

He also led the prosecution team in the criminal breach of trust case involving RM76.4 million against former Perwaja Rolling Mill and Development Sdn Bhd managing director Tan Sri Eric Chia Eng Hock and handled the corruption case involving former Land and Cooperative Development Minister Tan Sri Kasitah Gaddam.

Born on Oct 6, 1955, Abdul Gani began his career in the Judicial and Legal Service in 1980 before serving as a deputy public prosecutor at the Attorney General’s Chambers in Tawau, Sabah, becoming the first Sabahan to hold the position following the establishment of the federal Attorney General’s office in the state.

Throughout his career, he held several key positions, including Sabah head of prosecution in 1991, head of the AGC’s Prosecution Division from Jan 16 to Oct 14, 1994, and head and adviser of its International Affairs Division from April 1, 1995, to May 31, 1997.
He subsequently served as Commissioner of Law Revision from 1997 to 2000 before returning as head of the Prosecution Division on Feb 1, 2000.

On Nov 19, 2001, Abdul Gani was appointed Malaysia’s eighth Attorney General and officially assumed office on Jan 1, 2002, making history as the first locally trained law graduate to be appointed to the position and the first Sabahan to hold one of the highest posts in the federal civil service.

The appointment marked a major milestone in his legal career, which saw him helm the country’s foremost legal institution for more than 13 years before his tenure as Attorney General was terminated on health grounds, effective July 27, 2015.
However, he continued serving as an officer in the Judicial and Legal Service until reaching the mandatory retirement age on Oct 6, 2015.

Abdul Gani also contributed his legal expertise and experience through various other roles, including as a member of the Pardons Board for the Federal Territories of Kuala Lumpur, Labuan and Putrajaya.

He was also appointed an adjunct professor at the Faculty of Law of Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM) for two years from Oct 1, 2011, and served as chairman of the National Legal Aid Foundation (YBGK).
On Dec 23, 2016, he was admitted as an advocate and solicitor of the High Court of Malaya. — Bernama
e8f2e728e5a94b68: PETALING JAYA: Former Selangor menteri besar Khir Toyo has been appointed pro tem Tanjong Karang Wawasan chief.
In a statement, he described the appointment as a "great responsibility" and said he was focused on strengthening Wawasan’s presence in Tanjong Karang and serving residents in the area.
Khir joined Wawasan, led by opposition leader Hamzah Zainudin, last month.
He told FMT that he quit Bersatu just over a year after joining the party because it had lost its purpose and was plagued by internal infighting.
Khir, who was Selangor menteri besar from 2000 to 2008, served as Sungai Panjang assemblyman for three terms.
c73cbc2b483b2181: PETALING JAYA: Bekas menteri besar Selangor Khir Toyo mengesahkan pelantikannya sebagai ketua penaja Wawasan Tanjong Karang.
Beliau menerima watikah pelantikan rasmi daripada Presiden Wawasan Hamzah Zainudin.
Menurut Khir, jawatan itu disifatkan bukan sebagai satu kemegahan, sebaliknya satu amanah besar yang perlu dipikul bagi berkhidmat kepada masyarakat.
"Amanah ini untuk berkhidmat kepada rakyat, memperkukuhkan Parti Wawasan Negara di Tanjong Karang, dan membina masa depan yang lebih baik untuk semua," katanya.
Khir sebelum ini dilaporkan meninggalkan Bersatu untuk menyertai Wawasan, lebih setahun selepas beliau menyertai parti pimpinan bekas perdana menteri, Muhyiddin Yassin itu.

Beliau yang juga bekas Adun Sungai Panjang selama tiga penggal dilaporkan menyertai parti itu selepas PRN Negeri Sembilan pada 1 Ogos lalu, dengan alasan Bersatu dilihat sudah kehilangan hala tuju serta sering berdepan perbalahan dalaman.

Khir berkhidmat sebagai menteri besar Selangor dari 2000 hingga 2008 dan pernah cuba kembali aktif dalam pilihan raya pada PRU 2022 bagi kerusi Parlimen Sungai Besar, namun Barisan Nasional ketika itu memilih Jamal Yunos sebagai calon.
6b6a405e34e2ff13: PUTRAJAYA: Mahkamah Rayuan menolak rayuan Lembaga Hasil Dalam Negeri (LHDN) untuk menghidupkan semula sebuah syarikat yang telah dibubarkan bagi menuntut taksiran cukai pendapatan tambahan yang didakwa masih terhutang oleh syarikat itu.

Dalam penghakiman sebulat suara yang disampaikan Hakim Wong Kian Kheong, mahkamah memutuskan bahawa LHDN gagal membuktikan bahawa ia merupakan pihak berkepentingan yang berhak memohon pengembalian semula Mahabuilders Sdn Bhd mengikut Seksyen 535(1) Akta Syarikat 2016.
Hakim Alwi Abdul Wahab dan Aliza Sulaiman turut menganggotai panel berkenaan.

Wong berkata pemohon yang ingin menghidupkan semula syarikat yang telah dibubarkan perlu membuktikan kepentingan hak milik atau kewangan dalam pengembalian semula syarikat itu serta menunjukkan haknya berdasarkan imbangan kebarangkalian.

Beliau berkata LHDN gagal membuktikan bahawa Mahabuilders melakukan penipuan, keingkaran sengaja atau kecuaian dalam urusan percukaiannya, seperti yang dikehendaki di bawah Seksyen 91(3) Akta Cukai Pendapatan 1967 bagi membolehkan taksiran tambahan dikeluarkan.

Beliau turut menjelaskan bahawa had masa dua tahun di bawah Seksyen 535(1) terpakai kepada kuasa mahkamah untuk mengisytiharkan pembubaran sesebuah syarikat sebagai tidak sah, dan bukannya sekadar menetapkan permohonan perlu difailkan dalam tempoh tersebut.

Bagaimanapun, Wong berkata mahkamah tidak akan menggunakan budi bicaranya di bawah Seksyen 582 Akta Syarikat untuk melanjutkan tempoh yang ditetapkan undang-undang atau memperbetulkan ketidakpatuhan terhadap peruntukan berkenaan.
Beliau berkata pengembalian semula syarikat itu akan menyebabkan ketidakadilan yang besar memandangkan proses penggulungannya telah selesai dan asetnya telah diagihkan.

Wong turut menyatakan bahawa bekas pengarah syarikat itu dan individu lain yang termasuk dalam takrifan pengarah di bawah undang-undang berpotensi dipertanggungjawabkan secara bersama dan berasingan bagi cukai tambahan berkenaan mengikut Seksyen 75A Akta Cukai Pendapatan.
Beliau berkata tempoh masa yang telah berlalu juga akan menyukarkan bekas pengarah mendapatkan rekod dan bukti yang diperlukan untuk mencabar taksiran cukai tambahan tersebut.
Oleh itu, mahkamah mendapati tiada alasan untuk campur tangan dalam keputusan Mahkamah Tinggi yang menolak permohonan LHDN untuk membatalkan pembubaran syarikat itu.
Rayuan tersebut ditolak tanpa sebarang perintah berhubung kos.
bd22254991eaf109: MUNICH: Bayern Munich head to Hamburg on Saturday in the middle of a crisis which threatens not only to derail the club's sporting ambitions, but their identity itself.
Bayern, who are in the midst of an injury crisis which has decimated their forward line including Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane, sit two points behind Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga table.
But Bayern's treatment of midfielder Jamal Musiala by their hierarchy has led to a growing rift between the club and the playing group.

Shortly after Bayern lost 2-1 to Lille on Wednesday, ending their run as the final unbeaten team in Europe's top-five leagues this season, vice-captain Joshua Kimmich suggested the club had fallen out of step with their values.
"It's completely unacceptable and is not Bayern-like," Kimmich said on Wednesday, adding that Musiala's treatment was inconsistent with the club's "sense of togetherness".
'Mia san mia'
This week, Bayern's hierarchy suggested Musiala take a pay cut as the 23-year-old battles his way back from a neurological condition which causes absence seizures.

While the condemnation from media, player unions and former players was swift, Kimmich - who was wearing the captain's armband with Manuel Neuer out injured - was the first member of Bayern's current squad to speak out.

Despite their status as one of football's perennial heavyweights, Bayern have always sought to emphasise their Bavarian roots and member-ownership in contrast to the American and Gulf-owned behemoths that loom over the European landscape.
But their cold-hearted treatment of Musiala, a fan-favourite and popular inside the dressing room, threatens their carefully crafted identity.
The club's vaunted 'Mia san mia' motto, which appears on every modern Bayern kit, translates to 'we are who we are'.
Midfielder Aleksandar Pavlovic, a product of Bayern's youth system, in 2025 said: "For me, 'Mia san mia' means being a family, standing together in good times and bad.
"That's what we live by here from a young age, that we always stick together."
Musiala's return
Just two months after signing a contract extension in February 2025, Musiala began treatment for symptoms of the neurological condition.
After missing two months with an unrelated muscle injury, Musiala was warmly welcomed back by Bayern's 75,000-strong Allianz Arena on Friday.
Minutes after full-time, club powerbroker Karl-Heinz Rummenigge suggested Musiala's condition meant he might be unable to deliver on his lucrative deal and should take a pay cut.
"If he doesn't return to being the Jamal of old, then we need to have a conversation... because, frankly, the current financial figures would no longer be justifiable," he said.
The firestorm began to spread immediately, with Bayern's untimely announcement of a record turnover of close to one billion euros (US$1.1 billion) at their AGM a day later fanning the flames.
On Saturday, international player union FIFPRO said that Bayern "should know better", identifying a void between the German giants' values and their behaviour.
Former Bayern and Germany goalkeeper Oliver Kahn, who previously served as Bayern's CEO, issued a harsh critique.
"To put the player under pressure now and appeal to his decency through the public sphere, urging him to forgo part of his salary, is simply absurd," Kahn said.
But Kimmich's words have had the biggest impact as they provide a rare insight into the dressing room.
"It is understandable that the club might be concerned because of the illness. What I don't understand is the way this is being communicated publicly," Kimmich said.
"It must not happen that a player is made to bear the brunt of it."
e3cdd9f372753cc9: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 27 — The government has called on public-listed companies (PLCs) to adopt the RM3,400 living wage benchmark across their organisations.

Finance Minister II Datuk Seri Amir Hamzah Azizan said that fair and adequate wages would enable employees to meet their basic needs and maintain a decent standard of living. This, in turn, could lead to greater workforce stability, improved talent retention, and higher productivity.

“This is an important dimension of responsible business conduct, recognising that long-term corporate value creation must also take into account the well-being and economic security of the people who contribute to it.

“Paying a living wage is verifiable proof to investors, regulators and consumers that the social pillar of your sustainability report is backed by real conviction,” said Amir Hamzah in his speech at the National Annual Corporate Report Awards (Nacra) 2026 presentation dinner here today.
He said the government also remained committed to strengthening the institutional and policy foundations for sustainable and inclusive economic growth.

“Good governance, accountability and transparency are integral to this agenda, particularly as Malaysia seeks to move towards higher-value economic activities and strengthen its position in the global economy,” said Amir Hamzah.

He said stronger governance and reporting practices could help small and medium enterprises (SMEs) improve management discipline, assess business performance, access financing and engage more effectively with investors and business partners.
These capabilities are increasingly important as SMEs seek to expand their operations and participate in larger domestic and international value chains.

Amir Hamzah also said companies must invest in developing their workforce capabilities, particularly in data analytics, sustainability and environmental, social and governance (ESG) reporting, climate finance and digital finance.

“These competencies are important not only for meeting new reporting requirements, but also for understanding business risks, evaluating investment decisions and supporting long-term strategy,” he added.

Meanwhile, Nacra 2026 organising committee chairman Ong Chee Wai said high-quality corporate reporting was essential to building stakeholder trust, reinforcing investor confidence and supporting sustainable business growth among Malaysian companies.
“It also provides a competitive edge, helping organisations to attract investment and compete more effectively in an increasingly interconnected global economy.
“Through Nacra, we seek to recognise organisations that demonstrate these qualities and encourage continuous improvement across the corporate sector,” he said
Ong said the awards provided an opportunity for organisations to benchmark their practices against leading examples and raise the overall standard of corporate reporting in Malaysia.

Themed “Towards Accountability and Excellence”, Nacra 2026 is jointly organised by Bursa Malaysia Bhd, the Malaysian Institute of Accountants and the Malaysian Institute of Certified Public Accountants. — Bernama

7bf1de18245ec58e: LOS ANGELES, Nov 27 — Anita DeFrantz, an Olympic rowing bronze medallist who became a pioneering member of the International Olympic Committee, has died at the age of 74.
The IOC said in a statement yesterday that DeFrantz, the first African-American and the first American woman to hold a seat on the committee, had died. A cause of death was not disclosed.
”I feel an immense sense of loss at Anita’s passing,” IOC president Kirsty Coventry said.

”Anita was a mentor, a friend and a true inspiration to me, and to so many others around the world. From my earliest days in the Olympic movement, she showed me what courageous leadership looked like, and what was possible for women in sport.”
US Olympic and Paralympic Committee chief executive Sarah Hirshland and president Gene Sykes issued a statement hailing DeFrantz as “a giant of the Olympic Movement”.

”Anita DeFrantz was one of the most consequential Olympians our nation has ever known,” they said. “To those of us fortunate enough to work alongside her, she was also a mentor, a truth-teller and a steady source of wisdom and grace.”
DeFrantz captained the US rowing team at the 1976 Olympics, earning bronze in the women’s eight.
She served as vice president of Los Angeles’ 1984 Olympic organizing committee and was elected to serve on the IOC in 1986.
An outspoken advocate for women’s sports, DeFrantz spent 13 years on the IOC executive board, becoming the organization’s first woman vice president in 1997.
She also chaired the IOC’s Women and Sport Commission for almost 20 years.

”For all of her historic firsts, what we will miss most is Anita herself: her quiet strength, her sharp mind and her warmth,” Hirshland and Sykes said. “She asked the hard questions, always with kindness, and always brought the conversation back to the athletes.”
DeFrantz, who was born on October 4, 1952, and brought up in Indianapolis, Indiana, was introduced to rowing as a student at Connecticut College.
In it together
At her induction into the US Olympic and Paralympic Hall of Fame in 2025 she said she was shaped by the interdependence the “ultimate team sport” demanded.
”Unlike other sports, we can’t say ‘OK, I need a couple of strokes off. I’ll get back with you,’” she said. “We’re in it together, and that taught me so much.”

Qualified for the 1980 Olympics, DeFrantz was an outspoken critic of the US boycott of the Moscow Games that year and said the ultimately unsuccessful fight to get American athletes to Moscow had changed her life.
”Becoming an IOC member never crossed my mind,” she said. “But the path I took led me to that opportunity.”
DeFrantz was honored earlier this year at the Milan-Cortina Winter Olympics, where Coventry received the Olympic flame from her during the torch relay.

”Receiving the Olympic flame from Anita was a moment full of emotions,” Zimbabwe’s Coventry, a former Olympic swimmer herself, said at the time. “She really led the way for female leaders in sport globally.”
DeFrantz called seeing Coventry serving as the first woman IOC president “exactly how the world should be”. — AFP
bedf11acb59d79aa: BUENOS AIRES, Nov 26 — Former Argentina striker Carlos Tevez said yesterday Lionel Messi would appear in his testimonial next month and that he was confident Cristiano Ronaldo would be playing alongside them.
The 42-year-old Tevez played with Messi for Argentina and also lined up with Ronaldo at Manchester United.
Tevez started his career at Boca Juniors and returned there in 2018 before retiring four years later, and now his testimonial will be played December 20 at their Bombonera stadium in Buenos Aires.
Messi, 39, and 41-year-old Ronaldo have faced off against each other many times on the pitch, notably in several El Clasico fixtures during their respective times at Barcelona and Real Madrid.
If Tevez succeeds in luring the Portuguese forward to the Bombonera, it could be the first time ever that the pair who marked their generation play on the same side.
Other illustrious footballers scheduled for the match are the Italian goalkeeper Gianluigi Buffon, Argentine midfielder Juan Roman Riquelme and former England centre-back Rio Ferdinand. — AFP
b20daaa340e6f46b: PUTRAJAYA: The Court of Appeal has dismissed an Inland Revenue Board (LHDN) appeal to revive a dissolved company in order to pursue additional income tax assessments allegedly owed by it.

In a unanimous judgment delivered by Justice Wong Kian Kheong, the court ruled that LHDN failed to establish itself as an interested party entitled to seek the restoration of Mahabuilders Sdn Bhd under Section 535(1) of the Companies Act 2016.
Justices Alwi Abdul Wahab and Aliza Sulaiman were also on the panel.
Wong said an applicant seeking to revive a dissolved company must demonstrate a proprietary or pecuniary interest in its restoration and establish its entitlement on the balance of probabilities.

He said LHDN failed to prove that Mahabuilders had committed fraud, wilful default or negligence in its tax affairs, as required under Section 91(3) of the Income Tax Act 1967 to justify issuing additional assessments.

He also clarified that the two-year limitation under Section 535(1) applies to the court's power to declare a company's dissolution void, rather than merely requiring an application to be filed within that period.
Mahabuilders was dissolved on Aug 20, 2016, following the completion of its members' voluntary winding-up.
LHDN subsequently sought to issue additional tax assessments after investigations allegedly found that the company had understated its income for the 2012 and 2013 assessment years.
However, Wong said the court would not exercise its discretion under Section 582 of the Companies Act to extend the statutory period or remedy the non-compliance.
He said restoring the company would cause substantial injustice as its winding-up was complete and its assets had been distributed.

Wong also noted that the company's former directors and other persons falling within the statutory definition of directors could potentially be held jointly and severally liable for the additional tax under Section 75A of the Income Tax Act.
He said the passage of time would also make it difficult for the former directors to obtain the necessary records and evidence to challenge additional tax assessments.
The court therefore found no grounds to interfere with the High Court's decision to reject LHDN's application to invalidate the company's dissolution.
The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs.
571eceade4337142: ISTANBUL: Seorang pekerja maut, manakala beberapa lagi cedera dalam serangan ke atas sebuah loji penapisan minyak di wilayah Jazan, Arab Saudi pada Khamis, menurut Kementerian Tenaga negara itu.

Sumber rasmi kementerian itu dalam kenyataan berkata “projektil udara musuh” terkena loji penapisan minyak berkenaan menyebabkan kebakaran dan penggantungan sementara sebahagian operasi di kemudahan terbabit, lapor Anadolu Ajansi.
Sumber berkata, kebakaran itu telah dipadamkan.
Maklumat awal menunjukkan serangan itu mengorbankan seorang pekerja warga Nepal, manakala beberapa pekerja lain daripada pelbagai negara mengalami kecederaan tahap berbeza.
Pihak berkuasa mengucapkan takziah kepada keluarga mangsa korban dan mendoakan mangsa cedera yang sedang dirawat segera sembuh.
Pasukan tindak balas kecemasan dan teknikal khusus segera memulakan tugas susulan serangan itu.
Usaha sedang dijalankan bagi melengkapkan penilaian kerosakan dan memastikan keselamatan kemudahan berkenaan dengan kerjasama pihak berkuasa berkaitan, menurut sumber itu.
Kementerian itu tidak mengenal pasti pihak bertanggungjawab terhadap serangan berkenaan atau menyatakan jumlah pekerja cedera.
Pada Khamis, pakatan pimpinan Arab Saudi yang menyokong kerajaan Yaman diiktiraf masyarakat antarabangsa memaklumkan kumpulan Houthi menyerang loji penapisan minyak Jazan.

Pakatan itu kemudian memaklumkan ia memusnahkan sebuah pelantar pelancar peluru berpandu balistik di wilayah Al Hudaydah, barat Yaman, yang didakwa digunakan dalam serangan ke atas loji penapisan minyak berkenaan.
Serangan itu berlaku ketika konflik antara Houthi dan pakatan pimpinan Arab semakin memuncak, termasuk serangan yang menyasarkan lapangan terbang serta kemudahan tenaga di Saudi.
000e274fd7c14679: TBILISI, Nov 27 — Istanbul club Besiktas’ supporters unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during a Uefa Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia yesterday prompting a police response and sparking a diplomatic incident that led Turkey’s foreign minister to contact his Georgian counterpart.
Turkish football fans clashed with police in Batumi, temporarily halting the match, which had been moved from Istanbul over security concerns.

Images from the stadium showed Besiktas supporters displaying a banner reading “Revolt against the occupation, freedom for Palestine”, waving Palestinian flags and chanting anti-Israel slogans before police intervened.
Georgia’s interior ministry said in a statement that “three officers sustained various injuries as a result of the fans’ violent actions”, adding that 16 people had been detained.
It said some supporters had hurled stadium seats at officers and denied reports that police had used force in response to the display of pro-Palestinian flags and banners.

”We categorically deny these reports and emphasise that the fans’ violent actions and physical clashes with police began before the flags and banners were displayed, while they were still marching towards the stadium,” the ministry added.
Police used pepper spray against fans, some of whom required medical attention, Turkey’s private DHA news agency reported.
The match was suspended in the 26th minute because of disturbances in the stands, with Danish referee Morten Krogh sending both teams to the dressing rooms.
Turkey’s football federation strongly condemned what it described as the “unacceptable” conduct of Georgian police towards Besiktas supporters.

”We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the Uefa Europa League match,” the federation said in a statement.
Disproportionate use of force

Uefa announced last month that the fixture would be moved to Georgia after Turkish authorities informed European football’s governing body that, “for safety and security reasons”, the match could not be hosted in Istanbul.
Relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated sharply since the outbreak of the Gaza war.
President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a staunch supporter of the Palestinian cause, has repeatedly accused Israel of committing “genocide” in Gaza.
Pro-Palestinian banners and chants are seen or heard frequently at Turkish football matches, particularly since the start of the war.
Besiktas said they had lodged a complaint with Uefa over what they described as the “disproportionate” use of force by Georgian police.
”We have launched initiatives with our consulate general in Batumi and Uefa regarding the disproportionate use of force against our supporters by security forces,” the club said.
Besiktas added that they would closely monitor the situation until all of their supporters had returned safely to Turkey.
Erdogan spoke by phone with Besiktas chairman Serdal Adali and said he was closely following developments, the club said.
Messages of support
After the match, which finished 2-1 to Besiktas, Hapoel Beer-Sheva posted a message on social media directed to their travelling supporters.

”Please act responsibly, show restraint and use your best judgement as you leave the stadium and make your way to your accommodation. Follow the instructions of the Georgian security forces, who are responsible for ensuring your safety,” the club posted in Hebrew on X.
Messages of support poured in on social media from across Turkey, including from the sports minister and Ankara mayor.
Even Besiktas’s traditional Istanbul rivals, Galatasaray and Fenerbahce, as well as Black Sea club Trabzonspor, condemned the incidents and expressed solidarity with the club.
A Besiktas club employee told AFP that five supporters were receiving treatment in hospital.
Besiktas supporters scuffled with police and hurled objects at officers as they attempted to make arrests, according to live television footage.
The incidents prompted Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan to call his Georgian counterpart, Maka Botchorishvili.
”Officials from the Turkish embassy in Tbilisi and the consulate general in Batumi are at the stadium,” a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
”All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights.” — AFP
1ad09001caf799be: From William Ng

Malaysia’s ambition to move up the economic value chain is shared by every serious business owner in the country. We all want higher wages, greater automation and a workforce driven by skills rather than sheer numbers.

Yet, in our haste to reduce reliance on foreign workers, we risk confusing the symptom with the cure. Blocking or limiting the entry of foreign workers in unskilled and semi-skilled jobs across manufacturing, plantations, construction and food and beverage (F&B) does not automatically create higher-paying jobs for Malaysians. Instead, it disrupts the very businesses that keep our economy running and create higher-skilled roles for locals.
The myth of job substitution
The prevailing policy assumption is straightforward: restrict foreign workers, and local workers will step in to fill the gap. This is a myth born out of desperation.

Malaysia’s overall unemployment rate is at a historic low of 2.9%, effectively signalling full employment. Meanwhile, the economy produces hundreds of thousands of graduates annually, while youth unemployment hovers at around 10%. This gap is not caused by foreign workers taking jobs from Malaysians, but by a structural mismatch between job aspirations and skills. In short, our problem is underemployment, and foreign workers have little to do with it.

Critics often argue that Malaysians would readily take up 3D (dirty, dangerous and difficult) jobs if employers simply paid more, pointing to the hundreds of thousands of Malaysians working at F&B outlets, construction sites and factories across the causeway. But that comparison ignores basic arithmetic. An SME in Johor Bahru earns revenue in ringgit based on what local consumers can afford. It cannot charge in Singapore dollars to pay Singapore-level wages without triggering severe domestic inflation.

Even when vacancies are advertised on MYFutureJobs, young Malaysians with diplomas and degrees are not rushing to harvest oil palm bunches at remote estates, pour concrete under the sun, wash dishes in kitchens or operate repetitive manual assembly lines. Research by Khazanah Research Institute has shown that local and foreign workers occupy different segments of the labour market. They complement rather than replace each other.

When a restaurant is restricted from hiring foreign workers, it does not necessarily raise wages and recruit local graduates. Instead, it may reduce operating hours, delay expansion and eliminate supervisory, accounting and managerial positions that Malaysians actually want. Forcing SME manufacturers and F&B operators out of business because of labour shortages does not create automated alternatives. It reduces supply, weakens competitiveness and drives up costs for Malaysians.
The real cost of flawed policy design
Existing labour policies suffer from three structural flaws that penalise compliant businesses without resolving their dependence on foreign workers.

First, there is the assumption that taxing businesses more heavily for employing foreign workers will accelerate automation. The fact is, not every job can be automated. A high-tech semiconductor production line may be highly automated from the outset, but robots cannot climb hills to harvest durians, nor can a machine easily replace a barber.
During the pandemic, labour shortages cost the palm oil sector an estimated RM1 billion annually in unharvested crops. We are already seeing signs of repeating this self-inflicted damage.

Second, there is the misconception that requiring employers to advertise vacancies on MYFutureJobs will encourage locals to take up these jobs. In reality, very few of the positions intended for foreign workers attract applications from Malaysians. The requirement instead forces businesses to wait at least two weeks rather than fill vacancies immediately. The resulting revenue losses can be substantial and illustrate how poorly conceived policies can be when built on flawed assumptions.

Third, excessive restrictions on foreign worker recruitment are fuelling the shadow economy. When legal recruitment channels are frozen, approvals are delayed or worker-to-employee ratios become unrealistic, businesses do not simply shut down overnight. Instead, demand spills into the shadow economy, depriving the government of levy revenue and leaving workers without legal protection.
Why we cannot blindly copy other markets
Policymakers often point to Singapore, South Korea and Western economies as examples of how strict labour caps can force businesses to innovate and raise wages.
While the aspiration is admirable, importing another country's labour policies without replicating its economic foundations risks creating stagflation.
First, these economies began moving away from low-cost labour after building deep domestic capital markets, world-class research ecosystems and large-scale high-value export industries.

Second, consider how these economies actually operate today. Singapore remains heavily reliant on foreign workers in construction, marine and service sectors. Japan and South Korea have also expanded special technical intern and agricultural visa programmes over the past decade because of shortages of domestic workers willing to take up 3D jobs.

Even advanced economies recognise that modern service and technology sectors cannot function without an operational foundation. High-value engineers, chefs and supply chain planners cannot do their jobs if no one is clearing construction sites, preparing kitchens or moving freight.
A smarter path forward

Reducing dependence on foreign workers over the long term is the right direction, and most progressive businesses understand this. They also accept their responsibility to pay statutory wages, provide proper worker accommodation and healthcare and combat the employment of illegal foreign workers.

What we need is proper policy sequencing: reassessing sectors where cutting foreign worker numbers would be counterproductive and creating jobs that match the aspirations of Malaysians, rather than assuming the two are mutually exclusive.

When we treat foreign workers as a problem rather than vital contributors to the economy, and fixate on outward currency transfers while ignoring the far greater tax revenue generated by their economic output, we risk continuing to score own goals against our own economic growth.

Our businesses, especially SMEs, want to become the dynamic, high-wage companies policymakers envision. But restricting foreign workers in lower-skilled jobs is not the way to achieve that. Give businesses the workforce they need at the operational level so they can build the high-wage, automated economy Malaysia wants tomorrow.
William Ng is president of the Small and Medium Enterprises Association of Malaysia.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
73c26b52141b60f6: HONG KONG: Asian shares were set to end a bruising month on a steadier note as a holiday lull offered some respite from AI jitters, while the dollar reigned supreme, riding a wave of safe-haven demand and rate hike bets towards a third month of gains.

Oil prices were headed for the first weekly rise in four on renewed concerns about supply disruptions. Brent crude futures slipped 0.4% on Friday to US$96.14 a barrel, but were still up 3.9% for the week. For the month, they were down 18%.
Wall Street was closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday, but in Asia, S&P 500 futures were up 0.8% and Nasdaq futures were 1% higher.

Japan's Nikkei rose 0.7% to bring its gains for the week to 2.7%, clawing back only a fraction of its 8.4% loss for the month. Data showed on Friday that core inflation in Tokyo hit a 16-month high in November, bolstering the case for an interest rate hike from the Bank of Japan as soon as next month.
MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan edged up 0.5% to end the week 1.9% higher. It was still down 8.2% for the month.
Shares in South Korea rallied 2% and China's blue chips slipped 0.2%, after hitting the lowest level since June 2025 a day earlier.

"Barring a big shock that severely rattles a thin market, November is practically in the books and the markets limp into December where a seasonal 'Santa Rally' currently appears elusive," said Kyle Rodda, a senior analyst at Capital.com.
"For as long as the markets remain unsure about the growth trajectory for AI and lack clarity about where US rates may peak, uncertainty and therefore volatility is liable to remain elevated."

Tech giant Nvidia remained a source of unease after S&P put its credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade. The chipmaker told manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers containing its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, the Financial Times reported.
Elsewhere in tech, Elon Musk said that every child in the US would receive two shares in his space and AI company SpaceX, pledging a gift worth some US$18 billion.
Dollar reigns

The US dollar was headed to its third monthly gain on Friday, up 1.8% against its major peers at 103.8. It has been supported by expectations that the Federal Reserve is almost certain to lift interest rates in December, as well as safe-haven flows from the selloff in equities.
Futures imply a 99% chance the Fed will raise rates by 25 basis points in December, but speculation of a half-point increase has faded.

The euro was last flat at US$1.0964, after news that Spanish central banking veteran Pablo Hernandez de Cos would become the next European Central Bank president, a move that was well telegraphed and suggested policy continuity.

The kiwi edged up 0.2% to US$0.5482 after New Zealand's ruling centre-right coalition fell short of a parliamentary majority, leaving it reliant on negotiations with the centrist Opportunity Party to stay in power.
Bond investors are wondering if the broad losses in global stocks this month coupled with doubts about the durability of AI-driven business investment might temper the hawkishness of central banks.
"The Fed could, of course, still blink," said David Rees, chief economist at Schroders. "But a Fed put would not necessarily be unambiguously positive for markets."
"If growth and inflation data remain firm, in a game of cat and mouse markets could soon begin pricing a more hawkish Fed back in, potentially setting off the same chain of events all over again."
Two-year Treasury yields rose 3 basis points to 4.6705% as the cash market reopened after the US holiday. They were up 6 bps this week.
Benchmark 10-year Treasury yields rose 4 bps to 4.8918%, but were down 2 bps for the week.
2d5d412f1f98d7b7: From Samirul Othman
Pasir Mas MP Ahmad Fadhli Shaari asks why MISC should borrow RM2.27 billion to buy into Yinson Holdings Berhad, a company that owes billions. He asks if it amounts to a bailout.

My answer is that MISC can spend years expanding its overseas offshore business, one vessel at a time, or buy a stake in a platform which owns vessels already at work, with paying customers and teams that can compete for the next contract.

Take Yinson’s Agogo vessel in Angola. It is a floating facility that processes oil and gas at sea. It took 29 months from winning the contract to producing its first oil, even though Yinson delivered ahead of schedule. It is now on a firm 15-year contract.
In Brazil, Yinson’s Anna Nery is on a 25-year contract with Petrobras that runs to 2048. MISC would be investing in an established business with vessels already in operation and generating revenue.

The consortium of MISC, Yinson’s founding Lim family and the Employees Provident Fund is offering RM2.50 a share for the remaining 55.2% of Yinson. The RM4.03 billion goes to shareholders who sell their existing shares in Yinson.
MISC plans to put up RM3.03 billion, about three quarters of the sum it borrowed. Borrowing spreads the cost and keeps some of MISC’s cash available for the rest of its fleet.

The Lim family is not only keeping its money in the business but adding about RM1 billion in cash. This clearly doesn’t sound like a bailout. EPF is carrying over its roughly 17.1% stake without putting in fresh cash for the buyout. Again, no public funds are going into the deal.
Weighing acquisition against organic growth
Based on Yinson’s latest quarterly announcement, offshore production contracted revenue backlog amounted to approximately US$19.3 billion.

This represents future receipts from leases and charters that customers have committed to. That money will come in over many years, and the company has bills and lenders to pay. But it gives MISC a starting point for valuing the stake based on contracts already signed.

MISC’s first ultra-deepwater vessel began producing oil at Brazil’s Mero field in 2024. It already knows that market. The Yinson deal adds three vessels in Brazil and brings new relationships in markets such as Ghana and Angola.
In Ghana, Eni recently hired Yinson to expand the gas processing capacity of a vessel it already runs there. An operating fleet gives a supplier a track record that can win the next job.
The offshore industry rewards suppliers that can deliver the same kind of work again and again. In Guyana, ExxonMobil’s local affiliate recently awarded SBM Offshore its sixth vessel contract.

A builder that can build on proven engineering solutions, call on engineers who have worked together before and show that its vessels run reliably can make a stronger bid. That is the advantage I am expecting MISC to seek from Yinson.

MISC could also bid with Yinson on individual projects. Buying a stake not only gives it a share in contracts already earning money but gives both companies a reason to invest in engineering teams they can use across several bids.
For Petronas, that means its marine infrastructure arm can build a bigger business serving oil producers around the world, including on fields that Petronas is invested.

I take it that MISC has put a value on that head start. It can compare the price of buying into an operating platform versus the cost of building vessels, hiring the teams and waiting three to four years for contracts to start paying. It should run the numbers on both routes to see which brings in more cash, and how soon – balancing risks with expected long-term business impact.
The debt has to pay its way

Fadhli is right that Yinson’s lenders and holders of preference shares rank ahead of ordinary shareholders. In October, for example, Yinson announced a bond issue to replace existing debt on the Agogo vessel. That debt is tied to an operating asset with a paying customer. The proposed MISC loan has a different job. It would fund the share purchase, while Yinson continues to service its own debt.

What does the loan cost MISC? Its published illustration puts annual borrowing costs at about RM107 million. Using Yinson’s last audited results up to January 2026, MISC estimates it would have recorded about RM176 million as its share of profit. That offers an early indication of how the purchase could contribute even after interest. MISC still needs to show how much of that profit can reach it as cash.

Also, the full RM2.27 billion of borrowings quoted by Fadhli needs to be considered properly against Yinson’s equity value. Assuming a 16% premium using MISC’s announcement, MISC's borrowings to buy the Yinson shares at the current trading price would have been around RM1.96 billion.

Therefore, the real question is whether MISC’s borrowings for this premium, of around RM310 million, is more than that required to incentivise Yinson shareholders to sell their shares. This is something that MISC’s independent adviser would have to consider in its report.

RM3.03 billion is a lot of money, but this should be considered in the context of large offshore assets which can cost up to US$3 billion to construct. Also, the proposed RM2.50/share offer price doesn’t seem inconsistent with the RM2.26–3.83/share range of target prices that analysts had previously estimated for Yinson before the deal was announced.

Ultimately, MISC’s board should show that the vessels in the Yinson portfolio can generate cashflow to pay both the holders of preference shares and support a sensible return to MISC and its partners.
The writer is a Malaysian economist, international relations analyst and senior consultant.

babac6bd2e3fa552: Thanksgiving Day adalah hari kesyukuran yang diraikan di Amerika Syarikat dan beberapa negara lain. Dalam penulisan ini saya tumpu kepada hari kesyukuran di AS, yang disambut pada Khamis keempat bulan November setiap tahun. Bagi tahun ini, Thanksgiving Day ialah semalam yakni 26 Nov.

Thanksgiving Day pada asalnya merupakan perayaan kesyukuran atas hasil tuaian dan nikmat yang diperoleh sepanjang tahun. Tradisi ini dikaitkan dengan jamuan menuai pada 1621 yang menghimpunkan golongan Pilgrims, iaitu peneroka awal Inggeris di Plymouth, dengan masyarakat Orang Asli Wampanoag di kawasan yang kini dikenali sebagai Massachusetts. Pada 1941, AS menetapkan Khamis keempat bulan November sebagai tarikh rasmi sambutan Thanksgiving Day dan cuti umum persekutuan. Sempena Thanksgiving Day, rakyat AS berhimpun bersama keluarga serta rakan-rakan untuk jamuan Thanksgiving dinner. Hidangan yang lazim dikaitkan dengan Thanksgiving Day ialah ayam belanda panggang, sos cranberry, kentang lenyek dan pai labu.

Kebelakangan ini, dikatakan semangat di sebalik Thanksgiving Day telah hilang bagi sesetengah rakyat AS sejak Donald Trump menjadi presiden. Saya pun tidak tahu what Americans have to be thankful for. Kos jamuan semakin tinggi. Sambutan Thanksgiving juga menandakan bermulanya musim membeli-belah tetapi harga barangan pula melambung. Ini ada kena mengena dengan tarif yang dikehendaki Trump tidak berapa lama dahulu.

Menjelang Thanksgiving Day, pentadbiran Trump mencadangkan one more round of tariffs, dan barangan daripada 14 ekonomi termasuk Malaysia berdepan tarif tambahan ini. Menurut kenyataan Wakil Perdagangan AS Jamieson Greer, siasatan mereka mendapati strategi perindustrian tertentu yang diguna pakai oleh rakan dagang mewujudkan 'persaingan yang tidak adil' bagi pengeluar AS. Yang dimaksudkan termasuk keluaran melebihi kapasiti.

Ada lagi alasannya tetapi saya rasa tidak perlu dihuraikan kerana tidak mustahil langkah mengenakan tarif ini sekadar AS tunjuk kuat. Mungkin saya betul mungkin salah, namun China menyifatkan dakwaan lebihan kapasiti itu tidak berasas dan bermotifkan politik.

Cadangan oleh pentadbiran Trump ini telah meningkatkan ketegangan perdagangan sejagat, pun begitu diutarakan juga meskipun Trump berdepan tentangan politik, cabaran undang-undang, dan kebimbangan mengenai peningkatan kos sara hidup rakyat AS.

Trump mendakwa beliau mahu melindungi industri dan pekerja AS, namun pakar ekonomi memberi amaran langkah terbaharu ini berisiko meningkatkan tekanan inflasi, di samping kos sara hidup. Rakyat AS masih terkesan dengan first round of tariffs, and now this. Pun begitu, Trump teruskan jua.

Kita pun tahu parti Trump iaitu Republikan tewas teruk pada pilihan raya separuh penggal tempoh hari -- mereka hilang kuasa di Kongres dan Dewan Senat. Takkan Trump mahu 'menghukum' pengundi yang menolak Republikan?
Berita Harian Singapura menyebut China berdepan kadar tarif tertinggi yakni sehingga 40%. Jika benar, saya tidak terperanjat kerana China adalah pesaing AS. Mungkin ini cara AS melemahkan China?

Vietnam dikatakan kena 35% manakala Indonesia, Thailand dan Kemboja, serta Korea Selatan, Taiwan dan India berdepan kadar sehingga 25%. Singapura, Jepun dan Bangladesh, serta Kesatuan Eropah dan Switzerland dikatakan kena 20%.

Menurut Malaysiakini, AS mencadangkan tarif tambahan sehingga 18% ke atas barangan Malaysia selepas mendapati "dasar perindustrian dan amalan pembuatan Malaysia menyumbang kepada lebihan kapasiti dan pengeluaran berstruktur yang membebankan atau menyekat perdagangan AS."
Saya ulangi penegasan China, "dakwaan lebihan kapasiti tidak berasas dan bermotifkan politik."

Menurut Berita Harian Singapura, kadar sebenar yang dikenakan mungkin lebih rendah bagi sesetengah negara tertakluk kepada perjanjian perdagangan yang telah dimeterai dengan Washington. Menurut akhbar itu, tarif baharu dijangka berkuat kuasa pada 2027 selepas melalui proses mendapatkan maklum balas awam dan kemungkinan sesi perdengaran. Ertinya, negara-negara terbabit termasuk Malaysia akan terpaksa menghantar wakil ke Washington untuk membentangkan hujah masing-masing.
Menurut Reuters: "For Trump doubling down on tariffs is about power, not popularity". Sesungguhnya kuasa amat memabukkan. Tidak keterlaluan untuk kata Trump memang 'mabuk' dalam kekuasaan.

5f988667e680d566: When negotiators from Russia, the United States and Ukraine met in Abu Dhabi recently for peace talks on ending the Ukraine war, the Russians pushed a long-held demand for a new security architecture for Europe. Washington has appeared open to this, with US President Donald Trump touting a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. While little was revealed about what such a framework would look like specifically, a recent speech by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov provides some clues. Sergei Lavrov’s speech at the Minsk International Conference on Eurasian Security. At a security conference in Minsk, Belarus, earlier this month, Lavrov proposed a new security architecture for the entire Eurasian continent. Reiterating the claim Russia has long made to justify its war in Ukraine, Lavrov said NATO had repeatedly pledged not to expand eastward to contain Russia, but did so anyway. And, he said, the West is now pursuing a new “NATO-style military-political bloc in Asia”. In response, Lavrov said Russia wanted to build a new security framework that would encompass all of Europe and Asia – echoing the Soviet Union’s communist alliances during the Cold War. A new arrangement like this would be “committed to the principles of indivisible security, openness and equality”, Lavrov said, adding European nations were welcome to join. Russia does not “desire nor plan any war whatsoever with Europe”, he stressed. But he added: If Europe, as it threatens, is itself preparing for war and initiates one, we are ready. A security proposal based on “sovereignty” and “equality” may sound appealing to some states across the region. However, there are several reasons to be sceptical. What Europe wants The prevailing view in Europe is that Russia is the continent’s principal security threat. So, the idea of European states joining Russia in a new arrangement of any sort is unlikely to gain broad acceptance. And despite Russian President Vladimir Putin’s claims he is not against “having a dialogue with Europe, Moscow has made clear it does not want European representatives in the Ukraine peace talks. So it stands to reason Europe wouldn’t have a voice in a future security agreement either. That said, the political view towards Russia in Europe is evolving. As economic pressures continue to mount, support for right-wing, populist parties is growing, including one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters, Germany. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party opposes financial and military support for Ukraine, arguing the war is not in Germany’s national interests. In fact, its platform in one recent eastern state election where it finished first called for a revival of Russian language teaching, an end to sanctions and closer energy ties with Russia. This highlights the diversity of views in some countries on both the war and Europe’s broader strategic priorities. Some have raised the possibility of a more robust Organization for Security and Co-operation (the only European security group that Russia belongs to), or a revived NATO-Russia Council. However, this seems far-fetched in the absence of trust between the two sides. Many in Europe believe Russia’s true aims for a new security framework are to carve up the continent into Cold War-era spheres of influence and expand its influence beyond its borders. Read more: Russia wanted a new world order. This wasn’t the one it had in mind What China wants Second, it remains unclear how China, the region’s other major power, and its own security ambitions fit within Russia’s vision. Chinese foreign policy has long emphasised a principle of not interfering in the domestic affairs of other states. This has proven attractive to many authoritarian countries. At the same time, China has successfully advanced major global economic initiatives, notably the Belt and Road Initiative. And Beijing often promotes its own vision of the international order. As such, Russia’s proposed security framework would need to accommodate another major power with its own interests and priorities. Despite their growing cooperation in recent years, China and Russia are also competing for influence in a pivotal Eurasian region – Central Asia. While Russia has traditionally been the dominant power in the region, China has quietly advanced to the point where it can now compete with, if not surpass, Russia’s influence. What the rest of Asia wants Lastly, Eurasia is already home to a complex landscape of international organisations, blocs and multilateral security agreements. Beyond the European Union, these include the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, the BRICS (the group originally comprised of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), and the Gulf Cooperation Council, among others. Each of these groupings has its own distinct strategic interests and priorities. So, it remains unclear how a new Russia-led security framework would interact with these groups, or potentially compete with them. Indeed, there seems to be a growing preference, especially in Asia, for smaller alliances between countries with similar ideological world views, such as the new security pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey. At the same time, other nations, particularly those in Southeast Asia, have held fast to their non-aligned status, preferring to seek partnerships with an array of countries that suit a variety of interests. Read more: What Australia could learn from its Southeast Asian neighbours about power and the changing global order What comes next? We may be witnessing the gradual erosion of the post-second world war international order. Now, the big question is what comes next. While Russia’s aims seem reminiscent of Soviet influence during the Cold War, this is a new world, and there are too many hurdles for its vision of a new security framework to become a reality. New international orders do not emerge overnight. Rather, they evolve through the cumulative decisions of states pursuing their own interests, forming new alignments, alliances and partnerships along the way. Dilnoza Ubaydullaeva receives funding from the Japan Foundation Program.

c23365c8add12072: Eleven days. That is how long it took for a disgrace to become a homecoming.
On Nov 12, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as president and CEO, days after he admitted to an extramarital affair.

Reports linked him to Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials reportedly believe was recruited by Beijing to get close to him. China calls this a smear, and nothing has been proven in public. He confessed to it.

On Nov 17, board chair Harvey Jones told investors the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”. On Nov 23, the board voted unanimously to bring him back, calling him the “right person to lead Nvidia” and his return is “in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers”.

Stockholders first. Not one word about integrity, about the code of conduct the company itself said he had breached, or about a wife of four decades whose private pain became global headlines. The stock had fallen more than 16% after his confession. The board did the arithmetic, and the arithmetic won.
Surprise, surprise. Except, none at all.
When the powerful fall into scandal, it is our children left asking the questions.
Today, the Malaysian version is playing out in Jalan Langgak Duta.
Najib Razak was convicted in the SRC International case for misappropriating RM42 million. That conviction was upheld by the Federal Court, and he went to Kajang prison in August 2022.
In September this year he received a conditional royal pardon, allowing him to be placed under house arrest subject to payment of a RM50 million fine.
His party ran a crowdfunding drive in his name, succeeded and paid the entire fine. He has, since Nov 10, been serving what remains of his sentence under house arrest until August 2028.
Within days, the prisons department was explaining a nearly eight-hour outing for Friday prayers, a hospital appointment and other engagements.
And all this while he appeals a separate 1MDB conviction carrying 15 years' jail and an RM11.4 billion fine.

The king’s prerogative of mercy is enshrined in our constitution, and I do not question it. Nvidia's board answers to shareholders by law. An affair is a moral failing, not a crime. Najib's supporters sincerely believe he has suffered enough, and some believe he was persecuted.
All true. And all beside the point.
The question is not whether these outcomes are legal. The question is what they teach.
The lessons our children are learning
Children do not learn values from speeches. They learn from watching what happens to people who break the rules.

And what are they watching? A man who betrayed his marriage and allegedly let a suspected foreign agent into his inner circle is back on the throne within a fortnight, thanked for his “humility”. A former prime minister convicted of abusing public funds is welcomed home with prayers, crowds and political rallies in his name.

The lesson is clear: consequences are for ordinary people. The clerk who pockets RM500 from the till is sacked and never works in that industry again. The schoolboy caught copying in his SPM exam has his results cancelled.
But if you are valuable enough, powerful enough, connected enough, a conviction becomes an inconvenience and a scandal becomes a sabbatical.

Where is dignity in this? Not with the wife who learned of her husband's betrayal along with the rest of the world. Not with the rakyat whose money vanished into luxury and lawyers' fees. Dignity, it seems, has been outsourced to whoever holds the shares or the votes.
Where is respect? We now “respect” results. We have stopped respecting character.
What we must teach instead

So what do I tell my grandchildren? Talent without character is a loaded gun. Brilliance makes you useful. Integrity makes you trustworthy. The world will always try to sell you the first as a substitute for the second. Do not buy it.
Sorry is not the same as accountability. Anyone can issue a statement "with the greatest humility". Real remorse costs something, and it is paid before the comeback, not instead of it.
Do not cheer for the fallen powerful. When you clap for a convicted man, you are telling every corrupt official waiting in line that the crowd will forgive them too.
Judge leaders by how they treat people who can do nothing for them. A spouse. A taxpayer. A junior employee. That is where character lives.
The rules must apply to everyone. The day we accept two sets of rules, one for the rich and one for the rest, is the day our children stop believing rules matter at all.
Boards will chase stock prices. Politicians will chase votes. But families, schools and communities do not have to follow them.
The real test is not what Nvidia's board or Malaysia's political class does next. It is what we say at the dinner table tonight, when a child looks up from the news and asks: “Is that okay?”
Our answer will shape a generation. Let it be a clear, unashamed “No”.
