d7eb7800e9b4155a: Agentic AI has supercharged demand for inference infrastructure. According to Goldman Sachs, token consumption is set to jump 24-fold to 120 quadrillion tokens per month between this year and 2030. Enterprises, wary of frontier model sticker shock, are now building their own GPU estates to cope.

Those enterprises shouldn't blindly follow hyperscalers' lead when taking AI inference kit into production. The indicators of success for such companies are different than those for a frontier model provider, and so are the constraints. DIY AI infrastructure at the enterprise level has to earn ROI quickly, meaning that enterprises must focus on sustained operation. That makes engineering criteria such as uptime, heat and power, service windows, and deployment times doubly important. The performance benchmarks that hyperscalers focus on won't matter nearly as much to the average bank or retailer.

ASUS is presenting the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, built on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, as a worked example of sustained AI inference infrastructure. It announced two models at NVIDIA GTC Berlin in October: the 3U hybrid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BHFS and the 2U fully liquid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BLFS.
Agents change the compute bill

Agents represent a hockey stick curve for token consumption because an agent isn't a single prompt. It loops until the job's done, often spawning other versions of itself in the process. This is how it breaks a goal into steps and works through them iteratively.

While training is a batch workload, agent inference is a production service that runs around the clock and only gets bigger. NVIDIA is making each generation of systems more powerful than the last to keep up with the demands of both.

Running at scale, day after day, is another matter. A useful way to think about the infrastructure that does it is as a token factory: it takes in power, data and GPU compute and turns out tokens. What counts is throughput, meaning how many tokens, and how many users, the same power and floor space can serve, hour after hour.
Enterprises move from pilots to AI factories

Enterprises are moving ahead quickly with their AI factory projects. According to Deloitte's AI infrastructure survey, published in March, 64 percent of respondents have started limited or at-scale AI factory deployments, while 88 percent expect to do so by 2028. They are spending more on AI infrastructure to do it: 86 percent expect their budgets to increase over the next three years.

Enterprises have different problems from hyperscalers and frontier model companies, though. Model builders often get to design greenfield campuses around their GPUs. Conversely, enterprises are often working with small operations teams in existing datacenters that may not have been built with AI in mind. That means they need to think harder about maintenance windows, existing management tooling and predictable deployment. And they'll often be retrofitting halls whose racks rarely draw more than 30 kW.

In token factory terms, the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System is the core compute engine. Each system puts eight NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPUs on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, linked by sixth-generation NVLink. ASUS has designed its equipment to support the constraints above. Its customers can choose between the hybrid and fully liquid-cooled models, and they can opt for partial or full rack configurations by buying multiple trays. This enables them to match their facilities' needs.
Peak performance versus sustained performance

The other difference between model providers and enterprises lies in which numbers they care about. Peak performance is different from sustained performance. The first is a specification sheet number, while the second is what the GPU actually delivers hours into a heavy workload.

Production inference tends to run continuously, especially when it uses agents, as opposed to training, which is a sporadic job. So the sustained figure is the one that buyers pay for. Heat becomes a real issue here because when cooling can't keep up, GPUs throttle their clocks to protect themselves. In a token factory, a throttled GPU is a slower production line.

The more advanced the architecture becomes, the higher the stakes get. NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU has raised them to their highest point, delivering up to 400 petaflops of NVFP4 inference per eight-GPU board, according to NVIDIA's sparse specification. This is screamingly fast, but the increased heat per board means less margin before throttling.

ASUS designed both models to put direct-to-chip liquid cooling on every GPU. Only the 3U unit leaves the CPUs on air cooling. ASUS also says it puts every configuration through a 168-hour stress test.
Power and heat set the shape of the rack

As boards increase their compute density, pushing up the power and heat requirements, planning naturally has to move out of the server room and into the facility. That's the case whether you're talking about an entire NVL72 rack or a stack of eight-GPU servers like the ASUS systems.

There are other things to consider beyond heat. Few datacenters run racks drawing more than 30 kilowatts, says the Uptime Institute. Yet a single liquid-cooled tray of the ASUS systems draws up to 23.9 kilowatts, and a full rack of nine has a power budget of about 216 kilowatts.
Floor loading and power distribution matter as much as cooling.

NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU raises the stakes again. The eight-GPU format enables organizations to buy their computing power in more granular steps. That's where the two ASUS systems come into their own. With few enterprises needing a training cluster at NVL72 scale, the advantage is that an HGX box lets them buy AI compute in digestible pieces.
The ASUS systems also come with a 54V busbar and cable-free board-to-board design. ASUS says this simplifies assembly and improves reliability.
Connectivity, storage and management

So that's space, power and heat. But a GPU board won't produce many tokens if the network, storage or operational tooling can't feed it properly. Agent workloads move context and data all the time, so east-west bandwidth and local storage are key to effective utilization. Any new equipment should ideally slot straight into the enterprise's existing management and monitoring tooling.

ASUS ships the whole rack, including servers, networking, power and storage, as a single blueprint. ASUS pre-validates this AI Factory reference architecture at rack scale so that organizations can plan for future growth. That includes dedicated management nodes and a management switch.

Inside each tray, ASUS has sized the data paths to keep the GPUs fed. Eight OSFP ports on NVIDIA ConnectX-9 give every GPU 800Gb/s of east-west bandwidth to the rest of the cluster, and an NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPU adds two 400GbE ports. Within the board, the eight GPUs talk to each other over NVLink at 3,600GB/s, ASUS says. The 2U tray takes up to 4TB of DDR5 system memory and has eight E1.S NVMe bays for fast local data access, while the 3U model offers a choice of U.2 or E1.S drives.
Built to be serviced

The other issue for enterprises putting AI inference into production is service and maintenance. In a liquid-cooled box, routine fixes can mean draining a coolant loop, which is downtime, and lost token output, that most enterprises can't afford, especially when dealing with non-batch workloads such as inferencing. So ASUS set out to make components quicker to swap.

On the 2U fully liquid-cooled model, ASUS did it with independent, tool-less CPU and GPU sleds, each with its own direct-to-chip cooling. On the 3U hybrid, ASUS says the air-cooled CPU sled cuts maintenance time by up to 50 percent.
From loading dock to first token

Services aren't just about server maintenance. They're also about decreasing the time to value for AI. Most enterprises won't have in-house rack-scale GPU integration skills, which is why pre-validation and design services are so important.

ASUS says its services run from early facility assessment through to operations. Its professional services cover five offerings: infrastructure design, deployment, performance optimization, AI platform development and lifecycle management. For rapid deployment, ASUS uses its own automation platform, the ASUS Infrastructure Deployment Center (AIDC).
Production needs a partner, not just a part number

So, with an enterprise token factory judged on how reliably it keeps producing rather than on peak FLOPS, in-house AI deployment teams will be back to focusing on the basics, albeit while dealing with an innovative technology. That means they'll be asking questions about sustained performance, heat and power in existing facilities. They'll be looking at integration at the rack level and with management software, along with service windows and deployment time. ASUS is positioning itself as a partner that can answer those questions with the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, which it's making available this quarter.

d3ed840d59d336ff: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 27 — The Malaysian Palm Oil Board (MPOB) has been urged to clarify the rules on mixing palm oil products from different countries in the same vessel tank, especially how such cargo should be declared before export.
Maritime expert Datuk Seri Jeyenderan Ramasamy said clear guidelines were needed so that the country of origin, grade and quantity of palm oil cargo were recorded accurately.
He said the issue went beyond how palm oil was handled during shipping. It also involved export documentation, licensing requirements and Malaysia’s reputation as a major palm oil exporter.
“When palm oil from Malaysia is mixed with products from another country in the same vessel tank, what country of origin should be stated in the export documents?
“Should both countries be identified, or can the entire cargo be declared under one country? These are questions that need clear answers,” he said.

Jeyenderan said it was important to tell commingling apart from blending. Commingling mixes palm oil products of the same type and grade, while blending combines products of different types or grades.
He said MPOB should clarify whether both were allowed when the products came from different countries, and whether specific licences or approvals were needed.
The board should also explain the laws and regulations covering such activities, including how the grade and country of origin of the final cargo must be declared, he added.
Jeyenderan said physically mixing products did not automatically change their legal country of origin, which depended on the applicable rules of origin and trade requirements.
He said buyers relied on export documents to verify the source, quality and quantity of what they bought.
“Any difference between the actual cargo and the information stated in the documents could lead to commercial disputes, difficulties in verifying shipments and possible regulatory issues,” he said.
Jeyenderan also claimed that MPOB officers no longer routinely boarded vessels to check documents and inspect cargo after the Covid-19 pandemic.

“Before Covid-19, MPOB officers would usually come on board ships to check the relevant documents whenever commingling or blending took place. When Malaysian palm oil cargo was mixed with other Malaysian cargo, they would check the documents from both the ship and the shore to make sure the operation followed MPOB’s rules.
“But after the pandemic, we no longer see MPOB officers coming on board to carry out these checks,” he alleged.
He said MPOB should clarify whether its inspection procedures had changed, and what alternative arrangements were in place to verify cargo properly.

Jeyenderan said companies handling cargo from different sources should keep proper records of the quantity, grade and country of origin of each product loaded into a vessel tank, along with details of any later mixing or blending.
These records would let the authorities verify what a cargo contained and make sure export declarations were accurate, he added.
He said unclear requirements could also lead exporters, traders, cargo owners, shipping companies and vessel operators to read the rules differently.
Jeyenderan said a formal clarification from MPOB would give businesses more certainty, especially those in international palm oil trading.
“Seeking clarification is not about restricting legitimate trade. It is about ensuring that businesses understand the rules and that every cargo is properly declared.
“Malaysia must protect its reputation as a reliable palm oil supplier. Accurate documentation and transparency are essential to maintaining the confidence of international buyers,” he said.

114803e511063529: NEW YORK: Neither high fuel prices nor stubborn inflation are expected to stop US shoppers from spending robustly as their turkey hangovers wear off on Black Friday. But below healthy top-line forecasts lie signs of stress.

Holiday spending - which unofficially begins on Black Friday - is seen topping last year's strong figures by 4%-6%, several economic forecasts show. But most of the gains will be attributable to inflation which, at 3.8%, is about a percentage point higher than in each of the last two years.

The National Retail Federation sees November-December holiday retail sales rising 4.2% year-over-year, to just above US$1 trillion. The Mastercard Economics Institute and EY Parthenon each forecast sales to rise more than 5%.

Eventual final results often beat pre-holiday estimates. Still, consumer sentiment remains shaky. This month, voters punished US president Donald Trump for an Iran War that's pushed the cost of living higher, handing Democrats sweeping electoral victories.
A November survey by the National Retail Federation found that 82% of consumers are taking steps to manage holiday costs, like buying less expensive gifts.

Los Angeles resident Felicia Cox, 50, said that while her holiday spending will be roughly stable, inflation is impacting how she thinks. "I want to get more gifts that people will actually use or need," said Cox, a sales representative, while browsing in an L.A. Marshalls last week. "I feel like people aren't able to afford as much stuff."

Worries aside, some 87% of 1,200 consumers surveyed by Deloitte in October planned to participate in the five-day shopping period from Thanksgiving through "Cyber Monday," Nov 30 - the highest in a decade, according to Deloitte.

"People like to spend during the holidays," even when there's a "persisting undercurrent of stress,” said Katie Thomas, who leads the Kearney Consumer Institute, part of global consulting firm Kearney.
Middle- and lower-income shoppers - who have been trading down for months - were however more likely than wealthy ones to spend less, according to the Kearney survey.

Target, Dollar Tree and Kohl's have all pointed to belt-tightening during recent earnings calls. Kohl's CEO Michael Bender on Tuesday cited an "increasingly choiceful" consumer that is "looking to stretch every dollar."

Holiday spending forecasts mostly predated the recent stock market correction that followed the midterms, turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia, and mounting concerns around an AI bubble. The decline could dampen the wealth effect that has seen affluent shoppers splurge on gadgets and accessories, UBS analysts said in a note on Tuesday.
Higher input costs, particularly from petrol derivatives like plastic, are hitting some products more than others.
Prices of toys - generally high in plastic - have risen 13.2% since the start of the year, pushing Barbie maker Mattel this month to cut its annual forecast as consumers balked at higher costs.

Some unlikely products are buoying the toy category. Best and Target have both flagged trading cards - including Pokemon and Magic: The Gathering products - as a key growth driver. Squishy NeeDoh toys were selling for US$24.99 on Amazon in October, nearly triple the price a year earlier on hot demand, according to e-commerce marketing platform Omnisend.

Toy maker Learning Resources Inc - a plaintiff in lawsuits that overturned Trump's tariffs - is seeing demand roughly flat, said CEO Rick Woldenberg, though he added it's hard to predict demand before Black Friday.
"People can't shop until they have their turkey," Woldenberg said.

AI could also scramble the year's shopping dynamics. As shoppers use AI to find bargains or even complete purchases - and retailers become increasingly adept at altering price quickly through AI - the deepest discounts could come closer to Christmas, as consumers and retailers both wait out the market, said Ryan Orabone, a consultant at Spaulding Ridge.
"My advice to shoppers is to be patient," he said. "Don't jump on the first deal you see."
1ee2ba9889909398: BRASILIA: Luiz Carlos Trabuco, chairman of Brazil's second-largest private lender Bradesco, has agreed to become Brazilian finance minister next year when President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva begins a new term, the government said in a statement on Thursday.
Trabuco and Lula met at the president's official residence in Brasilia earlier on Thursday, the government said. Bradesco did not reply to a request for comment.
Trabuco will face the urgent challenge of convincing investors he can balance Lula's big campaign spending promises with pressure from financial markets to tackle snowballing government debt.
Investors have been concerned with the rise of Brazil's public debt, now at almost 83% of gross domestic product and up about 11 percentage points since the start of Lula's current term in 2023.

Brazilian financial assets, including its stocks and currency, have fallen since Lula beat rival Flavio Bolsonaro in October's presidential election, pushing the incumbent to seek a market-friendly figure for the finance role who could ease investors' concerns.

As rumours of Lula's invitation to Trabuco started circulating on Wednesday, markets responded positively, with the real BRL gaining ground while the Brazilian stock market's benchmark index rose 6% on Thursday.
Lula has said he wants to create economic conditions that would allow the central bank to bring down official interest rates, now among the world's highest at 13.75%.

The government announced a package of fiscal measures on Nov 11 to save around 0.5% of GDP in 2027 and ensure that existing fiscal targets can be met, while honouring Lula's campaign promises of more spending on social programs.
Analysts say further cost-cutting measures would be needed to stabilise Brazil's debt and bring down borrowing costs.
Economists polled by the central bank expect the economy will grow by just 1% in 2027 while inflation is forecast to hit 5%, above the official 3% target.

Trabuco joined Bradesco as a clerk at 17 years of age and spent more than four decades rising through its ranks. He was appointed chief executive officer in 2009 and remained in that position until 2018. His tenure at the helm was marked by the acquisition of HSBC's Brazilian operations in 2015.
He has long been regarded by Lula's allies as one of the president's trusted business interlocutors and has maintained a close relationship with Lula for many years.

19a7a89567588f35: From Boo Jia Cher
My blood boiled when I read that the works ministry had received several highway proposals from the private sector, supposedly to "tackle congestion" on the Federal Highway.
It is absolutely absurd that, in 2026, the government's response to the Federal Highway receiving an "F" grade for traffic congestion is to entertain proposals for yet more tolled highways.

Every Klang Valley commuter knows this movie by heart. A highway gets jammed. Private companies step in with glossy proposals for a new elevated expressway. The government approves it, tolls go up, concrete pours over whatever green space or neighbourhood buffer is left, and for a brief honeymoon period, traffic moves.

Then, the law of induced demand kicks in. More lanes simply invite more cars. Within a few years, the new highway is just as gridlocked as the old one, and taxpayers are locked into decades-long concession agreements. And then a new highway gets proposed.
Go to the comments section of almost any post about this news and you'll find Malaysians overwhelmingly questioning the need for yet more highways.
What people want is less road expansion and better public transport. Those at the top clearly aren't listening.
We are trapped in a cyclical, illogical and deeply regressive loop of highway expansion. More highways, more cars, more congestion, and somehow the answer is always another highway.
This needs to stop.
Outdated thinking

Our traffic planners are measuring the wrong thing. Grading the Federal Highway based on "level of service" is an outdated, car-centric metric that treats a road as a pipe for moving metal boxes rather than a corridor for moving human beings.
A single lane choked with single-occupant cars gets an "F", while a dedicated lane carrying thousands of commuters on buses gets ignored.

Our traffic engineers and highway authorities urgently need to update their playbooks, education and policies. Efficiency should be measured by how many people reach their destination on time, not how many cars we can cram onto a road.
Fragmented planning hurts rakyat the most
The left hand of the government clearly does not know what the right hand is doing.

While the transport ministry is pouring billions into rail networks like the LRT3 and MRT3 and the Selangor government is trying to improve first- and last-mile connectivity, the works ministry is still entertaining highway extensions that actively encourage more driving.
Planning transport and infrastructure in rigid silos guarantees failure. You cannot tell people to take the train with one breath while building brand-new highways alongside the tracks with the next.
Say no to 'private sector proposals'

Even worse are the endless unsolicited private-sector proposals. Private highway concessionaires have no business dictating public urban planning. Their goal is not to solve traffic; their goal is to collect tolls and guarantee returns for shareholders.

This broken system of letting private companies pitch "solutions" to public congestion is a symptom of crony capitalism that, since the 1990s, has carved up the Klang Valley into a spaghetti junction of tolled roads and destroyed walkable neighbourhoods.
Public infrastructure must be driven by public need, not corporate profit margins.
A real solution
The Federal Highway connects some of the densest, most economically vital areas in the country: KL Sentral, Bangsar, Petaling Jaya, Subang, Shah Alam and Klang.
Trying to solve congestion along this spine by adding more car lanes is like trying to lose weight by buying larger pants.
If the government wants a real, immediate and cost-effective solution, it should stop studying new highways and build a proper Bus Rapid Transit system right down the Federal Highway corridor.
Dedicated, physical bus lanes – protected from private cars – can move tens of thousands of people an hour at a fraction of the cost and construction time of a new expressway.

Pair that with reliable first- and last-mile feeder buses, safe and comfortable walkways, cycling lanes and seamless integration with the LRT3 and KTM Komuter, and people will willingly ditch their cars.
Let's stop regressing
Putrajaya admits that widening the Federal Highway is too expensive and socially disruptive. Good. Apply that same logic to the private highway proposals. Reject them.

The NPE2 is already underway, carving up yet more parts of Kuala Lumpur like Sri Pantai, Angkasapuri and Mid Valley. Yet we continue entertaining more highways while the Kelana Jaya LRT line keeps breaking down and our bus system – a vital artery of any functioning, major city – remains a joke.

Politicians across the political spectrum keep playing up race and religion to divide us but where is the same urgency in addressing the issues that affect every Malaysian, regardless of race or religion? Our transport, our neighbourhoods, our air quality and the future of our cities.
It is absolutely depressing that the government, supposedly the most progressive to date, is still regurgitating the same tired, discredited policies.
Tear down the silos between ministries. Retire 1990s highway-building dogma. Stop building cities around cars, and start redesigning them around people.
Boo Jia Cher is an FMT reader.

4d8ea6dd13887b6e: VIENNA: Members of the Opec+ alliance meet Sunday to hammer out production quotas for next year despite little visibility on the US war against Iran, which has roiled oil markets worldwide.
Ministers are also to set maximum capacity levels for each country, which aim to increase transparency of their industries and will form the basis for output quotas moving forward.
But some of the alliance's 21 members are already contesting the new levels, reached after two years of analysis by an outside consulting firm, US-based DeGolyer and MacNaughton.

"For the first time, the maximum sustainable production capacities have been assessed and established through an independent and objective process," Opec secretary general Haitham Al Ghais said in mid-November.
Iraq, one of Gulf countries most penalised by the de facto shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz by Tehran since the war began in February, has reportedly rejected its capacity level as too low.
It says its maximum sustainable output is 5.2 million barrels per day (bpd), not the five million set in the new study, according to a report by Bloomberg News this week.
"Iraq has long argued that production restrictions limit its ability to finance the country's reconstruction," said analysts at the investment bank DNB Carnegie.
Market disruptions from a flare-up of energy infrastructure attacks between Ukraine and Russia are also muddying the outlook, making for fraught talks on capacity and output calculations.
"Every country with a production shortfall has a credible argument that the shortfall is temporary," Jorge Leon, an analyst at Rystad Energy, said in a recent report.
He predicted the online talks Sunday would be "one of the most complicated Opec+ meetings in years".
Quota questions
Bloomberg has also reported that Opec+ could renew for January current output quotas given the geopolitical uncertainty, citing two unidentified delegates in the group.
But Iranian attacks on neighbouring Gulf infrastructure in response to the US attacks further complicate the picture, since many countries are producing far less than their capacity would allow.
But for Leon at Rystad, "The big question is Russia - they produced 8.4 million barrels per day in October, and their quota was almost 10 million barrels per day."
That raises the possibility its quota will be lowered as the Ukraine war drags on, potentially keeping oil prices high.
Higher energy costs have already weighed on worldwide demand, prompting countries and businesses to seek alternative sources.
As a result, the International Energy Agency forecast a return to a market surplus for the fourth quarter, as supplies rise and exceed forecast demand.
In the meantime, the risk of angering members with the new capacity and output levels has grown.
The United Arab Emirates withdrew from Opec earlier this year over anger at Saudi-led quotas, as it wants to sharply increase production in the coming years.
The move was a blow to Opec's market hegemony and its ability to regulate prices.
38eeadadb38c9316: In previous seasons, Arsenal v Manchester City was an early pointer in the title race; Sunday’s clash looms like a parting of ways.
Even without the elephant in the room, the gap between the new champions and the usual champions is wide and widening.
The Gunners now have the crown and look likely to hold it for the foreseeable future. City?
Even they don’t seem to know what they are. A vastly expensive work in stuttering progress? Or a collection of condemned men soon to be put out of their misery?
No club since Sheffield Wednesday in 1904 has won its first seven games and then lost its next three.
City have drawn a couple since, but even AI would struggle to make head or tail of those stats.
Indeed, the bravura of their early-season siege mentality, which many thought was their way of dealing with the guilty verdict, has disappeared.
And while the hierarchy remains defiant, it isn’t just the players who are struggling; it’s the fans.
On Tuesday, their ground could once again reclaim the title, ‘The Empty-had’.
After boos had greeted the draw with Fulham, at the next match, the huge upper tiers were eerie vaults of disillusionment.
Napoli, recently Italian champions with old City hero Kevin De Bruyne to salute, were not unattractive opponents.
As a bonus, a couple of former United players were along to jeer. But it was a poor turnout.
It’s as if the fans have eaten all those bananas they were waving and the players have slipped on their skins.
Or is the loss of their incomparable manager, combined with two iconic players, finally catching up with them?
Yes, to lose one icon may be unfortunate, but…
Saying adios to Pep Guardiola, who won six EPL titles in 10 years, including four in a row, was akin to Nvidia losing Jensen Huang.
If the results don’t compare, the loss is similarly incalculable.
And to lose Pep’s lieutenant, Spain’s World Cup-winning captain and former Ballon d’Or winner, Rodri, as well… no team can cope with that.
Not forgetting Bernardo Silva! He was just the guy who might have held the fort for a while – past his prime, but capable of acting as a manager on the field.
Like grief, sometimes it takes a while to sink in.
With wholesale changes, come fresh faces and a ‘new manager bounce’: between them, they may bring a honeymoon period.
But now, the realisation has dawned and, without Rodri protecting them, City’s defenders are no longer so surefooted.
Even the great Gianluigi Donnarumma is no longer looking like one of the world’s best goalkeepers.
England centre-back Mark Guehi is a shadow of the solid, cool ‘Mr Dependable’ of late last season.
And, in a team short of leaders, the armband has gone to Erling Haaland, who is finding captaincy isn’t one of his attributes.
For all his monstrous power and pace, the Norwegian’s reluctance to join the action often sees him setting records for the fewest touches.
He can get away with it as a member of the rank and file, but it’s not the sort of leadership that a crisis-ridden club needs right now.
A midfield that cost circa £300m still isn’t quite clicking, although Elliot Anderson is doing his bit and Ayyoub Bouaddi is finally getting a chance.
It’s Enzo Fernandez that isn’t justifying his £ 100m-plus fee.
In cool contrast, Arsenal motor on. If they win on Sunday, they could be looking at a 15-point lead by Christmas and a stroll to the title.
They are being compared to a smooth-running machine – a north London version of ‘Vorsprung durch Technik’, the label once associated with German cars.
Ironic, then, that their one potential weakness – the lack of a top replacement keeper – could haunt them on Sunday.
The brilliant David Raya missed the Napoli game with an injured shoulder and, all week, Gooners have been sweating over how long the Spaniard would be missing.
Early fears of serious damage were soon allayed and the latest news is that he’ll make it for the big game.
But it is a rude reminder that neither Kepa Arrizabalaga, who stood in against Napoli, nor former Leeds stopper Illan Meslier, fills the faithful with confidence.
If Raya’s shoulder does improve, it can expect a buffeting inside the six-yard box.
Even if he survives in one piece, don’t be surprised to see another keeper arrive in January. Mikel Arteta doesn’t need any more sleepless nights.
But just as Arsenal are what City are not, neutrals would much rather watch City.
In Bouaddi, Ryan Cherki, Jeremy Doku, they have players with a bit of flair, elan and unpredictability, qualities that Arsenal lack.
They don’t need the awful orange kit they introduced against Napoli as yet another blatant marketing gimmick.

Don’t be surprised if the orange goes the way of the bananas – Mancunians, who can be a tight-fisted lot, won’t be taken for fools and this is yet another insult to the sacred colours of a club. When will owners ever learn?
Perhaps they are thinking they might need the money soon. They’ve probably been told there are no potential colour clashes in the second and third tiers.
If we can forget the impending sanction and appeal process for a moment, from a football point of view, it would be good if City were to pull off a surprise.
A City win would close the gap with the leaders to three points while Liverpool, who go to Everton in the early game, could be just four behind at kick-off.
We could have a title race after all, and even if it’s rendered a non-event by the end of the season, it could be fun while it lasts.

Abolfath/WikimediaThis week, on the eve the Thanksgiving holiday, the United States Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s plan to launch one million “Starmind” artificial intelligence (AI) data centre satellites. This decision reflects the convergence of a satellite boom, an AI bubble and the Trump administration’s disregard for environmental regulation. If Starmind proceeds in full, the number of operational satellites will be multiplied by a factor of 50. Space and our night skies will become vastly busier places. SpaceX’s pitch is to take the impact of data centres away from Earth, using a million solar-powered satellites to do AI data crunching in space and beam the results to Earth. But what is the impact of one million satellites, both in space and on Earth? Why has the Federal Communications Commission made this decision? And will a million satellites actually end up in orbit? Ups and downs We are currently in a satellite boom, and constellations of hundreds or thousands of satellites are a key feature. The Starlink internet satellites (another SpaceX project) is the best known example of such a constellation. Orbital rocket launches have increased to almost one per day, while the number of operational satellites is creeping towards 20,000. But Starmind represents something else. A million satellites. To get so many satellites into orbit would be a vast undertaking. If the satellites have a lifetime of five years (similar to Starlink satellites), then roughly 500 satellites would need to be launched every day. This also implies that roughly 500 satellites would eventually need to be disposed of every day. For satellites less than 2,000 kilometres above Earth, disposal usually means reentry and burning up in the atmosphere. And this has consequences. When satellites burn up in the atmosphere, their materials react with and are deposited into the upper atmosphere. We now have satellites depositing far more aluminium, titanium, copper and lead into the atmosphere than the natural quantities from meteors. Aluminium is of particular concern, as alumina can lead to the destruction of ozone in the upper atmosphere. This could increase ultraviolet light on Earth and the risk of skin cancers. It’s getting busy Increasing the number of satellites by a factor of 50 is going to change our view of the sky. If you look up during the early evening, you will see the stars your ancestors saw. But within a minute or two you will see a satellite. A point of light silently moving from horizon to horizon. Satellites are already common enough, and Starmind would make matters worse. Our view of the night skies could fundamentally change. Each satellite would be 75 metres wide and in the early evening they will be brighter than any star. And with a million satellites in orbit, there will be hundreds of Starmind satellites above the horizon irrespective of where you are. The orbital clutter comes with real risks. Satellites travel at speeds of roughly seven kilometres per second, and collisions produce clouds of debris that can produce further collisions. A nightmare scenario is the Kessler Syndrome – a runaway cascade of debris producing collisions that render low Earth orbit unusable. Of course, SpaceX is aware of the risks of orbital collisions, and it already mitigates this risk with Starlink by manoeuvring satellites away from potential collisions. However, such manoeuvres require operational satellites and it is inevitable some satellites will fail. Those uncontrolled satellites will pose a real danger. Regulator or promoter? The Federal Communications Commission has been a key regulator for American satellites. This has included regulating the radio frequencies that satellites use for communications to and from Earth, the disposal of satellites at the end of their useful lives and environmental impacts. However, under the Trump administration, the commission is taking a looser approach to regulating satellites. This includes no consideration of environmental impacts, which is reflected in the commission’s decision on Starmind. It says the commission “will not require further environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act […] for SpaceX’s Starmind system”. There are also some statements from the commission on Starmind that are, quite frankly, bizarre. For example, it claims Starmind “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”. This is sci-fi silliness. A Kardashev II civilisation would need many trillions of square kilometres of technology in orbit around the Sun. Starmind is not a stepping stone to a vast “Dyson sphere” – a hypothetical megastrucutre that would surround the Sun and capture its energy. But can it work? One reason data centres are so unpopular on Earth is their use of precious resources, including water for cooling hot computer processors. But cooling in space is harder still. When stuck in a vacuum, one can only radiate heat away. And if you are familiar with vacuum flasks, you will know this can be a slow process. Of course, it is possible to regulate heat in space, and satellites do it all the time. But they typically aren’t pouring out heat like data centres do. Google recently launched an AI demonstrator satellite into orbit and tasked it with undertaking AI calculations. But it had to have downtime between calculations to dispose of excess heat. And apart from the physics there’s the finance. Right now we are in an AI boom, with the inflow of investment being vastly higher than revenues. And the cost of deploying AI in orbit will be vastly higher than equivalent AI on Earth. If the AI boom is a bubble, then the burst can bring Starmind back to Earth. Michael J. I. ef3aa3ba32752439: WASHINGTON: Elon Musk plans to gift every child in the US two SpaceX shares, as he attempts to build public support for his satellite and AI businesses during a period of intense public and political scrutiny of the technology sector.

The world's richest person announced the share giveaway, which is worth a total of around US$18 billion, on the eve of US Thanksgiving and just hours after SpaceX won US approval on Wednesday to deploy 1 million satellites for data centres in space.

Musk is seeking to expand SpaceX's role in the AI industry, even as the rapid growth of computing infrastructure raises concern about its environmental impact and the economic and political influence of technology billionaires.
Opponents of data centre development were among the biggest winners for the Democrats in this month's US midterm elections.
"The initiative clearly helps broaden public participation in the SpaceX story," Chez Anbu, head of wealth advisory at OCBC in Singapore, said on Thursday.
"Giving children a direct economic stake in the company creates a powerful narrative around broader participation in the benefits of the AI and space economy," Anbu added.
The Federal Communications Commission said it approved SpaceX's satellite constellation proposal to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing.
Astronomers have long been concerned about such developments in space and the American Astronomical Society said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the FCC's decision.

It warned the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky.
Share giveaway
Children would receive one share from SpaceX and one from him personally, Musk said in a post on X.
In a separate post on Thursday, Musk said he would continue the programme in future years.
"I will be donating another share of SpaceX to all kids in America every year," Musk wrote.
Musk earlier in the day said the SpaceX company shares would be transferred next month.
"The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," Musk added.

SpaceX said earlier on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account, adding that Musk would personally match the number of shares donated by the company.

A Trump Account is a programme designed to give Americans under the age of 18 a stake in the stock market and help build wealth from an early age. The White House said in October it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at US$127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly US$18 billion.
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment on whether Musk's SpaceX share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts.
"What it does is build a massive, long-term retail shareholder base," said Christopher Brankin, global markets advisor at brokerage Mitrade Group.
"It builds immediate market engagement and creates a massive, financially literate client pipeline for trading platforms as that generation comes of age," he added.
Musk, whose net worth is around US$824 billion, said last month he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America. He held about 6.42 billion shares in the company as of June.
"Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X at the time.

"Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way," said Musk, most of whose philanthropic efforts have been through the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds more than US$14 billion in assets.
SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and her husband in October pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under the Trump initiative.
Musk and AI rival Anthropic have sharply different blueprints for sharing some of the spoils of the AI boom.
Anthropic, which went public earlier this month, said in October that it was committing 5% of its shares to a new fund for the "public good."
Anthropic said its initiative, worth around US$54 billion at current prices, would give it more flexibility and scale to make donations for the benefit of humanity.

"It’s likely publicity for the Trump accounts ... and also a counter to the Anthropic philanthropy noise that is likely to emerge," said Mark Tinker, chief investment officer at Toscafund HK in Hong Kong.
"It is, after all, Thanksgiving!" Tinker added.

324933b619f6eefc: One of the quiet truths, or quirks if you like, that I have observed in life is that often - though not always - the more consequential moves are the ones we don’t make.

When Barisan Nasional and PAS announced they would sit out Sarawak’s coming state election, that restraint quietly handed Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) room to manoeuvre that it did not have to ask for.
Not to be outdone, Pakatan Harapan components PKR and Amanah followed suit by announcing that they too would not contest the state election.
At first glance, it is tempting to read such abstentions as a retreat, or even an admission of weakness.
Yet step back from the daily noise of Malaysian politics, and it looks far less like surrender and much more like a calculated gift.

Its real value lies not in Kuching today, but in Putrajaya tomorrow: whether the 16th general election ends in another hung parliament, just as GE15 did in 2022, continuing a pattern since 2008 where no coalition has managed to win a majority in Peninsular Malaysia on its own.

If that happens again, what keeps GPS’s price high is simple: freedom of choice. It can pick its federal partners without being tied down to any of them. Of course, if a single Peninsular bloc manages to cross the 112-seat mark by itself, East Malaysia becomes optional and this quiet advantage loses much of its shine.

Peninsular BN’s decision to stay away comes as no surprise. It rests on an old understanding — dating back to the days when Umno crossed into Sabah while leaving Sarawak’s local parties to manage their own house — that took on new form after GPS left BN in 2018.
Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi called it continuity, and he is right: BN stayed out of the 2021 Sarawak polls too, honouring an older convention that kept Peninsular parties off Sarawak’s turf.
What makes one pause longer are the decisions of PAS, PKR and Amanah.

GPS, meanwhile, will contest all 82 state seats on its own and politely declined formal pacts with any Peninsular party - just as it did in 2021, keeping even its federal partners at a polite distance.

To ask who looks weak in this arrangement is really to ask the wrong question. Peninsular BN no longer has the grassroots machinery in Sarawak that once belonged to its former local allies, while PAS faces steep odds and limited resources. Stepping aside spares both parties bruising fights they cannot win, while leaving GPS with a clear field and zero political debts.
PKR and Amanah too – which lost all the seats they contested in the 2021 state elections - have read the signs.

The logic becomes clearer when we look at how GPS has handled Putrajaya since 2018. It has backed three prime ministers in a row - Muhyiddin Yassin, Ismail Sabri Yaakob, and Anwar Ibrahim - without ever locking itself permanently into any camp.
That kind of agility requires peace at home. After all, it is never easy to sit across a cabinet table with people who were campaigning against you in your own backyard just weeks earlier.
Seen this way, these abstentions look very much like a low-cost insurance policy: a quiet premium paid by Peninsular parties to keep the door to Kuching unlocked after GE16.

We see this not so much in what politicians say, but in what they do. In 2021, BN stepped back and left the ground to GPS; this time, PAS followed suit, citing current political developments. For PAS, restraint avoids a campaign that could rally Christian and Dayak voters against perceived Peninsular Islamic overreach, while saving energy and funds for the peninsular battle.
By stepping aside, BN and PAS enjoy the optics of goodwill while keeping their lines to Kuching open. It is the same with PKR and Amanah.

But the DAP does not have the luxury of sitting out the polls because it holds two seats and has a following in urban areas. The party has announced that it will contest 12 seats, a modest number compared with the 26 it contested in 2026.

In the end, how much East Malaysia can ask for after GE16 comes down to a simple equation: how far the largest Peninsular bloc falls short of 112 seats. When the gap is small, GPS can fill it almost single-handedly - the strongest hand any negotiator can hold. When the gap widens, other parties and rival kingmakers enter the picture, diluting GPS’ federal hold.

Even so, what GPS has gained from a divided Peninsula is measured in status, influence, and revenue alike. It has secured senior federal posts — most notably Fadillah Yusof serving as deputy prime minister — alongside steady progress on rights under the Malaysia Agreement 1963.

While the long-standing call for a 20% oil royalty remains unmet and the 1974 Petroleum Development Act remains unamended, Sarawak has secured substantial financial and regulatory gains through other means, from its state sales tax on petroleum products to a stronger role for Petros in local gas distribution.

Before 2018, East Malaysia’s parliamentary weight was channelled through BN, which leaned heavily on Sabah and Sarawak seats to stay in power. That old order crumbled when BN fell in Putrajaya and Sarawak’s ruling parties walked out to form GPS.

Where once a strong federal centre under Dr Mahathir Mohamad intervened freely in East Malaysian affairs, especially Sabah, today’s fractured Peninsular landscape has given Kuching far more room to set its own terms. That advantage stands out even more by contrast with Sabah.

While GPS swept 76 of Sarawak’s 82 seats in 2021, Sabah’s 2025 state election left a much more divided assembly split closely between GRS and Warisan. A divided Sabah finds it harder to bargain with one voice, leaving GPS as East Malaysia’s steadier broker - though if Borneo’s leaders decide to speak with one voice, their combined weight would definitely be harder to ignore.

Yet nothing in politics lasts forever. GPS’s strength rests on delicate ground: unity within a coalition anchored by PBB, restraint from Putrajaya over federal fiscal levers, and a Peninsular electorate that remains split enough to keep kingmakers in demand.

By stepping aside in Sarawak, BN, PAS,PKR and Amanah have placed a quiet wager that they will need Kuching’s goodwill when the next general election arrives. Whether that bet pays off will not be decided in Sarawak’s polling booths, but in the shifting moods and quiet choices of voters across the South China Sea.

1c260427d34f2cc1: BERLIN: Powerful German trade union IG Metall and the employers' association for the metal and electrical engineering sectors reached a framework deal on salary rises Thursday, after marathon talks held against a backdrop of industrial crisis.
Employees covered by the agreement will receive an initial pay rise of 2% from next May, followed by a 2.3% increase a year later.
They will also receive, in March of next year, a one-off payment of between 150 and 450 euros, depending on the net profit margin the group obtains, IG Metall said in a statement.
This agreement runs to the end of November 2028, thereby covering 25 months, Gesamtmetall, the umbrella organisation for the sector's employers' associations, said in a separate statement.

Trade unions and employers have also agreed on a mechanism which, according to Gesamtmetall, permits the "use of collective bargaining measures to reduce costs in return for commitments regarding investment, products or technologies which offer long-term employment prospects" in Germany.

That agreement follows two rounds of strikes which IG Metall says involved nearly one million workers, as well as marathon talks lasting more than 24 hours in Mannheim, an industrial stronghold in Germany's southwest.

This second agreement is a pilot accord initially valid for two major industrial regions, but subsequently set to apply nationwide to 3.7 million employees in the automotive, electrical and electronics, aerospace, defence and mechanical engineering sectors.
IG Metall, which had demanded a 5% pay rise valid for one year, hailed the deal through its president, Christiane Benner, as "a solid agreement in turbulent times".
Gesamtmetall described it as a "painful compromise on pay".
"We are pushing the limits of what is possible and, for some of our companies, perhaps even going beyond them," said Gesamtmetall's president, Udo Dinglreiter.
Dinglreiter nonetheless said the accord was forward-looking and would "help to secure jobs and sites".
The annual pay negotiations proved particularly tricky this year amid challenges facing parts of German industry, particularly its auto sector under pressure from Chinese competition.
A week ago, IG Metall had threatened Volkswagen with a vast industrial dispute after the manufacturer called for a rollback of several employee benefits in order to cut costs.

INDIA needs to strengthen oversight and intensify surveillance of the packaged water industry, the food regulator has said in a confidential directive to all states, days after announcing that a sample of the nation's biggest brand was found to be unsafe.

The directive, dated Nov 25 and reviewed by Reuters, comes amid consumer worries after the regulator said this week it found one sample of Bisleri, the country's biggest and best-known bottled water brand, was unsafe due to the presence of chemicals that health agencies say may cause cancer.
Bisleri has said its water is safe to consume and its testing found no problems.

The new government checks will increase regulatory oversight of PepsiCo, Tata Consumer, Coca-Cola and billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Consumer, who have all bet big on India's US$3.5 billion packaged water market.
The scrutiny will also cover the booming natural mineral water sector, which targets wealthy, health-conscious consumers.
These brands are more expensive than the standard US$0.20 variety of packaged water.

"Considering the importance of ensuring the safety and quality of packaged drinking water and mineral water, there is a need to strengthen regulatory oversight and intensify surveillance and enforcement activities to ensure strict compliance," said the regulator, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI).

The letter orders state officials to hold "regular inspections and risk-based sampling of packaged drinking water and mineral water", adding that "appropriate action shall be initiated in cases of non-compliance".
In Bisleri's case, the FSSAI has publicly said it will soon initiate prosecution proceedings against the company for non-compliance with food safety laws.
The FSSAI and state regulators have conducted many raids and pulled up companies for improper labelling, affecting restaurants such as Domino's and liquor companies including Diageo. — REUTERS

49a49942d09a5e0f: BOLOGNA: Rafael Jodar fought back from behind to send Spain past Austria and set up a Davis Cup semi-final meeting with Britain on Thursday.

Spain were leading the tie in Bologna 1-0 when Jodar lost his first set to Austrian Jurij Rodionov, but he then closed out the match and the quarter-final, losing only one game in the next two sets for a 2-6, 6-0, 6-1 triumph.
"It was very difficult for me because the first matches in tournaments are not easy," said the 20-year-old Jodar, who only made his Davis Cup debut in the qualifiers.

"I couldn't find my rhythm. In the second, the start of the second set, I started playing better and more aggressive and more solid from the baseline. I think that's what really helped me get into the match."
As Daniel Merida had earlier beaten Joel Schwaerzler 6-4, 6-4, there was no need for the doubles, meaning Carlos Alcaraz enjoyed a rest.
"It was amazing for me to give the first point for Spain. I think we have a good team here. I didn't play my best level today, but I got the win," Merida said.
Spain captain David Ferrer said Alcaraz, who has won three consecutive individual titles, including last week's ATP Finals, may be able to play in the singles against Britain on Saturday.
"I will see on Saturday. I don't know yet. But yeah, could be possible," said Ferrer of the seven-time Grand Slam champion.
Spain are bidding for a seventh Davis Cup title but their first since 2019, when Rafael Nadal played a starring role.
BRITAIN DOWN ZVEREV'S GERMANY
Britain booked their place in the semi-finals earlier in the day with a 2-1 victory over Alexander Zverev's Germany.
The world number one won his singles match, seeing off Arthur Fery, the man he beat in the Wimbledon semi-finals, 6-3, 6-2.
But that was only good enough to level the tie after Cameron Norrie had beaten Jan-Lennard Struff 6-3, 3-6, 6-2 in the opening singles.
The tie came down to the doubles, which pitted Britain's Henry Patten, the world number one in doubles, and Neal Skupski, ranked third, against the German pair of Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz.
The Britons sailed through the first set 6-2 but had to work harder in the second as it went all the way to a tie-break.
Skupski served for the match at 6-5 but a nervy volley went wide to give the Germans a lifeline. His next serve was clean and gave Britain their second match point.
This time, a brisk cross-court backhand sealed a 6-2, 7-6 (8/7) victory to send Britain into the semi-finals for the first time in seven years.
"It helps having a guy who can hit a return like that on match point," said Patten. "It makes it a lot easier for me."
"We regroup, we relax tomorrow and practise a little bit, and then get ready for whoever we play on Saturday," said Skupski.
Three-time reigning champions Italy will take on the Czech Republic in the first semi-final on Friday.

2625416c89a6479b: MADRID: Spanish authorities raced to contain potential damage to ecologically valuable Mediterranean waters on Thursday after a tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel capsized off Ibiza, leaving one person dead.

The Maltese-flagged Med Emre, a chemical products tanker travelling from the southern port of Algeciras to Barcelona, suffered the accident in the early hours of Thursday north of the popular holiday island, the Balearic Islands emergency services said.
The ship's 17 crew members were rescued, but one was later confirmed dead in hospital in Ibiza, while six suffered "minor injuries", notably hypothermia, the rescuers said.
According to maritime data tracking firm Kpler, the vessel was transporting around 66,000 barrels of refined products.
Spanish government sources said the ship was "lying keel up, which indicates that it is not currently sunk", revising an earlier statement that reported it had sunk.
Images shared by Spanish media showed the grey underbelly of a ship visible above the waves.
It was unclear what caused the accident.
A boat and a plane belonging to Spanish maritime rescue service Salvamento Maritimo had been sent to assess possible environmental damage, the Balearic emergency services added.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the government was "closely following" the situation.

Valencia maritime captain Elena Delgado said the small slick that had formed around the vessel "disappeared" at the end of the day and the ship had been secured by cable to a vessel from the Spanish maritime rescue service.
"The situation is stabilised," she said.
She added that experts would inspect the hull and submerged section on Friday morning before a decision was made on the planned salvage operation to tow the vessel.
VULNERABLE WATERS
Any pollution entering the water could affect tourism, fishing and Mediterranean seagrasses, which absorb substantial quantities of climate-heating carbon dioxide.
The area includes sites protected by the European Union's Natura 2000 network and is home to the critically endangered Balearic shearwater, said SEOBirdLife.
"Contact with the fuel may alter the impermeability and the thermal insulation of the birds' plumage, causing heat loss and hypothermia," the NGO warned.
Marine conservation group Oceana noted that the time of year was "key" for migratory species, including turtles, sharks, red tuna, pilot whales and striped dolphins.

But Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the incident was not comparable to the 2002 Prestige oil disaster, Spain's worst environmental accident.
That vessel broke into two, spilling more than 60,000 tonnes of fuel and blackening thousands of kilometres of Atlantic coastline, affecting Spain, Portugal and France.
The Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkiye in 2019, with a double hull that acted as "a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment", Diaz said.

PRODUCER Datin Dr Wendy Wong took up scuba diving to better understand the challenges faced by her cast and crew while filming 'Takdir Terakhir: Last Dive'.
The 28-year entertainment industry veteran attended the course alongside co-producer Datuk Nancie Foo, with both women diving to a depth of 7m.

"Actually, the course requires at least five days, but I could only attend for three days due to time constraints," Wong said at the recent launch of the film's poster, trailer and soundtrack singing competition.
"I thought they would take me down just 3m, but we ended up reaching 7m. I was terrified, but the experience gave me huge respect for those who work underwater."

The experience gave her a better understanding of the strict safety protocols and time limits involved in underwater filming, as well as the additional challenges posed by unpredictable weather and murky waters.
"Previously, when the crew surfaced and needed an hour to rest, I might have wondered why they could not dive straight back in.
"But after taking the course, I began to understand. I would also become anxious whenever they spent a long time underwater, knowing their air supply was limited."
Working with five divers with disabilities also required changes to the production's logistics, including arrangements for accessible accommodation and toilet facilities.
"There were many details to consider. Some hotels had been booked, but we had to change them because their facilities were unsuitable.
"We learnt a great deal during filming. If we made any mistakes, we apologise and will strive to do better," Wong added.
The film also features special appearances by Datuk Dr Ras Adiba Radzi and Fauziah Latiff, and stars Shiqin Kamal, Aniq Durar, Fify Azmi, Amerul Affendi and Sandra Lim.
Ras Adiba said: "Hopefully, this film will open a new chapter for persons with disabilities, encouraging more productions to give them opportunities to act."

3b2b7b1913cdbfc6: Chinese and North Korean state-sponsored hacking crews are among the growing number of groups known for using the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft said this week.
ARTEX is an open source, AI-powered penetration testing framework that attackers have adopted to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks, and exploitation since its public release in July.

Campaigns that have been linked to ARTEX have targeted cloud environments, IT software like ConnectWise, and financial institutions globally, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours.

Salt Typhoon is arguably the most recognizable name on the list of ARTEX beneficiaries – the group responsible for attacks on telcos AT&T and Verizon, US government systems, UK prime minister's aides, and more.
The lesser-known Crystal Typhoon – the group behind the ArcaneDoor attacks back when Microsoft called it Storm-1849 – was also named alongside it, as were North Korea's Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet.
Microsoft also named China-state-aligned Storm-0940, linked to the ConnectWise compromise, and financially motivated, Cambodia-based Storm-3358. It had previously reported both groups' use of ARTEX.
Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November. GitHub user "Autumn-27" originally published its source code with a Chinese-language interface in July.
Various forks of the repo, which was taken down in October, have meant that the same framework is available in multiple languages.
According to Infrawatch, there are more than 130 variants of ARTEX in circulation, and it is the most widely used agentic offensive framework (AOF) at present.

Like other offensive security tools adopted by criminals, ARTEX can lower the effort required to mount attacks. Experienced groups can also use it to automate repetitive work and pursue multiple avenues at once.

As Microsoft echoed this week, after the FBI and AWS issued their warnings earlier this month, ARTEX is proving to be a useful tool for the more sophisticated groups to streamline and hasten their attacks too.
It's being used to help attackers steal AI and cloud credentials at "industrial scale," as AWS put it, which provide attackers access to advanced models for free.
Microsoft says ARTEX can progress from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on its configuration and the target's defenses.

"In the past few weeks, we've reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation," its threat intelligence team blogged. "These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain.

"Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack targets, create graphs to track discovered systems and results of actions, and report back to the threat actor."

Notably, ARTEX does not offer any new attack techniques. All of the tool's capabilities were previously known to the cybersecurity world, but its value lies in the automation capabilities it offers users, chaining attacks at machine speed.

In the UK NCSC's warning about AOFs this week, it said the key strengths of this technology are its speed, its thoroughness in probing target systems for weaknesses, how it learns from failures instantly, and that it is inexpensive to run at scale.
AOFs' speed comes at a cost, however. These tools are noisy, the NCSC said, making them easier to detect in network logs and by defensive solutions.

Some examples of the attacks in which the tool has been implicated include Storm-0940's hit on ConnectWise, which enabled attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, various financial institutions in South Korea and India, UK registrar 123 Reg, and the European Commission. ®

f97ba7ee0bd5f5eb: The independent Ladybird web browser has reached an important milestone: an alpha test version. What's more, it works well. These may not be the criteria by which some will judge it, though.

Earlier this week, the developer behind the Ladybird web browser announced that Ladybird is now in alpha. We've given it a brief test, and it performed very well. It's more stable and works better than its alpha label would suggest.
There are downloads available, covering macOS on Apple Silicon, as well as for Linux on x86-64; for the latter, there's a Flatpak package, as well as native Ubuntu and Fedora packages.

It's an open source project, so you can download the source code from the GitHub repository and compile it yourself, but in an unusual move, back in June the project announced that the developers would no longer accept public code contributions.

We first mentioned Ladybird as part of our early 2022 look at its original parent project – SerenityOS: Remarkable project with its own JS-capable web browser. Both the name and the date are significant: the former is a nod to the Serenity prayer, recited at the end of Alcoholics Anonymous meetings. The date of the article is because it's well before the launch of ChatGPT at the end of 2022.

About a year and a half later, we reported that Serenity OS turns five and emits first offspring, Ladybird. Both the OS and the browser were still hand-coded, but now the browser could be compiled and run on other OSes. That freed it up to call upon external libraries which didn't exist for SerenityOS.

Earlier this year, we wrote Ladybird flutters toward Rust with a little help from AI. At one point, developer Andreas Kling used Apple's Swift language, but this year, he changed course and adopted Rust instead, using LLM tools to convert some existing code. Some will dismiss Ladybird because of this, but as our first coverage shows, the browser and its original host OS were established projects before the current wave of AI-assisted development.

Kling does use LLMs, but Ladybird is not some sloppy vibe-coded effort. The macOS download is 68.4 MB in size, which in 2026 is remarkably small. The Flatpak is larger – about 111 MB – but it also pulls in some KDE dependencies which increase its size.

We tested it on Pop!_OS. It handles sites such as The Register and Hacker News and everything else we tried perfectly, and took just 6 percent of our Dell XPS13's CPU to play full-screen HD video from YouTube smoothly. In our short testing, we saw no crashes, hesitation, or any other problems at all.
The developers nevertheless warn that the alpha can crash, some websites will not work, and they make no security guarantees at this stage.

The use of LLMs will put some people off. However, this is not the only controversial thing about the project. As we have noted in our previous coverage, Ladybird belongs to the same political wing of the FOSS movement as Omarchy, XLibre, and other right-wing projects. If the LLM use doesn't put you off, the political views may. On the other hand, as we've seen from our earlier coverage of Omarchy and XLibre, the same factors also attract others.

The modern Web is an entire complex compute platform in its own right, and currently, only three tools support it – and two of those are interrelated. The dominant engines are Google's Blink, used by Chrome and other Chromium browsers; Apple's WebKit, used by Safari; and Mozilla's Gecko, used by Firefox. Blink was forked from WebKit.

Some day, when the Servo project matures some more, it may be another. Even so, today, the first preliminary release of Ladybird means that there are now four competitive modern browser engines. That's a significant step. ®

c6c514a3477bed88: FEW healthcare ideas have the potential to deliver such immediate benefits to underserved communities as the Health Ministry's proposed cottage hospital initiative.

At first glance, the concept appears straightforward. Selected rural health clinics will be upgraded with observation wards and enhanced medical capabilities, allowing patients to receive a broader range of treatments closer to home.
Yet behind this modest proposal lies a potentially transformative shift in how healthcare is delivered to some of Malaysia's most geographically isolated communities.

In his winding-up speech during the debate on the Supply Bill 2027 in the Dewan Rakyat recently, Health Minister Datuk Seri Dr Dzulkefly Ahmad said the Health Ministry has identified four existing health clinics under the concept: Sungai Asap in Sarawak; Telupid and Nabawan in Sabah; and Tekek on Pulau Tioman, Pahang.
Their selection is no accident. Sungai Asap is about 184km from Bintulu, while Telupid sits some 125km from Sandakan.
Nabawan, meanwhile, serves communities deep in Sabah's interior, far from Keningau, the nearest urban centre with more comprehensive medical facilities.
Together, they exemplify the geographical challenges that many rural Malaysians face in accessing healthcare.
The objective is clear: improve access to inpatient care, reduce the need for long-distance travel and ease congestion at larger hospitals.
These facilities are intended to serve as a bridge between ordinary health clinics and major referral hospitals, bringing healthcare closer to the people who need it most.
While each location has its own unique characteristics, they share a common challenge. Distance.

Nowhere is this challenge more evident than in Sarawak, whose immense land area, dispersed population and vast network of rural settlements mean that healthcare accessibility remains a constant concern.
Sungai Asap was established in the late 1990s as the resettlement area for communities displaced by the Bakun Dam, including many Orang Ulu families from the Sungai Balui basin.
Today, despite the area's development, residents of Sungai Asap and other interior settlements still face long journeys to major hospitals.
Such trips can be physically demanding, time-consuming and costly, particularly for the elderly, patients requiring regular monitoring and lower-income families.
The situation is equally relevant in Sabah.
Communities served by clinics in Telupid and Nabawan frequently live significant distances from specialist medical facilities.
Rural residents sometimes have little choice but to spend hours on the road to obtain treatment that could potentially be delivered closer to home if enhanced facilities were available locally.
For patients and caregivers alike, reducing travel time can greatly improve quality of life.
Pulau Tioman presents another compelling case. Islanders contend with geographical constraints that mainland residents rarely experience.
Accessing advanced medical care often means travelling by sea and then continuing onward to larger healthcare centres.
Weather conditions and transportation arrangements can further complicate matters.
Viewed collectively, these locations illustrate why the initiative deserves serious consideration. The Health Ministry is not simply upgrading buildings.
It is reimagining healthcare delivery in places where geography remains one of the greatest barriers to timely treatment.
The proposal is also notable because it emphasises the intelligent use of existing infrastructure.
Rather than embarking solely on costly new hospital construction projects, the government is exploring ways to strengthen facilities that are already embedded within communities.
This approach could shorten implementation timelines while delivering meaningful improvements in patient care.
Equally important is the potential impact on overcrowded hospitals.
Patients requiring observation, follow-up treatment or less complex inpatient care may no longer need to travel to major hospitals unnecessarily.
This would allow larger institutions to focus on highly specialised procedures and critical cases.
Success here will ultimately depend on execution. Adequate staffing, appropriate equipment, continuous training and sustainable funding will remain essential.
Rural communities deserve not only buildings, but also quality services delivered consistently and professionally.
Nonetheless, the underlying principle is both practical and compassionate. Communities should not face unnecessary disadvantages simply because of where they live.

If successful, the cottage hospital initiative under the Madani Reform Agenda championed by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim could emerge as one of the country's most meaningful healthcare reforms.
It reflects a simple but powerful belief: quality healthcare should reach the people, wherever they may live.

9c0e60c0432004ce: THE unexpected corruption investigation into Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, once seen as a strong contender for China's highest leadership body, challenges assumptions long used by diplomats and analysts to anticipate Beijing's opaque power moves.

Experts said the Shanghai party secretary post, a position once held by both President Xi Jinping and former president Jiang Zemin, was a well-trodden route to the party's top leadership posts that now appeared much less predictable.

"There is no more straight-forward pathway from Shanghai party secretary to the Politburo Standing Committee," said Wen-Ti Sung, a nonresident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Global China Hub, adding that political loyalty was the main criterion.

The sudden announcement of the investigation into Chen, an Imperial College London graduate in environmental engineering who stood out among his peers for having spent roughly a decade in Britain, surprised both the diplomatic and business communities.
Over nearly four decades, eight former Shanghai party chiefs were promoted to the Politburo Standing Committee. Chen's predecessor Li Qiang is now premier and sits on the current committee.
Chen, 62, was seen as a strong contender for elevation to the committee in the party's leadership reshuffle during the 21st Party Congress next year.
Xi is "clearing the ground" before the congress, sweeping aside entrenched political customs and older networks to build a more ideologically aligned leadership lineup, a senior Asian diplomat said.
China's anti-graft watchdog announced on Tuesday that Chen was under investigation for "suspected serious violations of discipline and law", a euphemism commonly used for corruption in China.
He had an unusual rise through China's official ranks. An environmental scientist by training, he rose through ​China's elite Tsinghua University, Xi's alma mater, to become its president.

He entered the government as China's environmental protection minister in 2015 — just as Xi made the area a priority — before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the Politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China's financial hub.

A champion for artificial intelligence development in Shanghai and Beijing, Chen was last seen in public last week holding separate meetings with Chinese shipping company COSCO and the chairman of Swiss pharmaceutical firm Roche.

The brief turnaround between Chen's last public appearance and the probe is unusual. Senior party officials usually disappear from public view for extended stretches before an investigation is officially announced.
Xi's dismantling of reform-era term limit norms and promotion of loyalists, together with the high-pressure anti-graft drive, have disrupted established routes to elevation and succession.
In 2017, Sun Zhengcai, a former Chongqing party chief and Politburo member, who was viewed as a potential future leader, was abruptly removed and later sentenced to life in prison for corruption.

Chen is the fourth Politburo member investigated in just over a year as Xi's anti-corruption purge reaches the party's innermost circle, having already ensnared Central Military Commission vice-chairmen Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.
"Chen's purge is particularly shocking in that he poses no military threat, and doesn't deviate from Xi on major symbolic issues like ethnic policy," Sung said.
"But he got purged anyway, so far without even an explanation. The shock is bound to reverberate."
