eefc75c7c3c24ae0: Years of technical debt, increasingly complex systems, and underinvestment in IT operations have left organizations vulnerable to major outages, according to Forrester.
The analyst pointed to a seven-day stretch in November when failures disrupted Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, banking, and other critical services.
The coinciding outages provoked "a slew of conspiracy theories about cyberattacks and AI," Forrester said.

"The real culprit is tragically mundane: the culmination of decades of technical debt, the frenetic buildout of massively complex and highly interdependent systems, the concentration of risk, and the underinvestment in advanced operations."

Forrester urged technology suppliers and in-house IT teams to prioritize resilience as their systems grow more complex. Otherwise, "the tech estate will collapse like a house of cards, taking down consumer and business trust with it."

Earlier this month, Microsoft was left struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became "overwhelmed" and its attempts to fix the problem failed. Some of its services did not recover for another 24 hours.

In October, Google Cloud blamed a "power event" for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe. Affected services included BigQuery Data Transfer Service, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, and Google Kubernetes Engine.
In October last year, a major outage impacted Amazon Web Services (AWS), with even Amazon's own web page reported to be offline and dozens of other online services and websites affected.

Aviation and banking were also hit this month. A communications outage triggered a nationwide ground stop in the US on November 13, while incidents involving JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, Apple, Workday, Gmail, and other services added to the sense of widespread instability.
"Claims that these were all part of one connected cyberattack or conspiracy are highly unlikely. The real story is much more mundane," the report said.
Forrester argued that organizations have prioritized visible improvements over repairs to the underlying technology.

"Modernization investments have favored visible change over structural renewal," wrote report authors Lauren Nelson and Mark Moccia. "Organizations routinely fund new customer experiences, cloud migrations, platform consolidation, and AI initiatives because leaders can connect them to growth or productivity.

"They are less enthusiastic about updating core systems, simplifying architectures, retiring obsolete components, and eliminating fragile interfaces. The result is a modern front end resting on an aging, brittle, and increasingly interconnected estate."

Forrester's recommendations are to map dependencies, test failures and recovery under realistic conditions, and use incidents and near misses to identify weaknesses before they cause another outage. ®

f823a3b94acced32: WEST PALM BEACH: US President Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Vladimir Putin to "pull back all military aggression" against Europe, in a fresh shift in tone towards the Russian leader he called his friend just last week.
Trump said he had made the request to Putin when they met in China last week, adding that he thought it would help lead to a deal to end Moscow's grinding war in Ukraine.
Trump's comments come a day after he hosted NATO chief Mark Rutte in Florida, after which the two leaders issued a joint statement calling on Russia not to expand the Ukraine war.

"During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe,"Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Trump said he had done so "in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly."
"I really believe this is a strong possibility – Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH – and will be a Great Tribute to everyone!"

The statement did not specify which territories Trump meant – and did not specifically include Ukraine, which Russia invaded in February 2022, kicking off the largest war in Europe since World War II.
But European nations have been increasingly concerned by what they regard as Russian provocations, including three Russian cruise missiles landing in Poland last week.
In their joint statement on Wednesday, Trump and NATO's Rutte said they "discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war."
Trump, who is spending the US Thanksgiving holiday at his Mar-a-Lago resort, reposted the joint statement with Rutte on Truth Social shortly before his new comments on Putin.
In a notable contrast with Trump's recent criticisms of Ukraine for striking targets deep inside Russia, the US leader made no call for Kyiv to show similar restraint.
'DEADLOCK'
Trump's tone appeared markedly different to when Trump met Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen last week, both face-to-face and together with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
On that occasion, a smiling Trump welcomed Putin by saying "Who is he? He's my friend," before warmly shaking hands with the Russian leader.
The "friend" comment in particular renewed concerns in Kyiv and European capitals that Trump was once again pivoting towards the Russian leader he has long been close to.

Trump has often appeared more willing to blame Ukraine for Russia's invasion, and has had tense relations with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky since their televised blow-up in the Oval Office in February 2025.
The US envoys on the Ukraine war, Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and business friend Steve Witkoff, have been accused of a similar willingness to take Moscow's side.
In an interview with the German MD Meets Podcast on Wednesday, Kushner said that Putin had "showed restraint" because he had "agreed not to use nuclear weapons."

Kushner also described the Russian leader, whom he has met several times, as a "grandmaster of politics" – while calling the Ukraine conflict "a proxy war where Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia."
But he acknowledged that the issue of territory in eastern Ukraine claimed by Moscow remained a sticking point with Putin.

"What Steve and I have deciphered from having many, many hours with President Putin and from the Russian team, is that you know the territorial issue is right now a little bit of a deadlock," he said.
And he warned against any downward spiral in the Ukraine war, saying it "it won't take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively."

0d6305ef5b11368c: HERE'S why many Malaysians lose their shirts to online scammers: they are lulled in, not because they are gullible — though some are — but because modern scams are skilfully engineered to exploit human foibles.
Scammers have found a sweet spot in exploiting trust and fear, routinely using online digital technology to deceive victims.

Take the case of the Johor woman who saw a RM10 maid-booking service as nothing more than a sweet deal — only to find more than RM15,000 surreptitiously drained from her bank account after several attempts to register.
Of course, the RM10 offer on social media was a tantalising bait. Scammers know the bait won't get any bite except from the naive.
Once they manipulated the woman into providing her private banking details, they transferred out her savings to temporary offshore accounts and disappeared for good.
Online fraud has cost Malaysians RM7.33 billion since 2023. About 192,869 complaints were filed until October this year.

While tracking these dastardly schemers is almost impossible, the authorities have made some headway. Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail revealed that 75,266 people were arrested during the same period while 69,665 charges were brought against people linked to 137,699 mule accounts.
Let's get something clear: online transactions and banking are generally safe, provided users exercise care and follow security rules.
But no secure website or transaction can protect a user who carelessly enters banking credentials into a WhatsApp link.
Web security is useless if users install APK files or apps pushed by online sellers.
Banking security collapses the moment users hand over one-time password, transaction authorisation code or banking approval codes.
These are basic precautions, yet most scam victims have, in one way or another, overlooked what is a powerful security force field.
To stay safe, users must check and recheck bank accounts and cellphone numbers through the government's Semak Mule portal as a second line of defence.
Verify any "attractive" online services and offers and do not rely on social media sales pitch.

If money is suddenly siphoned, immediately call the National Scam Response Centre at 997 and alert the relevant bank to freeze access. Finally, lodge a police report. Truth be told, the person on a video call with you may be computer-generated, even if they look and sound like a best friend or close relative.
Scammers are even brazen enough to impersonate officers from the police, Bank Negara Malaysia, Inland Revenue Board, High Court or government agencies.

These days, most deal with these slick scammers by ignoring them or having the intuition to spot the deception. Building experience, education and street savviness to install a mental scam detector may be the strongest psychological defence against ruthless online fraud.

3f1d3de01d29fe0e: KUALA LUMPUR: Throughout his more than three decades in the legal profession, former attorney general Tan Sri Abdul Gani Patail played a pivotal role in several high-profile cases that captured public attention, establishing himself as a prominent figure in Malaysia's legal landscape.

Among the high-profile prosecutions Abdul Gani handled were the corruption case involving former Sabah chief minister Datuk Joseph Pairin Kitingan in 1993 and the case involving the Al-Ma'unah militant group in 2000.

The Lahad Datu-born legal figure also led the prosecution team in the case involving 30 individuals, including Philippine nationals, charged with waging war against the Yang di-Pertuan Agong and involvement in various terrorism-related activities in Lahad Datu, Sabah, in 2013.
Abdul Gani, who served as Attorney General for 13 years from 2002 to 2015, died at a private hospital here tonight due to an infection.
Attorney General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar, who confirmed the news of his death, also extended his condolences to Abdul Gani's family.
"The entire Attorney General's Chambers (AGC) extends its condolences to his family and prays that Allah showers His blessings upon his soul," Mohd Dusuki said when contacted.
Abdul Gani was also part of the prosecution team in the 2006 murder case involving Mongolian national Altantuya Shaariibuu.

He also led the prosecution of former Transport Minister Tun Dr Ling Liong Sik, who was charged in 2010 with cheating the Malaysian government in connection with the Port Klang Free Zone (PKFZ) scandal involving the RM1.08 billion purchase of land in Pulau Indah.
Abdul Gani also handled the prosecution of former Selangor Menteri Besar Dr Mohamad Khir Toyo on corruption charges relating to a property purchase.

He also led the prosecution team in the criminal breach of trust case involving RM76.4 million against former Perwaja Rolling Mill and Development Sdn Bhd managing director Tan Sri Eric Chia Eng Hock and handled the corruption case involving former Land and Cooperative Development Minister Tan Sri Kasitah Gaddam.

Born on Oct 6, 1955, Abdul Gani began his career in the Judicial and Legal Service in 1980 before serving as a deputy public prosecutor at the Attorney General's Chambers in Tawau, Sabah, becoming the first Sabahan to hold the position following the establishment of the federal Attorney General's office in the state.

Throughout his career, he held several key positions, including Sabah head of prosecution in 1991, head of the AGC's Prosecution Division from Jan 16 to Oct 14, 1994, and head and adviser of its International Affairs Division from April 1, 1995, to May 31, 1997.
He subsequently served as Commissioner of Law Revision from 1997 to 2000 before returning as head of the Prosecution Division on Feb 1, 2000.

On Nov 19, 2001, Abdul Gani was appointed Malaysia's eighth Attorney General and officially assumed office on Jan 1, 2002, making history as the first locally trained law graduate to be appointed to the position and the first Sabahan to hold one of the highest posts in the federal civil service.

The appointment marked a major milestone in his legal career, which saw him helm the country's foremost legal institution for more than 13 years before his tenure as Attorney General was terminated on health grounds, effective July 27, 2015.
However, he continued serving as an officer in the Judicial and Legal Service until reaching the mandatory retirement age on Oct 6, 2015.

Abdul Gani also contributed his legal expertise and experience through various other roles, including as a member of the Pardons Board for the Federal Territories of Kuala Lumpur, Labuan and Putrajaya.

He was also appointed an adjunct professor at the Faculty of Law of Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM) for two years from Oct 1, 2011, and served as chairman of the National Legal Aid Foundation (YBGK).
On Dec 23, 2016, he was admitted as an advocate and solicitor of the High Court of Malaya. -- BERNAMA

8030417e575dab36: Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.
Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.

Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment."

That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to."
The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried.

It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged.

Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination.
The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review.

Monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs.

And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report.
The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions.

Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model.
The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November.
"We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," said DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy.
The watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®

1ec52ab2acfcb198: Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) says "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack.
The Brisbane-headquartered company said the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents.
Its disclosure [PDF], filed with the Australian Securities Exchange today, added that it was aware that records were accessed, but cannot definitively say how many were exfiltrated.
Flight Centre is working with the supplier and incident response specialist Mandiant to establish the scope of the incident.

An initial review suggests most accessed records contained only customer names, some with basic travel information. A "very small percentage" may also include birth dates, email addresses, limited passport details, phone numbers, or, in rare cases, health or mobility information.
Flight bookings and corporate travel use separate systems and are unaffected, the company said.

"FLT values customer privacy and data security," the company said in its disclosure. "The company understands that an incident like this can be unsettling for customers who may be affected, and we apologize for any concern this causes."
Investigations remain ongoing, but FLT has already contained the attack, rotated keys and credentials, and increased system monitoring, it said.
The company said it would contact affected customers directly. Its brands continue to operate normally, and travelers should proceed with their plans.
Customers should independently verify unexpected messages about their bookings before clicking links, opening attachments, or sharing personal information.
The attack on FLT follows others that have hit booking systems in the past year, including those on Booking.com and BWH Hotels.
More recently, another Australian business, RMS Cloud, which provides booking software to travel and leisure companies, also acknowledged a breach that led to WhatsApp scams in late October.
Numerous reports of travelers being targeted with messages that contained their names and booking details hit local news outlets at the time.
Customers were sent convincing messages seemingly from the hotels they had booked, and according to Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre, the scams appeared to be financially motivated.

Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, said attackers targeting booking systems is a "familiar supply chain story" that has a greater impact than simple data theft.

Speaking generally about the risks of exposed travel records, Patel said: "Unlike a compromised email address or phone number, a passport can't be changed easily or quickly. For affected customers, the practical risk extends well beyond the immediate breach.

"Passport details combined with names, addresses, and travel history create a comprehensive identity profile that enables document fraud, identity theft, and targeted social engineering that could persist for years." ®

fb38117fe35cda86: KUALA LUMPUR: The Health Ministry will coordinate an integrated enforcement operation with relevant agencies following a viral video showing rats eating bean sprouts at a premises in Pudu Market.

"The ministry will also strengthen coordination with DBKL to ensure that market cleanliness, waste management and rat population control are addressed comprehensively.
"The ministry, through the Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya Federal Territories Health Department, has conducted an initial inspection at the premises and found that the issues raised were substantiated.
"Traders must ensure their premises are free from pests under Regulation 16 of the Food Hygiene Regulations," it said.
The ministry said compounds could be issued for offences, while premises that posed a risk to public health could be ordered to close immediately for up to 14 days under the Food Act 1983.
It reminded traders to keep their premises clean and free of pests, store food in covered containers, manage waste properly and carry out regular rat control measures.
"Any food exposed to rats or suspected of being contaminated must be discarded and must not be sold or used for food preparation.
"The ministry also advises consumers to choose clean food that is stored in covered containers and protected from pests," it said.

Last week, a video showing rats roaming around and eating bean sprouts at a premises in Pudu Market went viral.
The video, taken from a TikTok livestream, was shared by a user on Threads, raising public concern over hygiene standards at the market.
The footage purportedly showed several rats on a container filled with bean sprouts, eating its contents.

394e9f5b4e5d096c: Rackspace is shutting down its low-cost Spot cloud service after a security breach, giving customers two weeks' notice to move their workloads and retrieve their data.

In a notice posted on Tuesday, the cloud computing biz said its Rackspace Spot service will cease operations at 1700 Central Time (2300 UTC) on December 8. Any workloads still running at that point will be terminated, and customers will no longer be able to access their data.

"Following the recent security incident affecting Rackspace Spot, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the service," the company said. "Spot customers are being notified with the wind-down timeline, instructions for retrieving their data and steps to secure their environments."
Customers will have to contend with the fallout from the breach while simultaneously trying to get their applications and data off the platform.

According to a customer notification seen by The Register, the attackers used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot over a period of almost 22 hours on November 17. Rackspace only learned of the intrusion the following day, after a customer raised the alarm.
The intruders impersonated legitimate users, created pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, gained access to stored credentials known as Kubernetes Secrets, and listed nodes and storage volumes.
"With that access, they could have read any Secret in an affected user's clusters, and any Spot API token or refresh token that user held," Rackspace told customers.

Rackspace has since revoked the affected tokens and sessions, removed the pods planted by the intruders, and changed the affected platform and storage keys. Customers must also reissue API tokens, download new Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their clusters, including database passwords and third-party API keys.
Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and chief growth officer of Platform9, which co-developed Spot with Rackspace, shed some light on the root cause in a November 20 GitHub post.
"An observability system was breached using a compromised credential," Raghuram wrote. "This was obviously a critical error on our part and we are very sorry we let this happen."
Raghuram said the incident necessitated significant changes to the underlying infrastructure clusters, prolonging the outage.

Spot's selling point was cheap compute. The service operated an auction-based pricing model, allowing customers to bid for cloud infrastructure at a fraction of the cost of conventional on-demand instances. Rackspace advertised savings of up to 90 percent for customers willing to tolerate interruptions to their workloads. A permanent interruption probably wasn't what they had in mind.

Rackspace hasn't explained why it chose closure over recovery, revealed how many customers were affected, or said whether it will offer migration extensions. It did not respond to The Register's questions. ®

"He breathed his last around 9pm," he said.
Abdul Gani's second child, Faezul Adzra Patail, told Bernama that his father died at Prince Court Medical Centre at 9.15pm.
"He died due to an infection and will be laid to rest at the Precinct 20 Muslim Cemetery in Putrajaya tomorrow morning," he said.

Among the high-profile cases he handled was the prosecution of 30 individuals in connection with the Lahad Datu intrusion in February 2013.

The Australian uranium producer said on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project.

Peninsula Energy said it believes the attack is "confined to the plant and wellfield operating and control systems," and that back-office functions, such as payroll and other corporate systems, in both the US and Australia, remain unaffected.

"The company's immediate priorities have been to protect the safety of its employees, secure its operating systems, and work towards the restoration of operations in a safe and controlled manner," it said in an update to the Australian Securities Exchange.
The notification [PDF] went on to say that Peninsula Energy's investigations into the attack, including whether any data was compromised, remain ongoing.

Peninsula has not given a restart date and says it cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 production guidance. Operations will remain suspended until recovery and safety checks are complete. "Peninsula will provide further updates to the market as material information becomes available," it said.
The disclosure of additional information came two days after Peninsula secured a short trading halt, which referenced a cybersecurity incident at its Wyoming site.
The November 23 filing [PDF] dated the incident to Friday evening in Western Australia. Wednesday's update clarified that Strata detected it on the morning of November 20, local US time.
Peninsula subsequently requested a voluntary suspension of trading until the earlier of November 30 or an announcement on restarting operations and any resulting change to production guidance.
Peninsula's Lance project is a uranium mining operation, extracting the element from underground deposits and turning it into uranium concentrate, aka yellowcake or U₃O₈.
Uranium concentrate is feedstock for nuclear fuel production, typically undergoing conversion, enrichment, and fabrication into uranium dioxide pellets before use in reactors.
The Lance central processing plant was constructed to produce a maximum of 2.0 million pounds (Mlb) of U₃O₈ annually, and is licensed for 3.0 Mlb.

Peninsula previously forecast production of 500,000 to 600,000 pounds in 2027, having withdrawn its 2026 guidance earlier this year following operational problems at Lance. It now says it will reassess the 2027 outlook once operations resume. ®

ec9fbbb151b965da: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account. But neither of those common occurrences is what we’ll be talking about today. Instead, our subject broke the number-one rule of backups: you gotta keep ’em separated.

Our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a company that provides data protection and recovery software. At one point, a partner called him into a case where a Chinese vehicle parts manufacturer fell victim to a ransomware gang. Unfortunately, its backup was compromised too.

The manufacturer had religiously backed up its manufacturing execution system (MES) and SAP orders, inventory, and finance systems every night. There was even a green dashboard that showed the backup process had succeeded, and someone checked that every morning.

However, one Friday evening, crims broke into the network and found out that the backup server was joined to the same Windows domain as the rest of the network. The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a domain admin account.
So the first thing the crooks did was delete every restore point on that backup server. Then they started encrypting the production servers to ransom them.
“Every backup job had succeeded for three years,” Li said. “The failure was that the thing meant to save them could be reached with the same keys as the thing being attacked.”
The results were devastating. With the MES and SAP data both gone, the plant couldn't schedule production, ship parts, or track them.

By the time Li was called in, the plant had already resolved its ransomware situation. We don’t know whether it paid or not. The manufacturer did ask Li and his company to make sure that this couldn’t happen again.

Li’s fix was not radical, but it was instructive. He made sure that the company now keeps its backup system outside the production domain, uses unique credentials, and requires MFA to reduce the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised. He also made sure that the company keeps at least one offline backup and runs a test restore quarterly to ensure it’s prepared for emergencies.®
354cbb8728340d15: UK public sector websites are directing visitors to gambling promotions through old links to defunct local enterprise partnerships (LEPs), research by digital consultancy Digital Royalty has found.
The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies.

LEPs brought together councils and businesses to promote economic growth in England under a coalition government initiative launched in 2010. Central government funding ended in April 2024, with their core functions transferred to local and combined authorities.

Among other things, Digital Royalty builds and looks after websites, which means chasing down old links. In August, it found that a link on Surrey County Council's website led to a former LEP address now displaying casino content. It went looking for more.
Digital Royalty founder Alex De Sousa said: "Slow is usually a sign of caution and diligence, but 31 months after the LEPs wound up, it's crossed into inefficient and dangerous."

The consultancy offered The Register four examples of websites run by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), Hull City Council, Parliament, and the Local Government Association. One example is a government page about the Digital Skills Partnership, originally published under an earlier incarnation of DCMS.

The page includes a link that appears to be for the Humber Digital Skills Partnership within the Humber LEP website, but in fact takes users to a site advertising "Independent Non GamStop Casinos UK – New Casino Sites Outside GamStop." GamStop is the self-exclusion scheme designed to help people restrict their online gambling, which makes the links more concerning than ordinary website clutter.
The same link appears on the Hull City Council website under a list of Joint Committees, Partnerships and Trusts where it appears as Local Economic Partnership (Humber LEP).

An old page for the Parliament website detailing the Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy committee's Industrial Strategy report includes a footnote (135) that appears to be for the Business Central funding finder service, but takes the user to the "Highest RTP Non GamStop Casinos for UK Players."

The Local Government Association's (LGA) sustainability and waste route map included a link to the former York and North Yorkshire LEP website. The destination initially appeared legitimate but contained links promoting crypto casinos. The LGA now appears to have removed the link.
All the organizations mentioned have been contacted by The Register to offer them the opportunity to comment.

Digital Royalty checked former web addresses associated with about 70 LEPs and growth hubs, then used a backlink index to identify roughly 3,000 incoming links from public sector sites. Most were simply outdated rather than leading to gambling content.
The findings are not exhaustive: the index may miss pages, and the research did not cover other types of defunct public body whose domains may have been repurposed. ®

55fdee707b66a112: Microsoft has released an out-of-band hotpatch to fix a bug in November's Windows Server 2025 security update that could crash some servers when an IPv6 route expires.

The patch for the patch, KB5138318, addresses crashes on systems with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes. When a route timer expires, affected servers can halt with error 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE).
Issued on November 25, the corrective update takes effect without requiring a restart, according to Microsoft.

KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE means the kernel has detected corruption of a critical data structure and stopped the system. Microsoft has identified route-timer expiry as the trigger but hasn't explained the underlying coding fault.
Good to see the operating system being protected against the impact of the corruption. Less good for administrators wondering why their servers have suddenly misbehaved.

Lansweeper puts Windows Server 2025 at 7 percent of the servers it monitors, compared with 32 percent for Server 2022 and 33 percent for Server 2019. Only systems with the affected hotpatch and networking configuration are implicated.

Microsoft's Windows Server updates have not gone well over the last few months, with out-of-band updates issued in September, October, and November. An out-of-band update to deal with a problem introduced in a hotpatch (in this case, KB5131077) therefore carries with it a certain sense of inevitability.

Hotpatches are a way of getting OS security updates on a Windows Server without requiring a restart and so are, in theory, a boon for administrators keen on maximizing uptime. According to Microsoft, in addition to faster installations and better protection, there is "lower workload impact with less need to restart your machine."
Avoiding a planned restart is less of a selling point when the alternative is an unplanned crash. ®

c9d929f7e8b12eb6: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.

A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

db125f4552756b9b: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Grand Theft Auto VI is 2026’s breakout entertainment event. By the numbers, it made roughly $3.79 billion in revenue at launch, outpacing the lifetime earnings for megahit films like Avatar, The Odyssey, and Avengers: Infinity War. PlayStation called it their biggest launch of all time with over 39 million players on the platform alone. It’s the center of the current cultural zeitgeist, whether it’s because of the game’s controversy, music, love story, cultural legacy, or its accolades.

Entire households are playing GTA VI with one slight hitch: unlike movies, TV shows, or even books you can read side by side, a single-player, 40+ hour experience is tough to enjoy when you live together.

For some couples, the solution has been using more than one console or even multiple copies of the game. Married couple Meagan Kelley and Kyle Prahl typically switch between playing different games in the same room, or the same platforms in different parts of the house. The two are parents who find time to game after putting their son to bed. “The nice thing about having really young kids is they do go to bed super early,” Kelley told me. “Usually [my son] goes down and is asleep before eight, so then that's kind of like our prime gaming time.” The couple often plays different games in the same room, but for GTA VI “we're playing separately, so that kind of sucks because it's like we don't get a lot of time for each other,” Kelley said.

Although some men online have whined about Grand Theft Auto VI’s central romance, complaining about doing favors for their in-game girlfriend Lucia (“cuck simulator” being one common refrain), Kelley says the benefits to her real-life relationship are only positive. “It's funny that there's so much online discourse about GTA splitting up relationships and stuff when it's like something that can bring Kyle and I closer,” Kelley said. “Especially as we become parents and need to have more perspective on making sure that we're making time for ourselves.”

Dividing up time to play and sharing their experiences, she said, adds a new dimension to their mutual hobby. “When we are together taking care of our kid or having conversations, it's almost like book club,” Kelley said. “We share the different ways that we're experiencing the game with choices and stuff like that.”

Justin Massongill, another GTA VI player, and his wife recently had their second child. “She's taken on a lot,” he said. He bought the game for her, giving her priority to play so she could de-stress.

Massongill watched his wife play the first hour of the game; the next morning, he started his own. “We're kind of trying not to look too much at the other player's screen,” he said. “I don't want to, you know, get spoiled on things. But it's also such a massive game that what are the chances that we're going to see the same thing in the first place?”

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> Madeline Blondeau and her fiancée decided to buy their copy of Grand Theft Auto VI together. The $80 price tag wasn’t so bad between the two of them; they downloaded the game, knowing that even with a PlayStation 5 and a PlayStation 5 Pro, they’d have to divvy up time between their single copy.

“We have been alternating our schedules,” Blondeau said. Her fiancée wakes up at 5 a.m. to start her IT job. Blondeau’s shift starts around 10 a.m. “We've sort of worked this out—me playing while she is working, and then her playing while I am finishing up my shift, trying to tiptoe around spoilers.”

Even as a queer couple, there’s an equality and care for each other in the experience Blondeau finds reassuring. “I think there's these very gendered expectations in relationships in terms of who games, who is the gamer of the household,” Blondeau said. You even see it in Grand Theft Auto, she adds, where Jason, the game’s male protagonist, will be the one with a controller in his hand. “Breaking down the gendered expectations of who is the gamer in the relationship really opens up a whole avenue for not getting into fights with your partner over video games,” Blondeau said.
“It feels like two people who figure their shit out, working out equitable time to experience something they've liked their whole lives, and talk about it.”

This past weekend, Blondeau’s fiancé left to grab groceries. She came back with something extra: the Grand Theft Auto trilogy for Nintendo Switch, a consolation prize for whoever wasn’t playing their shared copy of GTA VI. “I was in the mood to play Vice City,” her partner said. “We can trade off."

— Narendra Modi (@narendramodi) November 19, 2026

Indian politician and frequent Modi critic Jairam Ramesh mocked Modi for the posts on social media. “The PM in a desperate bid to reach out to the youth has resorted to GTA V and GTA VI imagery on social media,” Ramesh said in his post. “Recall that this video game follows a criminal duo. How very appropriate.”

On Instagram, Singapore’s Land Transport Authority made fun of people who can’t navigate the country’s rail system. “If he can memorize the entire GTA6 map, he can memorize the Singapore MRT System Map,” the post said. “Bro knows every corner of Leonida but still saves the SG MRT System Map on his phone to get to Orchard. 💀”
View this post on Instagram

NATO posted its attempt at being part of the cultural conversation on Instagram. “Wanted level: NATO,” the post said above the pink-hued cross cut collage of military images in the GTA style. “The final boss of wanted levels. Think you could fend off the most successful Alliance in history? NATO isn’t part of GTA6 of course, but if it was, we think even the best gamers would have a challenge with this one.”
View this post on Instagram

In Scotland, the Scottish National Party (SNP) posted GTA 6 memes so cringe that they talked about it on the floor of parliament. On November 19, the SNP social media accounts posted AI-generated pictures of Boris Johnson and Margaret Thatcher in the GTA style. “When the loading screen so long you start seeing characters you’ve never seen before,” one image said over a picture of Thatcher pouring a bag of “Scottish oil money” into the UK treasury.

Scotland’s Green Party didn’t find the memes funny. Rockstar is originally Scottish, was founded in Edinburgh, and still maintains a significant studio there. In parliament, Green co-leader Gillian Mackay said she was proud of what all of Rockstar’s workers had done to stand up against bad working conditions and produce a work of art like GTA 6. Then she made comments about SNP leader and Scottish First Minister John Swiney.

“Last night the SNP angered anti-AI campaigners by posting AI-generated GTA memes on its social media despite huge concerns about the impact of AI and AI data centers on artists, workers, and the environment,” Mackay said in the parliament session. “Does the first minister understand why people are concerned about his government’s approach to AI and the big companies behind it.”

The SNP deleted the memes and Swiney apologized. “First of all, let me say that I don’t want to offend anyone by anything that we get up to, so if I’ve offended anyone about that, I’m sorry about that. It was not my intention,” Swiney said in the Scottish parliament. Then he said he shared concerns about AI but defended the technology’s use for healthcare.

There will be more bad posts like this. Grand Theft Auto VI hasn’t been out for even a week and the memetic landscape around it will shift and change. We don’t even know what the dominant memes for the game are yet, let alone the innovative ways posters will iterate on them. Rest assured, however, that the governments of the world are watching and waiting to post their own variations and make it all cringe.

d0bc4ea904511dad: The UK government is working "around the clock" on contingency plans for Capita contracts after the outsourcer's CEO quit and its shares plunged, a Cabinet Office minister told MPs.

Capita announced plans this week to raise around £190 million through a share issue in the first half of 2027 after warning of sharply lower profits and further costs linked to its Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) contract.
The outsourcer "should be absolutely ashamed of its performance" on the £239 million contract, Sally Jameson, parliamentary secretary in the Cabinet Office, told MPs on Tuesday.
"We have seen evidence that it has stepped up in recent months and begun to rectify the problem, but it is inexcusable that it let the situation get to this point," she said.
Adolfo Hernandez stepped down as CEO with immediate effect on Monday, with finance chief Pablo Andres taking over. Shares fell around 70 percent following the announcement.
In the House of Commons, Jameson was asked about the government's plans if Capita were unable to carry out the remainder of its contract given the outsourcer's performance on the CSPS.

"On contingency planning, it is important that we stabilize the situation and that Capita can continue to deliver the pension scheme. However, the government is working across departments, as we do in relation to all strategic suppliers, to ensure that the relevant contingency plans are in place. People are working around the clock on that," she said.
Jameson said contingency planning for the pension scheme was already underway before Monday's announcement, describing it as standard practice for major government suppliers.
She told the Chamber that the Cabinet Office was "currently arranging to meet the new CEO in the coming days" following Hernandez's departure.

The Register first exposed problems with Capita's CSPS portal last December. The site, serving 1.5 million current and former public servants, rejected login details even for newly created accounts, contained broken and circular links, and displayed dummy text.

In January this year, the Cabinet Office was forced to promise "interim support measures" for the CSPS following Capita's botched takeover, including 150 additional government staff to clear the backlog in cases.

Speaking in Parliament, Conservative MP Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the Public Accounts Committee, said there had been "some tragic and dreadful cases" since Capita took over administration last December.

"I heard of one poor lady who was living on benefits because she could not get the bereavement payments she needed after her sister's death. I have heard of a member of parliamentary staff, not far from this Chamber, who is having to delay his retirement by a year because he cannot even get a statement from the scheme."

The government has withheld nearly £10 million in contractual payments over Capita's performance. It is currently locked in negotiations over further penalties following the appointment of an auditor, first revealed in July. At the time, Hernandez apologized for Capita's performance but refused to commit to further compensation.
The National Audit Office and Public Accounts Committee have both launched probes into Capita's handling of the CSPS and its appointment as a contractor.

In February, The Register revealed a legal challenge to the government's award of the separate Synergy shared services contract to Capita. The deal covers HR and finance services across four Whitehall departments and associated arm's-length bodies. Rival bidder Sopra Steria, which owns incumbent provider SSCL, alleges Capita's bid was abnormally low and its proposed staffing raised concerns about delivery. Capita and the Department for Work and Pensions, which led the procurement, deny the allegations and say the competition was fair and open. Capita values the contract at £370 million.
The Public and Commercial Services Union is now calling on the government to scrap Capita's shared services contract with the DWP, citing the outsourcer's troubled handling of CSPS. ®

3e44a71fc7f63f38: More than eight years after Rodrigo Duterte announced the Philippines would withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), the country’s former president is about to begin his trial in The Hague. Duterte faces charges of crimes against humanity over alleged killings carried out during his deadly war on drugs. The trial, which begins on 30 November, comes at a precarious moment for the court, as the United States ramps up its efforts to undermine the institution. “Nothing has really quite approached this level of hostility we’re seeing coming from President Trump, or more particularly Marco Rubio,” explains Carrie McDougall, an associate professor at Melbourne Law School, speaking on The Conversation Weekly podcast. The US has never joined the ICC, citing concerns about politically motivated prosecutions of its nationals. But the court can investigate alleged war crimes committed by Americans on the territory of its member countries. McDougall says the US has “made no bones” about its opposition to the investigation of US nationals and the prosecution of Israeli nationals. In October, the Trump administration extended sanctions against individual ICC judges and prosecutors to the court as a whole. The sanctions threaten the court’s access to banking and IT services, as well as its ability to engage with victims and witnesses, McDougall says. The US has also been pressuring countries to withdraw from the court. McDougall attributes the decisions by Venezuela, Chad and Nauru to withdraw from the ICC to that pressure. Meanwhile, Duterte’s case illustrates both the powers and limitations of the court. “The reality is that the court itself doesn’t have any enforcement powers,” McDougall says. Instead, it relies on the Security Council – which has never used its enforcement powers to assist the court – and countries to cooperate with it. Duterte was arrested by his own country’s authorities. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu are both subject to ICC arrest warrants, but Russia and Israel have refused to cooperate in the arrest of their leaders. Neither country is a member of the ICC. While the ICC doesn’t have its own enforcement powers, arrest warrants still have some power; they can restrict leaders’ ability to travel overseas and potentially deter others from committing crimes. And, McDougall says: There is no statute of limitations, so those ICC arrest warrants can be enforced after individuals have lost power and lost the protection of their states. Duterte’s case also demonstrates that withdrawing from the ICC does not necessarily shield political leaders from prosecution, explains McDougall. Once a state … files a notice of withdrawal, it takes a year to become effective, and the ICC retains jurisdiction over any crimes committed up until that effective withdrawal date. So will the ICC survive? McDougall says the US sanctions “will impede the court’s ability to fulfil its mandate” and that the threat is “very serious.” She also warns that US attacks on international institutions risk emboldening other countries, including China and Russia, that want to reshape that order. “I think we are facing something of a crossroads,” she says. McDougall describes the ICC as the “canary in the coal mine” for the international legal order: It is required to hold to account those responsible for international crimes, particularly when we’re talking about the leaders of states. And so that puts a really big target on its back for would-be spoilers. Ultimately, though, McDougall does not expect a mass exodus from the ICC. I think a lot will actually hinge on how robustly other ICC states’ parties stand up for the court. 7ada5ec3997421d7: 1Password is reassuring customers that their vaults remain secure after an attacker breached its systems and stole account information and private source code.

The Canadian security biz disclosed this week that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, made off with private source code, and deployed malicious code to its backend services to siphon off customer information.

1Password, which began investigating the intrusion on November 19, hasn't said how many customers were affected, but confirmed that the stolen data includes names and email addresses used to sign in to the service, account identifiers, timestamps showing when users created and last accessed their accounts, and various pieces of non-secret account metadata.

The company insists the information that customers actually pay it to protect was beyond the intruder's reach. "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password said.

Arguably more troubling is the revelation that the intruder gained access to 1Password's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) infrastructure, which houses credentials used to keep its products running. The company says it has rotated or revoked potentially exposed credentials and that neither its apps nor its browser extensions were affected.

1Password hasn't explained how access to an employee's GitHub account enabled the attacker to deploy malicious code to its backend services, nor has it detailed the extent of the attacker's access to its software build and distribution infrastructure. The company did not respond to The Register's questions.

The miscreant also got their hands on tokens embedded in emails sent to some customers as part of account invitations, provisioning, and recovery processes. These tokens aren't enough to access an account on their own, according to 1Password, as users must also authenticate via single sign-on or enter a verification code sent to their registered email address.

The company says it specifically notified the small number of users with affected provisioning or recovery processes underway. It found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed provisioning tokens.

Still, the breach has prompted the password management biz to beef up those verification codes, replacing the six-digit numeric variety with ten-character alphanumeric codes to make brute-forcing them considerably more difficult.

1Password has booted the intruder out of its GitHub environment, revoked the stolen token, and rolled back the affected backend services to clean versions of the code. It's since shored up security around its development infrastructure and employees' devices, and brought in outside security specialists to review its handiwork.

The incident recalls the first stage of LastPass's 2022 breach, when an attacker compromised its development environment and stole source code. Information obtained in that intrusion helped enable a second attack that exposed customer vault backups, including encrypted passwords.

The UK Information Commission's Office slapped LastPass with a £1.2 million ($1.6 million) fine last December over the incident, which compromised the personal information of up to 1.6 million UK users. Among the regulator's gripes was that LastPass had fallen short of the higher standard of security expected of a company entrusted with people's passwords.
Customers aren't being asked to change their account passwords or Secret Keys, neither of which 1Password stores, although the company is warning users to be on the lookout for phishing attempts.

A list of email addresses belonging to people known to use a particular password manager is a handy thing for a phisher to have, especially when said password manager has just given them a plausible pretext for getting in touch. ®
38bebe8b01f35c10: TOKYO, Nov 26 — US President Donald Trump’s fresh tariff blitz aims to pressure Asian countries into sealing trade deals with Washington so as to avoid unfavourable duty rates, analysts said on Thursday.
The proposed levies announced on Wednesday affect a range of nations in the region, from long-time US competitor China to allies like South Korea and Japan.
They could result in rates of up to 20 per cent on exports from the targeted countries, but face a period of public comment before taking effect, at the earliest in January.

The announcement came after Washington concluded a months-long probe into alleged excess production in the targeted economies, which itself followed the US Supreme Court’s decision ruling that Trump’s previous “Liberation Day” duties were illegal.
But “several of these economies already have prior negotiated tariff rates with the US, which would effectively cap the appliable rate”, said MUFG economist Lloyd Chan in a note.
The US has also indicated that the new tolls will not stack on top of other tariffs already imposed on 60 countries over forced labour concerns. Instead, the higher rate will apply.
“In all, that should help contain the incremental tariff shock, assuming prior negotiated commitment remains in place,” Chan said.
However, it does mean that Washington has established higher tariff ceilings that can be activated “should trade negotiations or existing commitments break down”, he added.
Stephen Brown of Capital Economics also noted that “the US has left open its ability to hike these tariffs if trade agreements fall apart”, particularly with China.
Room for leverage
In Beijing’s case, the new levies stand at 20 per cent, meaning the total rate could jump to 40 per cent if its current trade truce with Washington, set to expire in January, is not extended.
Such a scenario “could take the two largest economies back to the trade wars of 2025”, Josh Lipsky, of the Atlantic Council, wrote in a note.
However, that is not something Trump wants, he added.
Instead, the US president is banking on an extension of the truce, though this is “far from a sure thing”, Lipsky added.
Trump and China’s Xi Jinping are set to meet next in December at the G20 summit in Miami.
“Tariff wars and trade wars are not in anyone’s interest,” Beijing’s foreign ministry warned on Wednesday.
Other Asian economies, also in Trump’s crosshairs due to significant trade imbalances, are likewise under pressure.
Vietnam faces a maximum additional tariff of 35 per cent on goods, which could be cut to 20 per cent if a trade deal is reached.
Hanoi reiterated on Wednesday that it has made commitments under a framework agreement in October 2025, and that it is working for a final deal “as soon as possible”.
India uncertain, Taiwan bullish
India said on Wednesday that trade concerns should be addressed in ongoing talks with Washington for a bilateral trade deal.
The US has proposed a 17 per cent rate on Indian goods, rising to a possible 25 per cent if no deal is reached.
The countries reached an interim agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.
But the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s levies days later, fuelling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.

“By deploying a dual-rate structure — threatening steep baseline tariffs against countries that refuse a pact while offering lower rates to those that sign — Washington reclaims the bargaining power to impose duties at will and extract unilateral concessions,” Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative, told Bloomberg News.
In contrast with Indian uncertainty, Taiwan, which reached a deal with Washington in early 2026, struck a reassuring tone.

“We are confident that when tariffs are finalised early next year, we will return to a 15 per cent non-stacked tariff under the agreement between Taiwan and the US,” Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun told a news briefing. — AFP

18cfa8107ce61490: SC25 in St. Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall. Pipes, pumps, manifolds, quick-disconnects, and a lot of people who clearly spend more time thinking about pressure drop than floating-point. I kept expecting to see a booth selling industrial fire hoses. Chicago is a much bigger building – McCormick has roughly four times the exhibit space St. Louis had – so the pre-show question was whether SC26 will still look like that or whether the hall is large enough to dilute the effect.
If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago. The heat problem didn't get smaller just because the building got bigger.

We also saw a lot of new companies displaying their cooling wares at SC26. I follow this stuff closely and see two broad trends. First: consolidation with big industrial suppliers buying up the liquid cooling pioneers. Second: anyone with an angle is heading into the market. Both trends were visible on the floor in Chicago, and everyone had something to say about higher inlet temperatures, whether they have a real story or not.
Game changing news

The real news, though, is a number Nvidia dropped earlier this year: 45°C (113°F) liquid inlet temperature for their parts. That's not a small tweak. Most liquid-cooled systems have been living in the 30-35°C (86-95°F) world because that's what the chips would tolerate. Jump to 45°C (113°F) and a whole bunch of datacenters that currently need chillers suddenly don't.

If AMD, Intel, and the Arm folks can match it – and we’d be shocked if they aren't already working on exactly that – then free cooling stops being a cool climate thing and becomes the default for a lot of places.

Rooftop dry coolers can reject nearly any incoming fluid temperature and bring it below 45°C (113°F). There are few places in the world where ambient temperatures approach 113°F, and for the hours when outside temps spike, adiabatic assist is available. This is where water is trickled through a mesh surrounding the dry coolers, which drops the effective temperature another 10–20 percent.

So, in our new cooling world, there are two closed loops: one taking heat from the server gear and then passing it to a second, different loop that takes the hot water to the roof, cools it, then brings it back again.

What's missing here? It's the chillers. You won't need them anymore. These are essentially huge rooftop refrigerators that cool water even more after the dry cooling. They're expensive, need a lot of maintenance, gulp electricity and are thankfully unnecessary now for new datacenter builds.

The power and water savings are not trivial. Legacy designs that rely on chillers and open evaporative towers commonly put 20 percent to 40 percent of total facility energy into cooling. A large share of that is the chiller plant itself – compressors, pumps, and cooling-tower fans. Move to dry coolers running at 45°C (113°F) inlet and that slice collapses.

Published estimates and vendor modeling for high-temperature liquid loops put the reduction in cooling energy in the 50 percent to 70 percent range versus a conventional chiller-plus-tower plant, which translates into a 10 percent to 20 percent drop in total datacenter power – depending on the starting PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) and climate.

Water use falls even harder. Traditional evaporative towers can consume millions of gallons a year at a mid-size site. Dry coolers use essentially no outside water in normal operation; adiabatic assist only wets the mesh during the hottest hours, cutting annual water consumption by 80 percent to 95 percent in most climates. Those are the numbers that make the 45°C (113°F) inlet such a big deal.

The same shift also changes the economics of the mechanical plant itself. A chiller plant is not just an operating cost; it is capital equipment that has to be sized, installed, maintained, and eventually replaced. Dry coolers are simpler, cheaper to install, and have far fewer moving parts. When the chips will accept 45°C (113°F) fluid, the business case for putting a mechanical refrigeration plant on the roof of a new build gets hard to defend in most climates. That is the part that has not yet fully registered outside the cooling specialists.
Getting to 45°C isn't free

Designing systems around these higher inlet temperatures still takes real engineering work – sizing the loops, choosing the dry coolers, and making sure the facility can run at the new set points without surprises. Existing buildings add another layer. Many were built with pipes, pumps, and heat exchangers sized air cooling or lower temperature liquid. Raising liquid inlet temperature means checking flow rates, pressure drops, and making sure the existing set-up delivers.

At SC26 I had meetings with a couple of companies that do this work and buttonholed more in their booths. My top-of-mind questions were: Are the 45°C (113°F) inlet temps for real? Yes, they are, and are being used as a design basis to an extent – they need to leave headroom, of course.

Any news on whether the other chipmakers are going to hit the Nvidia number on inlet temperature? Attendees were closed-lipped on this one. Nothing public from the other vendors (AMD/Intel/Arm). But on the cooling vendor side, they are happy to see the increase and will comply.

My instincts are telling me that the other chipsters may have been caught flatfooted by Nvidia's 45°C stake in the ground, but those same instincts also tell me that handfuls of Peanut M&Ms healthy snacks. I’ll nose around more.

There's real money at stake here from a TCO standpoint. One cooling vendor reports that their initial testing shows 3 percent to 4 percent cooling energy cost decrease for every additional 1°C inlet temperature increase. That's a significant number at scale.
We're approaching a point where industry advances are answering many of the objections (the real ones, not the hysterical ones) raised by the anti-data center movement.
