a65f509715b5b41f: Patrick T. Fallon/GettyIt’s hard to think of Nvidia without picturing Jensen Huang. Rarely seen without his signature black leather jacket, Huang has led chipmaker Nvidia since co-founding it in 1993, turning it into a central player in the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Earlier this month, Huang resigned as president, chief executive officer and a member of Nvidia’s board, in the wake of a bombshell scandal involving affairs and alleged corporate espionage. Days later, the board linked his departure to “personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”. It said it did “not intend to reinstate” him. This week, however, it voted unanimously to bring him back, following a remarkable intervention by US President Donald Trump. Many analysts have already weighed in on why the US government intervened. But there’s a deeper, more fundamental question here about corporate power. If a chief executive is seen as too valuable to lose, can a company’s board still hold them to account? If it can’t, what exactly is the board for? Read more: Trump had 4 reasons to ‘convince’ Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang. Here’s why it matters globally The ‘key person risk’ Sometimes, the “hero” leader of a company can become its biggest vulnerability. In corporate governance, this is called “key person risk”. It is the danger a company comes to depend so heavily on one person that losing them would do serious damage. This problem often grows out of success. A founder who builds a business and shapes its culture becomes its public face. Staff, customers and investors start to see the person and the company as one. Think of Steve Jobs, co-founder and longtime chief executive of Apple, or even the fictional media magnate Logan Roy in the TV series Succession. Nvidia itself recognised this risk before Huang’s brief removal. Its 2026 annual report warned the company was “highly dependent on the services” of its longstanding executive team, and that failing “to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions” could hinder its success in the long term. Despite this, when Huang left, no permanent successor was ready. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, stepped in temporarily while the board searched for a replacement. Who’s watching the boss? So, what is a board actually for? Shareholders can’t supervise the managers in a large company like Nvidia; instead, they elect a board of directors to do it for them. While the board isn’t involved in daily operations of the company, it approves big decisions, watches the chief executive and, if needed, replaces them. It’s designed to solve something economists call the “principal-agent problem”. A company’s managers (the agents) may put their own interests ahead of the owners’ (the principals). That’s why independence matters. Independent directors don’t work for the company and have no close financial or personal ties to its management. Filling a board with the chief executive’s employees (such as other senior executives) and friends is like letting students mark their own exams. Nvidia’s U-turn shows how fragile independence can be. A committee of independent directors is still investigating claims that Huang was targeted by China’s top spy agency. Huang is also due to answer questions from US lawmakers behind closed doors on December 1. The board brought him back before either had finished. The board acknowledged that its decision to rehire Huang was heavily influenced by the US government. It said it was “confident” Huang posed “no national security risk”, based on “input from senior US government levels”. We have seen other boards cave under pressure before. In November 2023, OpenAI’s board fired its chief executive, Sam Altman. Within days, nearly all of its 770 staff threatened to quit. Altman returned, and the board that sacked him was replaced. Independent of whom? On paper, there are strong safeguards to protect board independence. For example, the Nasdaq stock exchange, where Nvidia is listed, requires most directors to be independent. The committees that check a company’s accounts and set executive pay must be fully independent. But these rules fall short in three ways. First, the board itself gets to decide who counts as “independent”. In 2024, a US court found several Tesla directors who approved Elon Musk’s pay deal were too close to him to be independent. A higher court later restored the deal on other grounds. Second, directors get much of their information from the very executive team they are meant to be keeping in check. And third, a board without its own independent leader often struggles to push back against a chief executive. Nvidia only appointed its first-ever board chair on the day Huang resigned. Why no one should be irreplaceable “Key person” risk can’t be removed, but it can be managed. Boards can train a credible successor, appoint an independent chair before a crisis hits, and finish investigations before deciding. They should also explain their reasoning in public. An independent board that isn’t able to fire and replace a chief executive is just a cheer squad – not the umpire it’s supposed to be. This matters well beyond Silicon Valley. Many retirement funds around the world own shares in Nvidia. For the sake of protecting millions of people’s long-term savings, retirement funds and others representing shareholders should be advocating for better governance than we’ve seen at Nvidia so far. Anish Purkayastha does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

3fa3cdca329aa8c5: Ironi adalah perkataan yang sepatutnya sinonim dengan politik. Apa tidaknya, musuh boleh jadi kawan, kawan boleh jadi musuh, orang yang ditentang reformasi dia pula yang memenangkannya.

Dulu tahun 80-an dan 90-an, saya menyokong Dr Mahathir Mohamad 100%. Kemudian saya amat membenci beliau dari tahun 1997 hingga 2016, berlatarkan reformasi ketika itu. Apabila beliau bekerjasama dengan Pakatan Harapan, saya menyokong Mahathir sehinggalah 2020 apabila beliau ditikam belakang oleh parti sendiri -- sedap juga melihat Mahathir ditikam oleh gengnya sendiri. Sekarang saya menulis pula bahawa pandangan beliau tentang PAS jelas lebih benar berbanding tanggapan saya terhadap parti itu, sejak dari 1997 hingga PAS berkawan dengan Umno dan Najib Razak.

Tujuan saya menulis artikel ini adalah kerisauan saya tentang nilai dan sikap orang Melayu. PAS kini memperlihatkan nilai yang cukup membimbangkan tetapi yang peliknya tak ramai agamawan akademik yang menegur secara langsung. Maka terpaksalah saya mencari orang yang orang Melayu hormat lebih daripada orang kerdil dalam politik seperti saya untuk memberi kesedaran tentang bahaya parti yang menunggang agama demi kuasa.

Baru-baru ini kita membaca tentang seorang pemimpin PAS yang mengatakan pemberian derma untuk membayar denda RM50 juta yang dikenakan ke atas seseorang yang didapati bersalah dalam kes penyelewengan dana adalah perbuatan yang dapat pahala. Sebelum ini, rasanya tahun lepas, PAS menjayakan tabung jihad untuk membayar saman fitnah untuk seorang wakil rakyatnya. Kedua-dua kes penyelewengan dana dan fitnah ini boleh kita telusur tanpa was-was. Kemudian, kita dapat tahu bahawa orang yang memfitnah serta orang yang pecah amanah dan salah guna kedudukan tidak menyatakan penyesalan, jauh lagi berikrar tidak akan mengulang lagi perbuatan.

Tidak cukup dengan itu, kita juga mendengar PAS menggunakan istilah munafik semasa membahaskan Belanjawan 2027 yang dibentangkan perdana menteri baru-baru ini. Ada pula presiden PAS menyifatkan Perjanjian Keyakinan dan Perbekalan yang ditandatangani antara kerajaan dan beberapa Ahli Parlimen pembangkang sebagai pendekatan dajal. Kita sudah pun maklum tentang peristiwa membaca doa qunut nazilah terhadap orang yang tidak sehaluan dengan PAS. Isu mengkafirkan orang sudah pun tercatat dalam sejarah negara.
Maka itu saya menyingkap dua ucapan Mahathir dalam Perhimpunan Agung Umno pada 1984 dan 1999. Dalam ucapan 1984, Mahathir mengecam PAS seperti berikut;

"Umno adalah parti politik orang Melayu. Oleh kerana orang Melayu semuanya beragama Islam, maka Umno dengan sendirinya menjadi parti orang Islam Semenanjung Malaysia dan berjuang untuk agama Islam. Tetapi Umno bukan hipokrit dan berpura-pura menafikan yang ia adalah parti orang Melayu seperti yang dibuat oleh sebuah parti lain.

"Umno dengan jelas mengakui yang ianya parti kebangsaan Melayu di samping menjadi parti Islam. Menafi hakikat ini akan menjadikannya hipokrit atau munafik -- dan orang munafik tidak menjadi orang Islam yang jujur.

"Tidak ada cara yang lebih berkesan untuk mengekalkan kelemahan orang Melayu daripada menggunakan orang Melayu sendiri untuk melawan orang Melayu. Dengan tertubuhnya PAS maka terbentuklah alat utama musuh orang Melayu. Malang bagi mereka, kebanyakan daripada orang Melayu dapat meneka strategi pecah-belah ini dan telah terus menyokong Umno.

"Sekarang ini usaha ditumpukan kepada melemahkan semangat kebangsaan Melayu dengan mendakwa Islam menentang kebangsaan. Bahawa kebangsaan orang Melayu adalah satu alat mempertahankan diri bagi orang Melayu yang semuanya Islam, sama seperti kebangsaan Mujahidin mempertahankan orang Islam Afghanistan, dan tidak menjadi satu keangkuhan yang mengenepikan agama Islam dan orang Islam lain, tidak disebut. Mereka yang mendakwa bahawa mereka cuma mengakui keislaman mereka dan kononnya menolak semangat kebangsaan Melayu, tidak pula berani mempertahankan orang yang seagama dengan mereka di Afghanistan, atau di Lubnan atau di lain-lain tempat. Keislaman mereka terhad kepada kegiatan di Malaysia sahaja di mana kebangsaan Melayu Umno dapat memberi perlindungan kepada mereka. Sifat mereka ini adalah sifat hipokrit atau sifat talam dua muka. Dan mereka adalah begitu fanatik kepada parti mereka sehingga mereka tidak menyoal sama ada pendirian parti mereka baik atau tidak. Mereka inilah yang sebenarnya dari golongan asabiyah."
Jelas siapa sebenarnya hipokrit yang dimaksudkan Mahathir ketika itu. Namun demikian kita dapat merasai kesamaan mesej tersebut dalam tindak tanduk PAS ketika ini.

Dalam petikan kedua ucapan yang sama, Mahathir mempertikaikan PAS bahawa mereka sahaja yang tahu Islam manakala orang lain seperti Umno ketika itu yang juga mempunyai barisan pemimpin seperti Anwar Ibrahim tidak mencerminkan Islam sebenar.

"Sebagai satu lagi usaha untuk menentukan kejayaan orang Melayu, kita telah berusaha menerapkan nilai-nilai Islam. Kita tidak syak bahawa nilai-nilai Islam akan menjadikan orang Melayu orang yang lebih berjaya di dunia dan di akhirat. Pentadbiran yang diasaskan kepada nilai-nilai Islam tetap akan menjadi pentadbiran yang kukuh, adil dan berjaya.

"Di sini nilai-nilai Islam tidak bermakna rupa bentuk dan kebudayaan Arab yang menjadi tumpuan setengah-setengah orang Melayu di Malaysia. Memang benar rupa-bentuk boleh dijadikan simbol Islam dan ditiru dengan mudah. Tetapi rupa-bentuk tidak akan membawa kejayaan kepada kita. Yang akan membawa kejayaan ialah amalan nilai-nilai Islam seperti amanah, disiplin, taat setia, rajin dan tekun, bersaudara antara orang-orang mukmin, berani kerana benar, bertoleransi dan bertimbang rasa, adil, insaf dan syukur dan lain-lain lagi nilai yang mulia yang tidak begitu mudah diamal atau dipamerkan.

"Dalam ucapan saya di perhimpunan agung 1982, saya telah menjelaskan tentang hasrat kerajaan untuk menerapkan nilai-nilai Islam ke dalam pentadbiran negara. Maksud saya ialah supaya kita akan mentadbir dengan amanah, jujur, disiplin, setia, bertanggungjawab, cekap, bersih, dan lain-lain lagi nilai Islam yang akan menjadikan pentadbiran negara ini satu pentadbiran yang berkesan dan adil.

"Malangnya hasrat ini telah dijadikan alasan untuk ajaran dan tindakan yang membawa masalah dan mengganggu pentadbiran. Islam sengaja digambarkan oleh kumpulan-kumpulan tertentu sebagai agama yang tidak toleran, sehingga kakitangan kerajaan yang beragama Islam dilarang dari berkawan dengan yang bukan Islam dan melawat mereka di hari kebesaran mereka. Tumpuan diberikan bukan kepada soal khidmat yang baik dan pegangan kepada janji dan ikrar, tetapi kepada soal haram-halal, di mana tafsiran dibuat mengikut nafsu.

"Demikianlah ekstremnya tafsiran yang dibuat sehingga ada pegawai yang tidak mahu menyentuh kertas yang ada tertulis di dalamnya perkataan 'babi'. Ada yang sanggup menukar arahan ketua kerana tidak secocok dengan fahaman ekstrim mereka. Ada yang berpendapat bahawa penerapan nilai Islam bermakna memakai cador, tetapi kerana gaji, mereka masih sanggup bekerja di pejabat."

Dalam petikan ucapan 1999 sewaktu era reformasi dan Mahathir berseteru dengan Anwar, beliau juga menyerang PAS yang bekerjasama dengan DAP. Di sini Mahathir menyebut bahawa PAS adalah parti yang boleh mengubah haluan mengikut citarasa sendiri dan memfatwakan apa saja bagi niat politik kuasa;

"PAS adalah sebuah parti yang mudah menukar haluan mengikut kepentingan semasa. Demikian pada mulanya PAS mendakwa bahawa orang Islam yang bekerjasama dengan orang bukan Islam menjadi kafir dan dengan itu PAS menolak kerjasama dengan bukan Islam. Kemudian PAS menyertai Barisan Nasional dan bekerjasama dengan orang bukan Islam dalam BN. Pada masa itu PAS tidak lagi mendakwa bahawa orang Islam yang bekerjasama dengan bukan Islam menjadi kafir. Ternampak jelas tafsiran agama oleh PAS boleh ditukar untuk kepentingan semasa.

"Kemudian PAS keluar daripada BN dan menganggap orang Umno tidak Islam sehingga ahli dan pemimpin PAS sanggup sembahyang berasingan di masjid yang sama dan membina masjid lain bagi orang PAS. Tetapi apabila pilihan raya hampir tiba, PAS mengadakan pakatan dengan DAP yang bukan Islam. Bagi PAS, orang Umno yang Islam tidak boleh dijadikan sahabat seperti PAS bersahabat dengan orang bukan Islam dalam DAP."
Kini kita melihat kebenaran kata-kata Mahathir itu apabila PAS menghumban Bersatu dan memeluk Umno serta kini memperjuangkan nasib Najib.
Akhir sekali Mahathir menyinggung isu PAS yang suka merendahkan umat Islam lain dan menampakkan diri mereka seperti orang Islam terpilih dan special dalam ungkapan seperti di bawah;

"Hari ini kita lihat kesan daripada kesanggupan PAS bekerjasama dengan syaitan. Nik Aziz dan pemimpin PAS yang lain sanggup mengeluarkan kata-kata yang buruk kononnya Badawi Malaysia menjadi gembala babi. Sindiran ini tidak mempunyai asas kerana Abdullah Badawi telah ditugaskan untuk menyelaraskan kerja-kerja menghapuskan penyakit JE (Japanese Encephalitis), bukan untuk menjaga babi. Lebih dari itu dakwaan dibuat kononnya tuhan mencarut dan kita orang Islam patut mencarut.

"Tetapi orang PAS akan terus setia kepada PAS kerana mereka fanatik dan taasub kepada parti mereka. Mereka adalah daripada kumpulan asabiyah, kumpulan yang terlalu fanatik dalam menyokong kumpulan mereka sehingga tidak mengambilkira kumpulan mereka baik atau jahat, benar atau salah. Demikian apabila ahli PAS berkhalwat, mereka tidak bersalah. Kesalahan hanya ada pada orang lain, tidak sama sekali kepada orang PAS dan parti PAS. Inilah orang yang keterlaluan dan termasuk dalam golongan asabiyah."

Mahathir cukup benar bacaannya tentang PAS serta ahli-ahli yang mempunyai sentimen kefanatikan yang cukup besar. Sikap ini bukan sahaja ada pada golongan tidak berpendidikan tinggi, golongan kelas pertengahan dan akademik berjawatan tinggi di universiti pun sama saja kefanatikan mereka.

Saya menyokong PAS selama 20 tahun, sebagai ahli dan penyumbang wang serta pemikiran. Saya juga membenci semua tuduhan Mahathir terhadap PAS dahulu, tetapi hari ini saya terpaksa mengakui bahawa bacaan Mahathir tentang PAS ternyata benar dan saya dapat melihat dengan sendiri kebenaran tersebut hari ini.

Sebagai ringkasan ucapan Mahathir di atas, beliau membawa mesej tentang bahaya kepercayaan fanatik kepada agama dan parti politik yang boleh merosakkan orang Melayu dan pembinaan negara bangsa serta pembangunan ekonomi untuk semua.

ec7b63860efa33d3: Malaysia Athletics cannot claim to have put its house in order while Karim Ibrahim remains president of one of its affiliates despite his disqualification by World Athletics.
Karim is not only the former president of Malaysia Athletics. He also heads Perak Athletics Association (Perak AA), a member of the national body.
MA’s endorsed constitution appears clear on the eligibility of people in such positions.

Article 13.2.8 bars anyone disqualified, removed or suspended by MA, the Olympic Council of Malaysia, the Asian Athletics Association, World Athletics or another local or international sports authority from being nominated, elected, appointed or holding office as an affiliate’s office-bearer, council member or committee member.
That restriction remains until the relevant authority lifts the sanction or the person succeeds in an appeal.

World Athletics has disqualified Karim. He has not appealed, and the sanction remains in force. The provision expressly covers office-holders in MA’s affiliates, not just those serving on its national executive council.

His position in Perak AA therefore puts MA’s responsibility to enforce its own constitution squarely in focus. The national body cannot leave the state association to decide whether it wishes to observe a rule that binds its members.
Affiliation carries obligations
MA’s authority to demand compliance rests on more than the eligibility provision.

Article 18.3 gives its constitution and by-laws precedence when they conflict with those of its members. Article 18.4 requires MA, its affiliates and people holding positions under its rules to comply with Malaysian law and the regulations of OCM, the Asian Athletics Association, World Athletics and other relevant international sports bodies.
Together, these clauses establish the obligations that come with membership. A state association cannot claim the benefits of affiliation while disregarding the rules governing the sport.
There is, however, a difference between requiring an affiliate to comply with MA’s constitution and automatically rewriting its registered rules.
If Perak AA’s constitution conflicts with the national one, it may still have to follow its own amendment procedures and the requirements of Malaysian law.

That does not excuse inaction. MA should formally notify Perak AA of the eligibility provision, explain its application and require the state body to address the position of its office-holders in accordance with the rules.

The same scrutiny should extend to every affiliate. MA must identify conflicting provisions or practices in state associations and set out what they need to do to comply. It should not wait for another dispute to expose weaknesses in its governance.
The council must be prepared to act
The executive council has a clear role in this process.

Article 18.1 gives it sole authority to interpret MA’s constitution and by-laws. Article 16.2 provides a mechanism for disputes between MA and its members, or between members. The council may seek OCM’s advice before making its final decision by majority.
These provisions give the council a way to resolve disagreements. They also place responsibility on it to address non-compliance.

That does not give the council licence to impose whatever penalty it chooses. It must identify the relevant breach, follow the proper procedures and give the affiliate a fair opportunity to respond. Any action must also comply with Malaysian law.
But procedural requirements should guide enforcement, not become an excuse to avoid it.

In Perak AA’s case, the council should establish the facts, determine the application of Article 13.2.8 and set out the steps needed to bring the state body into compliance. If Perak AA disputes the interpretation, the constitution provides a route to resolve the matter.

The same standards must apply to every affiliate. Perak AA should not receive special treatment because Karim once led the national association. Nor should any state body enjoy an exemption because of its influence or leadership.

This is not about stripping state associations of their autonomy. They should remain free to run their programmes, develop athletes and manage their affairs. But autonomy does not mean freedom to disregard the rules of the national and international sport.
The Karim episode exposed the consequences of a national body allowing its own rules to fall short of international requirements. MA must not allow that failure to continue at state level.
Its constitution gives it the authority to demand compliance. The executive council must now show that it has the resolve to use it.

b879995cf1e26209: Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.

The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001 and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.

The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.
44f6d57a797b432e: According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.

Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Henderson wrote.

The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company's post-incident report, dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.
1479a2d5f1158c80: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field."

73155e0b93283f09: Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water.

The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23. Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died.

On November 23, Pennsylvania's health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death, an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child. New York has also reported a death, which was of a 7-month-old baby. On November 20, Virginia reported the death of a child between the age of 0 and 4.
58c64dd3bfb5f2ac: In 2017, Apple removed the home button from its iPhones. Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges). We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness. A new system called “TangiMap,” co-developed by an MIT graduate student and researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), helps bring tangible control back to your software. The system personalizes the physical controls on everyday devices by mapping digital widgets onto tangible inputs, turning things like editing photos, animation, performing music, and creating 3D models into more dynamic and tactile experiences. Just as a DJ’s pads switch between triggering cues, loops, and samples, TangiMap gives a device’s controls entirely new roles. But how, exactly? TangiMap relies on an AI agent, or semi-autonomous programs that “think” and complete well-defined tasks, to find and act on context about the software you’re using, your tendencies, and the device used to control that program. To gather the required context, the agent can draw on sources such as the program’s API (the rules that let programs talk to each other), an MCP server (a standard that connects AI agents to apps), or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model. Then, the agent uses a large language model to put all the info it's gathered into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls. “TangiMap builds on our broader vision of reprogramming common objects to be more dynamic,” says Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21, a doctoral student in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a CSAIL researcher whose advisor is MIT Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller. “Here, AI agents help us adapt physical controls to whatever we’re working on. We want to bring back physical controls so we can interact with our devices eyes-free, the way you adjust a car’s volume without looking away from the road. Physical controls also let you adjust several settings at once, like tweaking brightness and contrast together when editing an image, which is hard to do on a screen.” The system helped the researchers turn a standard mixer into a photo-editing controller. That way, they could adjust color in Adobe Lightroom, with a complementary visualization of those controls displayed on their screen. The team did the same with sound-mixing software, so that performers can adjust their music in real-time with their own inputs to knobs and faders.  The researchers also reprogrammed a simpler mixer to work with the 3D modeling program Blender. Their interface included an area where users can type in a prompt, and once the model was generated, users could adjust features like shininess on a mixer using physical controls. Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live. Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology earlier this month. Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture. The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing. Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious. “The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.” A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life. Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.
e41a71b86838ecc4: Extraordinarily harsh droughts and heavy flooding have become more common around the globe this year due to an unusually strong El Niño. AP Photo/Charlie RiedelThe extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples. But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather. To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027. That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in. But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses. As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices. Gaps in climate science grow In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts. The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars. This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record. While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024. For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity. Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data. Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening. In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites, which feed forecast models. Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit, while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database. El Nino’s effects, especially strong in 2026, have disrupted crops and supply chains around the world, including a delayed monsoon season in India. Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images What this means for supply chains The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling. In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains. Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models. When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services. While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t. And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin. What it means for consumers Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves. Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year. And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026. A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth. fdd5f51e8fafafb3: Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the company is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists.

Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn't enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated.

As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal's total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it's only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements.
22995c289ab600a9: By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide. The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution. Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted. Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights. Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions. Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life, the Rohingya faced restrictions on movement, education and health care while families were restricted to a two-child limit. Returning to Myanmar just to face the same conditions of life is not an option for many Rohingya. The repatriation conundrum It’s unlikely, however, that Myanmar will agree to grant citizenship to the Rohingya. Since the 2021 coup d'état that ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her National League for Democracy, the military has had sole control of the government. Gen. Min Aung Hlaing is seen at the IX Moscow conference on international security in Moscow in June 2021. (AP Photo/Alexander Zemlianichenko) Earlier this year, Min Aung Hlaing, the architect of the Rohingya genocide who had been commander-in-chief of the Myanmar Forces since 2011, stepped down from his role and was subsequently elected president by a military-dominated parliament. This makes the prospect of a safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya to Myanmar a near impossibility. The Myanmar military and government aren’t the only entities complicating the return of the Rohingya. Since late 2023, vast swaths of Rakhine state, where most Rohingya resided until 2017, have been under control of the Arakan army. The army is the largest and most powerful non-state armed group in the country and it is vying for the independence of the Arakan region, where Rakhine is located. The Arakan army is openly hostile to the Rohingya, and those residing in the territory it controls are facing many of the same restrictions that were previously imposed by the state. The enforcement deficit The ICJ established Myanmar’s responsibility for the genocide, and consequently ordered it to provide reparations and compensation, with details still to be decided. But, in practice, there is little the court can do to compel Myanmar to take accountability and pursue justice if it refuses to do so. The ICJ has no independent enforcement mechanism; it only relies on states’ willingness to obey international law. Only the United Nations Security Council could decide to take coercive action against Myanmar, but China and Russia, which both hold veto power, are likely to oppose it. The two states have provided Min Aung Hlaing’s regime with political, diplomatic and military support over the years. Each also has its own issues with international human rights law, namely Russia’s war in Ukraine and China’s treatment of the Uyghurs. How the ruling might help the Rohingya The ICJ ruling has brought much-needed attention to the plight of the Rohingya. Renewed interest in the Rohingya crisis is expected to draw donations that could help alleviate some of the more pressing needs. Funding for the refugee camps has dwindled in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and the dismantlement of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID). Currently, the Rohingya in Bangladesh only receive US$7-$12 per person per month in food assistance. Read more: Thousands are feared dead in Myanmar’s quake. Trump’s USAID cuts will cause even more unnecessary deaths Combined with the lack of income-generating opportunities, the cuts to food rations are frequently identified by refugees as the most severe challenge they face in the camps. For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English. Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue. A country of 124 mother tongues Nepal is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world, though the state has not always acknowledged it. The 2021 census recorded 124 mother tongues. Fifty years earlier, in 1971, when the Panchayat regime was promoting Nepali above all other languages, the census counted just 17 languages. Today, Nepali is the first language of just under 45 per cent of the population. I have worked in Nepal since 1991, first as a volunteer schoolteacher and later as a linguist and anthropologist. I have spent decades researching the country’s linguistic diversity. The census numbers reflect a shift I have witnessed on the ground, in communities. In 2021, for the first time, the census asked people about their ancestral language as well as their mother tongue. Nearly three million more people name Nepali as their mother tongue than they name it as their ancestral language, a sign that many families have shifted to Nepali. For other languages, the gap goes the other way. Some 300,000 more people name Nepal Bhasa, the language of the Newar community, as their ancestral language than name it as their mother tongue. Nepali is also spreading as a second language: 46 per cent of the population now speaks it that way, up from 33 per cent in 2011. Whatever pressures Nepal’s other languages face, Nepali is certainly not a language at risk. Rights on paper On paper, Nepal’s laws side with children. The government’s School Education Sector Plan 2022-32 commits to scaling up early-grade teaching in children’s mother tongues. In practice, implementation has been sluggish and uneven. As comparative education scholar Uma Pradhan has shown, policy has long treated mother tongues as a bridge to Nepali, a stepping stone to be left behind, with the state offering little support. In a 2026 study from Tanahun, one grandparent spoke about a granddaughter in Grade 2 who was being taught only in Nepali and English: “She [does not have the] opportunity to study in [her ancestral] language; so, there is a gap.” Grade 1 students at Shree Sahara Bal Primary School in Pokhara, Nepal, in June 2013. (Photo by Jim Holmes for AusAID), CC BY The evidence for local languages A 2024 study commissioned by UNICEF Nepal examined language use in 30 schools across all seven provinces. Its conclusion was unequivocal. When children learn in their mother tongue or a familiar language, they take a more active part in lessons and do better in assessments and exams. Many schools have rushed to switch to English-language teaching, often for financial reasons and with little teacher training. Yet students taught in Nepali outscored their English-taught peers in Nepali, in science and even in English, according to the study’s analysis of school assessment results, which was limited in scale. In Dailekh, in western Nepal, principal Sher Bahadur Rana told UNICEF that teachers once corrected children who used their own “language or dialect.” After training in multilingual teaching, he said, “we learned that children learn faster and feel more confident when we teach them in the language they speak and understand best.” Obstacles to implementation A recent review by education researchers Pariksha Onta and Amado Padilla, covering 111 studies and policy documents, points to a “persistent disconnect between constitutional commitments, classroom practice and targeted funding.” Where mother tongues are taught at all, they are usually a subject rather than the language children learn in. Textbooks in children’s mother tongues remain scarce, and most of those that do exist are translations of Nepali materials with little locally relevant content. Far too few teachers who speak local languages are recruited or trained. Parents, meanwhile, are caught in the middle. Many see English-language schools as a marker of quality and employability. And funding is lacking: in 2026–27, education and sports together received around 10.3 per cent of Nepal’s national budget, well below the international benchmark of allocating at least 15 per cent to education. Onta and Padilla’s review also highlights what works. In some Kathmandu Valley schools, children learn in Nepal Bhasa for their first three grades before Nepali and English are phased in. A strong foundation in the mother tongue supports learning in the other languages, which means families don’t have to choose between them. From paper to practice As I argued previously with colleagues Lava Deo Awasthi and Yogendra Prasad Yadava, rights “do not implement themselves.” Children should begin school in the language they understand best, with Nepali and English introduced gradually, building on that foundation. Making this work requires sustained funding, teachers trained to teach in children’s languages, and materials that reflect their lives and communities. Some municipalities have introduced local-language education programs, while Nepal’s Curriculum Development Centre has developed curricula for elementary education in more than 20 mother tongues. Language policy can sound technical, but at heart it is about whether a child’s first experience of school is a welcoming one. In Renuka Dahal’s classroom in Rautahat, where children now teach their teacher, the message is simple: their languages belong in school, and so do they. Mark Turin receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC).

0fc51390fa9c3aee: About half a million Californians were affected by the state's hike in minimum wage for fast-food workers. AP Photo/Jae C. HongEven before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers’ purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries. As the example of California shows, however, these initiatives can produce mixed results. In April 2024, California began requiring fast-food chains with at least 60 locations nationwide to pay a minimum wage of US$20 an hour, $4 above the statewide minimum at the time. The governor’s office estimated that more than 500,000 workers would be covered by this mandate. As a researcher of health and labor markets, I joined with economists David Neumark, Gary Wagner and Vitor Melo to run a study measuring the impact on California’s fast-food industry – specifically, whether restaurants employed fewer workers because of the ensuing higher labor costs. We found that the answer depends on which establishments you look at. For the state as a whole, the law didn’t affect employment in any statistically detectable way, we concluded. But smaller chains did take a hit, with employment falling by roughly 20%, while the number of locations dropped by about 10%. New openings fell by 17%-20%, and closures rose by 9%-21%. This employment decline comes almost entirely from fast-food chains ceasing to operate in California, rather than from staffing cuts at the locations that remain. The impact of minimum wage hikes holds importance far beyond the fast-food sector. Their proponents point to the fact that the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour has stayed unchanged since 2009 and argue that states and municipalities need to take action on their own. Los Angeles is phasing in a $30 wage for hotel and airport workers, while California’s healthcare workers just received another scheduled increase. Vermont lawmakers have proposed a $20 fast-food wage of their own. In addition, a total of 16 states will raise their minimum wages across the board on Jan. 1, 2027. With the federal minimum wage unchanged since 2009, many states and municipalities have raised the wage floor on their own, including for specific sectors. AP Photo/Andrew Harnik Smaller chains see an impact The question of whether and how minimum wages affect employment still provokes a vigorous debate among economists. In California’s case, some researchers have found that lifting the minimum wage caused small declines in employment compared with other states; others contend that the effect on jobs is essentially zero. More broadly, some researchers have found that minimum wage hikes cost jobs. But the time horizon matters, and effects tend to get larger in the long run. Our study didn’t try to settle that disagreement. Instead, we wanted to find out how employers did adjust, and whether large and small chains responded differently. What happens when higher minimum wages raise one sector’s costs and prices while its closest substitutes – such as sit-down restaurants – keep paying the lower statewide minimum wage? We relied on a database that recorded every business location in the country by name, along with the number of employed workers, each year. That let us directly identify the chains that were subject to California’s law, count each chains’ national footprint to apply the 60-location rule, and track outcomes from 2019 through 2025: total employment, employment at locations that stayed open, the number of locations, and openings and closures. We also compared California with other states and separately compared each chain’s California restaurants with the same chain’s restaurants elsewhere. Finally, we divided the covered chains into two groups: The 20 largest, which account for about 60% of covered jobs, and the 261 smaller ones. For the state as a whole, we found that employment at covered restaurants was basically unchanged, and employment at restaurants that stayed open didn’t change. Among the 20 largest chains, there was no detectable effect at all for any of the measures we tracked over this period. But the smaller chains tell a different story, recording substantial declines in employment, locations and openings, while closures rose. How to reconcile the flat statewide numbers with the sharp effects on smaller chains? The largest chains employ most of the workers affected by the new minimum wage rule, so the statewide total is dominated by them. And the reduced entry and higher exit among smaller chains may have eased competitive pressure on the largest ones. A final point: The biggest chains tend to be the most automated, relying more on equipment such as self-serve kiosks that can reduce the number of workers needed. That may help explain the muted employment response among these larger businesses. Taking the longer view First, we caution that the absence of a clear short-run effect on total employment doesn’t prove that the policy won’t cause bigger job losses over time as companies adapt to the new law. We also can’t answer what happened to the workers at the most affected restaurants or what happened to prices at those establishments, although other research suggests they rose by 3% to 4%. That said, the law was implemented barely 2½ years ago, and some of the larger effects that economists might expect – such as the closure of labor-intensive restaurants or fewer openings – are already apparent among smaller chains. Second, it’s important to remember that California’s fast-food minimum wage applies only to chains with 60 or more locations. So the smaller chains in that range likely lack the scale, automation and pricing power of the national brands and are most sensitive to the new wage floor. Indeed, the law appears to have shifted California’s fast-food market toward its largest chains, a pattern that other researchers documented in a similar study that looked at Germany’s national minimum wage. For the cities and states now weighing wage floors of their own, the California evidence isn’t a slam dunk either way. It shows that the costs, broadly speaking, fall first on the smaller chains covered by the law – but whether it meaningfully impacts the largest chains is unclear. Liam Sigaud is affiliated with the Paragon Health Institute, a not-for-profit health policy research organization.

84edfb5a38475599: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”
60e8aadceb71593e: From Ann Teoh
Today marks exactly 10 years since Amri Che Mat went missing.
A Suhakam public inquiry unanimously concluded in 2019 that Amri was a victim of enforced disappearance – specifically by state agents, namely the police's Special Branch.
It was past 11pm on Nov 24, 2016, a Thursday, when Amri drove out of his house at Padang Behor in Kangar, Perlis, to have supper with a friend.
Just minutes later, less than a kilometre from his house, his Toyota Fortuner was boxed in by three four-wheel-drives. Screeching sounds, glass breaking, and that was it. It took less than a minute.
Providence would have it that the incident was witnessed by a passing motorcyclist and a restaurant owner across the road from where it happened.

Amri’s Fortuner was found abandoned at a construction site in Bukit Chabang, Kedah, a few hours later. His wife, Norhayati Ariffin, did not realise Amri hadn't come home until the next morning when she received a call about the abandoned car.
Before Amri took a nap at 7.30pm, he had asked his wife to wake him up at 10.30pm. That was the last time Norhayati saw her husband.
This sounds like a bad conspiracy novel, but reality is stranger than fiction.

DNA swabs were taken from the Fortuner when the car was found, but were sent to the chemistry department only five months later. Amri’s family also did not get the police support they wanted. Instead of trying to locate Amri, Norhayati was queried about her husband’s involvement in Shia activities.
Shia Islam is prohibited in Malaysia and Amri was watched by religious authorities and the police, but was never arrested or charged. Instead, he disappeared.
How do we know Amri was being watched? Would he have disappeared at a different time if he didn’t go out that fateful night? It's quite possible judging by the circumstances.
A car workshop owner across Amri’s house later testified that unknown cars, with engines running, took turns parking outside Amri's house day and night for three days before he went missing.
One of those cars was a gold-coloured Toyota Vios with a Penang number plate, which was also spotted when Pastor Raymond Koh was abducted 81 days later.

The Vios belonged to an operative of the Special Branch in Kuala Lumpur. He was identified as Saiful Bahari Abdul Aziz, but the police always had an excuse for why the key witness could not be present to testify.
Koh was abducted the same way on Feb 13, 2017. His car was also boxed in as men in black rushed out from three black four-wheel-drives. There was also a gold-coloured Vios nearby.

Koh’s abduction was more audacious than Amri’s; it happened in broad daylight on a Monday morning in SS4, Petaling Jaya. Amri’s case only had eyewitness accounts but Koh's case included video evidence.
Besides witness Roeshan Celestine Gomez, a chambering student who happened to be driving behind Koh's car, the pastor's abduction was caught on the CCTV cameras of two houses nearby.

Strangely, the police didn’t rush to get the CCTV recordings. It was Koh’s family who looked for them once they knew about Roeshan’s police report. After the CCTV recordings were spread through the media, the case couldn't be hidden any longer.

With two Malaysians abducted this way – and Joshua Helmi and Ruth Sitepu also missing since end-November 2016 – and a growing suspicion they were abducted, a group of civil society groups sent a memo to Suhakam seeking action.

Suhakam then carried out public inquiries on both Koh and Amri’s disappearances. Amri’s case took Suhakam 10 months to complete starting from January 2018, with 27 days of hearings and 24 witnesses summoned.

Suhakam's final reports said evidence pointed to Amri and Koh being forcibly abducted by the Special Branch. It also stated that in both cases, the police failed to investigate the disappearances properly.

The Cabinet then set up a special task force in 2019 to look into the matter. Its report in 2020 stated that it was “highly probable that Amri’s disappearance was caused by rogue police officers acting alone or in a group with unidentified individuals from religious groups".

Three years after Amri disappeared, Norhayati, who became a single mother to their four daughters, sued the police and government for malfeasance and failure to investigate his abduction properly, among others.

The civil suit filed on Nov 18, 2019, took six years, partly because the government initially refused to release the special task force's report. By the time the High Court made its decision, nine years had passed since Amri disappeared.

On Nov 5, 2025, the High Court awarded Norhayati general and exemplary damages totalling RM3 million, and another RM14,457.52 mainly for the children’s education expenses. The court also ordered a re-investigation into Amri’s disappearance.

Justice Su Tiang Joo said the police breached their own SOPs, citing severe delays in handling DNA evidence, failure to investigate the Vios owner, and failure to investigate CCTV recordings, among others. The police also made almost no effort to keep the family updated.

Su said Norhayati’s mental anguish, pain and suffering included having to dissolve her marriage under fasakh – as advised by the Perlis religious affairs department – “to bring succour to the needs of the four daughters".

Norhayati was unable to get welfare aid as a single mother if she remained married to Amri. Secondly, the divorce dispensed of the need for Amri to be a wali for one of their daughters who was getting married.
Perhaps it was to be expected that the attorney-general would appeal the High Court decision. With that, the award was stayed while Norhayati and her daughters continue to wait.
Today, we want to remember Amri.
Whatever wrongs he allegedly committed, Amri deserves a fair chance at defending himself in a court of law.
That’s the basic minimum of a modern democratic society proclaiming the supremacy of the constitution and rule of law as two of its five Rukun Negara tenets.

Abducting Amri was cowardly and dastardly because the government has the machinery, laws, institutions and manpower resources to frame a legal case against him and prosecute him, if he indeed did wrong.
The police chose a shortcut instead, and the executive arm of the government allowed that shortcut. This was a betrayal of the rakyat's trust.
Today, we remember Amri Che Mat, a Malaysian, a father of four girls (now grown women), and surely, a friend to many through his NGO, Perlis Hope.

9c8bf06abbbe421e: Complaints include marriage disputes, unfair trial, unlawful land grabs, corruption, torture, and more
Originally published on Global Voices
An old man in the Talas province addressing Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov during a public meeting. Photo from the Presidential Administration's website. Fair Use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In October and November 2026, Kyrgyzstan’s president, Sadyr Japarov, held public meetings with the population in all seven provinces of the country. What were meant to be formal events turned into quests for justice by people driven to desperation.
The meetings revealed the ineffectiveness of the existing justice mechanisms and showed how people saw the president as the only guarantor of justice.

The effectiveness of Kyrgyzstan’s law enforcement and judicial bodies was people’s most common justice-related complaint. During a meeting with residents of the southwestern Batken province on October 11, a woman complained to the president about her former husband, who accused her of forging their marriage certificate and framed her for crimes she did not commit to avoid the division of assets after their divorce.

She also said her former brother-in-law provided false testimony to back up his brother’s accusations. She now lives in an apartment with their three children in constant fear that her former husband may kick them out because he allegedly bribed police and courts.

This trivial legal dispute reached the point where the woman had to beg the president to ensure a just investigation and ruling. Japarov condemned her former husband and said that he should have left everything to her and their kids after the divorce.
Here is an Instagram reel with his response to the case.
View this post on Instagram

On October 26, Japarov met with residents of the Kazarman district in the southern Jalalabad province, where Shirimbek Abrahmanov told the president about his father, who was imprisoned for allegedly offering a bribe of KGS 2,000 (USD 23) to a police officer during a traffic stop. The district court acquitted him of the charges.
However, the local prosecutor’s office appealed the decision in the provincial court, which found Abdrahmanov’s father guilty and sentenced him to two years in prison.
Here is an Instagram reel with the complaint and Japarov’s response.
View this post on Instagram
Japarov could not hide his anger when he heard the story, especially after finding out the provincial court took seven months to issue a verdict. In reply, he confronted local authorities and said:

Are the traffic police officer and the prosecutor in cahoots? Does that mean they’ve ganged up on him? If it were a large bribe, that would be one thing. But to have someone imprisoned over two thousand soms — that’s a disgrace.
The man was released from custody shortly after Japarov’s intervention and subsequent pardon.
Similar complaints resurfaced multiple times during presidential meetings in other provinces, highlighting systemic problems plaguing the judicial and law-enforcement systems.
The message is clear: people have lost all hope of finding justice at the hands of local police and courts.

Surprisingly, following his meetings with the public, Japarov concluded that the level of distrust towards courts has decreased, but admitted that problems in the judicial system remain and must be solved quickly.

On the one hand, the lack of justice and the dysfunction within the courts and police bodies, which are plagued by corruption and bureaucracy, are real pressing issues affecting millions of people across Kyrgyzstan. However, the current political regime led by Japarov, who came to power in October 2020, has made little tangible progress.
In 2026, Kyrgyzstan was ranked 99th out of 144 states in the Rule of Law Index compiled by the World Justice Project. For comparison, in 2020, it was ranked 87th.

On the other hand, people’s desperate appeals for justice helped Japarov sustain his man-of-the-people image. By listening to people’s requests and swiftly resolving their issues, the president can reinforce his popularity. In turn, this leads to the maintenance of the personalistic regime built around Japarov since his arrival to power.
Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev
